[SPEAKER_00]
It was a pleasure and I also really enjoyed the chat. It was as simple as Chang told me.

[None]
Well, had

[SPEAKER_03]
a good one on the topic of differential privacy, Chang and I, and I would encourage folks who haven't listened to the former series on differential privacy, they should take a listen to that one because it's good stuff.

[SPEAKER_00]
Perfect.

[None]
Thank you. you.

[SPEAKER_03]
All right, everyone. That's our show for today. For more information on Perrines or any of the topics covered in this show, visit twimlai.com slash talk slash 208. Thanks once again to the good folks over at Georgian Partners for their sponsorship of this series. As always, thanks so much for listening and catch you next time. Ones.

[None]
For
sources.title: Trust and AI with Parinaz Sobhani - TWiML Talk #208

sources.text:
[SPEAKER_00]
This is just the beginning.

[SPEAKER_02]
Hi, and welcome to another Axios Live virtual event. I'm Dan Primack of Axios, coming to you from my house in Southboro, Massachusetts. And today we're going to be talking about inequities in venture capital, specifically racial inequities in venture capital. Big thanks to everybody joining us, whether you're on YouTube or Twitter or Facebook or the Axios.com homepage. And be sure to follow us on Twitter at hashtag Axios events. Thank you to Cooley for sponsoring, without whom we wouldn't be able to do this. And just to give you a little run of show, we will have 30 minutes today together, three segments talking specifically about Black Americans' underrepresentation in venture capital. And to start, I want to bring in from San Francisco, Sarah Kunst, the founder of Clio Capital. Hey, Sarah.

[None]
Hi,

[SPEAKER_00]
how are you?

[SPEAKER_02]
Good. Good. Good. so let's start here. Clio is a firm you founded in early 2018. And there seems to be, there's really some Twitter conversation, particularly among Black founders and venture capitalists about this question. Sure. Is the best way to get more Black representation of venture capital for people to join existing firms or to start their own? Now, you started your own, but I get the sense you don't think that is the right path for everyone.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yes. I mean, I worked at a big Sand Hill Road fund, right, as an analyst prior. And I think that it's incredibly hard to do venture capital, incredibly hard to raise a fund if you,

[None]
you know, one,

[SPEAKER_00]
don't have millions of dollars, but two, if you don't have kind of the experience and network of having already been at a fund. And so, or at least angel invested, right? So if you have hundreds of millions of dollars and you want to jump into VC, great, go, go, you know, start a fund and hire somebody out of an existing one to help you. But if you're looking at both raising a fund while learning how to be a VC, you know, in our business, we call that threading two needles at once. And as you can imagine, it's pretty hard.

[SPEAKER_02]
So I wonder then for you, what do you think is, or is what you're saying you think the best path for folks who are black folks who are getting, who want to get into venture capital? Is it to try to get into a existing venture capital firm? if so, why has that proven seemingly so hard over the years?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, I certainly think angel investing or going directly into venture capital at a fund is the sort of most efficient route to learning about how to be an investor. Obviously, the funds haven't done a good job hiring diverse candidates, even though they're there, right? A lot of venture funds hire post MBA associates every year, know, GSB, Harvard, those schools are full of amazing black talent and other industries are finding them and venture just hasn't, you know, made that leap to make it a priority in recruiting.

[SPEAKER_02]
And you're kind of, as a piece of that, I mean, there's also this intersectionality thing, right? You're a black female venture capitalist. And honestly, I think I can count the number of black female venture capitalists, if not on one hand, definitely on two. As a piece of that, again, is this, you're arguing this is not a pipeline problem. Is this really a lack of venture capital firms just paying attention?

[SPEAKER_00]
I think it's, yeah, I mean, it's easy to hire what we know, right? It's easy to go out and say, I like this person. I've worked with this person. I've worked with, you know, this, this person's brother or dad. And because of the way that our country has worked for 400 years, when you hire people from your neighborhood, from your fraternity, from, you know, whatever your summer camp, you're not going to end up with a lot of diversity for the most part. And we're still a deeply segregated society socially in a lot of ways, and certainly socioeconomically. And so, you know, it requires making that commitment and understanding that, hey, this matters. And we know that diversity drives better returns. So let's go get better returns. That's our business.

[SPEAKER_02]
So you say it matters and you say it matters because of better returns. Can you unpack that a little bit for me? Why does having, say, more black investors around the table at a Sand Hill Road firm or some other venture capital firm, why does that help drive better returns?

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_00]
a ton of studies have shown that diversity drives better returns, right? And so diversity isn't just having one group, right? It's having a diversity of experiences around the table. And certainly in America, race and ethnicity drives a huge amount of diversity, diverse experiences, which drive diverse opinions and insights, which are going to drive better results, right? The joke I always make is I would be a terrible person to road test sunscreen, right? I've gotten one sunburn in my life. It was horrible, but it's just not something that I have experience with. And so if I'm looking to say, hey, should I invest in the sunscreen brand? I want somebody who has deep experience with sunburns to tell me if it works or not. And it's the exact same thing that we see at these companies, right? When you have a more diverse group around the table, you're more likely to spot ideas that aren't going to work. And candidly, you're more likely to spot ideas that will work that just aren't exactly in your wheelhouse or your experiences.

[SPEAKER_02]
So let me ask, I'm curious what you think about this concept of title. I don't even want to say inflation, but kind of title confusion, right? It used to be if you looked at a venture capital firm website, there'd be a group of partners or general partners and principals or analysts or some lower titles. Now, really, almost kind of since the Me Too era, which seems to be why this maybe began, you now see lots of people called partners at venture capital firms who don't necessarily have check writing ability, which is what a partner used to mean. Do you feel are venture capital firms messing around with titles to make them appear more diverse than they really are?

[SPEAKER_00]
You know, the genesis of the title inflation wasn't so much that. It was actually pre me too. And it was so that, you know, and associates could get meetings because it used to be that people only wanted to meet with partners. And so the fun solution for that was to make everybody a partner. Right. And since then, I do think that you're right, that the vast majority of women, of black people and Hispanic people at these funds, you know, they don't necessarily they're not general partners. And even if they are, they don't necessarily have equal economics to some of the other general partners. And often to your point, you know, they're 25 year olds who aren't allowed to write checks. And so I certainly don't think that's been the genesis of this, but it is one of those consequences that I think some funds are probably pretty comfortable with that they get to look diverse while not actually having to have a diversity of thought around the table in terms of who can write checks.

[SPEAKER_02]
Sarah, you're unique among the three people we're talking to today in part because you're also a limited partner. I'm working on the LP side of things and limited partners, for those who don't know, are the institutional investors who invest in VC funds. When it comes to the diversity issue around the table that we're talking about with direct investors, do you think limited partners are paying enough attention to this when they're deciding which funds to support or not support?

[SPEAKER_00]
You know, I was on a limited partner board at a university, and I don't think that it was I don't think that most limited partners are paying enough attention. I think they're very afraid if they're in a top fund that if they if they disturb the peace and if they ask hard questions, if they're going to get pushed out the next time because top funds tend to be oversubscribed. But I definitely think that limited partners, particularly family offices, can play a massive role in this. They can invest in whatever they want, and they need to start wanting to invest in what drives the best returns, which is diversity.

[SPEAKER_02]
Sarah, quickly, we have 10 seconds. Give me one portfolio company of Clio Capital that most people haven't heard of but will hear about.

[SPEAKER_00]
Lunch Club.

[SPEAKER_02]
Lunch Club. Easy. There it is. Sarah Koontz, thank you so much for joining us. Thank you. And I'm pleased to be joined now by somebody else in San Francisco, Elliot Robinson of Bessemer Venture Partners. Hey, Dan. How's it going? Good. Hey, Elliot. Thank you so much for joining us. So, Elliot, you have a different background than Sarah in kind of how you got to Bessemer, which you joined, I guess, last year, right? To help kind of run its growth fund. Can you talk a little bit about your history? Because you've talked to me and publicly a little bit about how you were searching for a venture capital job and had a very, very hard time finding one.

[SPEAKER_01]
Sure. I'd love to delve into that. So, to start, I started in venture in 2006 at what still stands today as the largest black -owned venture fund in the country, Syncom Venture Partners. It's been around for about 45 years now. So, that's where I got my start. And then after taking a break, we had an IPO in a company called Iridium Satellite. And then I took a break to do my MBA at Columbia Business School. And what was so shocking, I think in my class of 800 -ish students, only six of us had pre -MBA venture experience. I had the most. And I couldn't get a job at all the same venture firms that were recruiting out of my school. However, I could get a lot of offers doing just about everything except for investing. So, whether it was a marketing partner role or portfolio kind of platform community role. And again, not begrudging those roles or saying that folks that look like me don't want opportunities at that role. But for someone that had been investing for four or five years and had some success, it was almost impossible for me to get a job here in the States.

[SPEAKER_02]
I wonder, know, Elliot, when you fast forward, I guess, 14 years from 2006, and you think about the conversations we're having now. You're part of BlackVC, which had a big event a couple weeks ago. We do seem to be having a moment nationally, but also within venture capital. Do you believe, how do you feel we kind of, and you guys put an infrastructure into place, the industry puts an infrastructure into place, so that in three years, in four years, in five years, there are more Black venture capitalists and we're not having this conversation again?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, so what's so confusing to me about the current moment is that the infrastructure has existed for decades. Before BlackVC, there were organizations like the National Association of Investment Companies or the Marathon Club that worked with both LPs and GPs and the pipeline to start to solve this problem. For fundraising, for new GPs, for people trying to break into the industry, the infrastructure has existed. It's really a heart and minds problem and a bit of a will problem that hasn't changed, unfortunately.

[None]
Do

[SPEAKER_02]
you, are you optimistic about what's happening right now or do you feel that this is just a moment in time and we'll all move on to something else in a couple months and this will be forgotten?

[SPEAKER_01]
That's a great question. I am optimistic and I'll tell you why. So, you know, when much of this conversation started happening maybe six weeks ago, a lot of GPs and funds started opening up office hours for more diverse entrepreneurs. I just kind of matched it and said, hey, I'd love to open some office hours to talk to some non -diverse venture funds around the country. I assumed maybe two or three might reach out. had over 80 funds reach out, including some search firms and some LPs that wanted to have the conversation. I've now done 16 kind of conversations slash consultations. I'm not a diversity expert, but as someone who's been in venture capital for this long across a number of funds, I'm happy to kind of dispel many of the myths around there's a pipeline problem. We can't find people who are talented. Where can we find these entrepreneurs and these investors? And it's gone really well. And just to be clear, you know, the conversations have gone everywhere from the top Sand Hill Road funds to some more of the regional funds. And then, you know, what I'm really most excited about is that LPs are really engaged in the conversation and hopefully they'll start asking some harder questions.

[SPEAKER_02]
Oh, such as what? What would you like LPs to be asking that you don't think they're currently asking?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, so the biggest one is really the term that I talk about a lot, which is diversity theater. I know there was a prior conversation around kind of title inflation. We can argue where the genesis is, but I've seen it and I've kind of lived it where for both, you know, black and brown investors as well as female investors. We've done this thing where we will give you a quote unquote investing role, but we won't let you touch things like carry, real check writing, sitting on boards and the like. As you know, this industry is really an apprenticeship model. It takes, I've always believed it takes kind of six or seven years to even know if you're good at this thing and then another fun cycle to figure out whether you're great at it. And if you don't give people like me or folks that look like me that opportunity to go through a full fund cycle, we'll never really start to solve that problem. And I am excited about funds that are, you know, really going out and making an effort to diversify their investment staff. You know,

[SPEAKER_02]
when you talk about the apprenticeship model between Georgian Partners and Bessemer, you spent time at M12, which is Microsoft's corporate venture fund. And you and I were speaking yesterday about how from your perspective, it's corporate venture capital funds where black investors have had the easiest time getting a foot in the door. Can you explain that a little bit? Why corporate venture funds as opposed to any other?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, so there's a high correlation between some of the most well -known and prominent black GPs and their time spent at corporate venture funds. And it really happens because we hit these glass ceilings inside of, you know, non -corporate venture funds, to be totally honest. You can spend two or three years at a Sand Hill Road or Sand Hill adjacent road firm, not get to check writing. And as you get closer to check writing, it gets harder. And then corporate venture capital firms have actually, you know, really held the position that we don't really care where you come from. We've got capital, whether it's off balance sheet or some corporate firms have a mix of LPs, balance sheet and outside of the org. And it's much easier to get to a check writing position, whether it's at M12 or Intel Capital or Comcast Ventures. There's like a long legacy of black investors building their track record there, whether it's leading investments, co -leading or following on. And then using that track record to kind of leverage into other funds or their own.

[SPEAKER_02]
Elliot, there's been, obviously, over the past couple of weeks, there's been a handful of new efforts that have been launched specifically at funding black and brown founders. Obviously, SoftBank created a fund and recent board, which created a small fund. As somebody who is at Bessemer, which is a generalist firm, which is going to invest in theory, at least in founders of all colors and creeds. Do you feel that those efforts are worthwhile is the wrong word? But do you think that is the right way for the venture capital market to be going? Or should it be saying, no, we've got a 500 or a billion dollar fund. We need to do a better job finding different founders within this main vehicle.

[SPEAKER_01]
Sure. So, you know, you'll never find me in a position where I say, you know, more capital, more effort, more commitment to funding diverse founders is a bad thing, particularly black founders. What I will say, however, back to that comment around it is a hearts and minds thing and a will thing. Most of the funds that you've seen step forward manage billions and billions of dollars, Bessemer included. And what's most important is that we don't create a separate line for investors based off of, you know, where they come from, the color of their skin, because that's the same thing that we've been talking about on the investment side. What's most important is if we start there at step one, very quickly, we move to a position where the main fund vehicle is treating everyone equitably, because that's really the spirit of this conversation and hopefully where the industry goes. L.A. Robinson of Bessemer Venture Partners,

[SPEAKER_02]
thanks so much for joining.

[None]
Thanks,

[SPEAKER_02]
Dan. I'm going to turn it over now to my colleague, Ina Freed.

[None]
Thanks,

[SPEAKER_03]
Dan. So I'm excited to continue this conversation. I cover tech for Axios, and obviously there's a huge line between what happens in BC and what happens in tech. I'd like to bring on Charles Hudson to talk about sort of why this intersection matters. Thanks, Charles. Thanks for joining. Thanks for having me. So this may be obvious, but I want to take a step back and talk about why representation matters. Can you help draw this through line of why it matters having Black investors in terms of supporting Black founders and diverse founders, and then ultimately into the products that these companies make, which can either further or limit institutional racism? Like, why does it matter having diverse VCs other than the fact that it matters having diversity in every industry?

[SPEAKER_04]
Well, think capital allocation is a big part of how companies get started. And I think having Black and Brown venture capitalists at the table means that folks who look like me are more comfortable, means you're going to get a good audience. I think it's a strong signal to Black and Brown founders when you look at a firm's webpage or you look at an industry where you say there's almost no one who looks like me. think it can send a pretty strong signal to founders that perhaps I'm not welcome here. Perhaps this is an industry or business that doesn't value my talents and abilities. And so what I think is there's this notion that, founders should only start companies that serve Black audiences and Black VCs should only invest in Black founders. I think one thing that's worth considering is I think it's also important for White founders and Asian founders who might not have much social or professional experience with Black people to have access to that. And I think venture capitalists, it's a unique opportunity to influence a lot of people. And having Black and Brown venture capitalists influencing a wide variety of founders, including Black ones, is I think an important way for us to get to know each other better as people and to show the industry that we have a lot of untapped talent.

[SPEAKER_03]
And how important is this moment when people are finally paying a little bit of attention to what seems like centuries of institutional furthering of an initial racist society? How important is it for not just venture capital, but the broader economy and tech ecosystem to make use of this moment?

[SPEAKER_04]
I think it's really important to make good use of this moment. And I think for me personally, it's been pretty jarring. I think, you know, within the Black community for some time, we've been making the argument that a lot of these things that seem like isolated incidents, whether it's police brutality or just microaggressions or the everyday frustrations you experience as a person of color in this country, that there was a through line that connected all these things. And that through line was systemic racism. And I think for a long time, the conversation was, well, there's no pattern. These are isolated incidents. This is one bad police officer. This is one bad person. This is one bad incident. Don't create a pattern where one doesn't exist. And it's very jarring to go from a world where there is a broad lack of willingness to acknowledge the pattern to a world that feels like almost overnight, everyone's eyes have opened and said, wow, this systemic pattern that people have been talking to us about, we suddenly believe that it's real. And it's been, for me, least kind of a jarring thing to go from a world where it was a hard argument to make to one where I think it's being widely embraced.

[SPEAKER_03]
And where do you see the biggest real interest and momentum and changes happening? It seems like every brand in the world changed their social media profile to, you know, a black border with some white text. The NFL, for example, I think was the classic one saying, oh, we're totally opposed to systemic racism. How many people are actually going beyond sort of that black box? What are the really encouraging signs you've seen of institutions that are taking more significant action?

[SPEAKER_04]
I really think the institutions that I think are doing the best job are ones who are not saying, well, what can we do to get likes on social media or what can we do to get public praise? But they're looking inward at their own processes. And, you I've been talking to quite a few venture firms. And one of the nice things I think that's come out of this moment is a handful of firms have reached out to me and just said, hey, we don't think we're a racist firm. We don't think we're discriminatory. But when we look at our portfolio and we look at our team, clearly something's wrong because the companies that are getting to the end of our investment process and the people that end up on our team don't reflect our values. And I think this is one of those few times I've really seen across society and particularly in my business in venture capital, a real reexamination of the outputs of the process and who's getting hired, who's getting funded. And I think these old arguments about it's a pipeline problem where we look at everybody equally. I just think those don't hold water anymore.

[SPEAKER_03]
In my experience covering tech, certain issues tend to get fleeting attention, social issues prominent. But I even remember privacy and other issues, security that just, you know, there's a big incident. Everyone pays attention for a second and then they move on. And it's historically diversity has fallen into that. What are the most important things you think need to happen while we are paying attention? What do we need to be doing right now so that we're not having this conversation so that we can't have an event two years from now where we're saying nothing's changed?

[SPEAKER_04]
I think in general, people have short attention spans. And so my, the one thing I've seen when you get sustained change, it's usually because people are organized. And if I look at sort of the progress that venture capital as a business has made with gender, we're still a long way away from where we need to be. I think a lot of that came from folks who cared about the issue organizing themselves. And I think if we're going to make real progress on racial justice in venture capital and society as a whole, it's going to be through organized efforts and sustained pressure. So I think we have to keep our foot on the gas here. And I think the folks who really care about changing the organizations that they work for and the industries that they work in need to really apply pressure. And we need to find each other and hold each other accountable and support each other in our efforts to drive real change.

[None]
What

[SPEAKER_03]
are some of the tech things that you've seen, given your vantage point, that you think are ordinarily missed by traditional venture capital? And what are sort of the upside? You know, part of sort of getting the change is a values commitment. And part of it is recognizing economic missed opportunities. What are some of the missed opportunities that traditional venture capital has missed because it's not diverse?

[SPEAKER_04]
I think one of the biggest ones is, and I say this with full acknowledgement of myself as a two -time Stanford graduate, that I probably contribute to this problem to some degree. We're an industry that really only hires people from very narrow set of backgrounds, whether it's academic or professionally. And one of the things we've tried to do at Precursor is expand the aperture of who we think can be a successful founder and also who we think can be a successful investor. And that's meant that we've looked in new places for both talent for our team, as well as for the founders that we back. And I think as long as we're focused on what's perceived to be low -risk pedigree hiring, we're not going to change anything.

[SPEAKER_03]
Thanks so much, Charles. I really appreciate the conversation and hopefully we continue it and we're not having the same conversation a year or two from now, but a better one fueled by some progress. Thanks so much, Charles. Thank you. So I want to bring back Dan Primmick so that we can talk a little bit about the why it matters and where we go from here.

[None]
We have

[SPEAKER_02]
some audience questions. And one of the things, I guess, I'm curious, you know, our conversations with Sarah and with Elliot and with Charles just now, a lot of it was around this question of, is this a moment that is going to be sustainable? Is infrastructure going to get put into place? And for you, who covers big tech companies in Silicon Valley, particularly given how many venture capitalists come out of those companies, do you believe that Silicon Valley tech companies are serious about improving their diversity numbers, their racial diversity numbers? Or do you think this is something that they are giving lip service to right now, maybe even sincerely, but are going to move on quickly?

[SPEAKER_03]
I think the danger, I think it is sincere, but I think the danger is that companies move on before making much progress. You know, I think companies have been committed, if you will, to diversity for a while now without making significant change. You know, we've heard a lot of talk from tech companies about the problems, about how committed they are. They've been putting out reports. And that is a step forward because if we don't see the numbers, we can't track progress, obviously. But that progress has been pretty limited. So I think the real hope is that out of this movement actually comes progress. And I think some of the most successful companies have put dollars behind it and accountability. They've tied executive pay to boosting diversity. I think when you pay somebody for it, you get results a lot more than if you don't. You know, as a piece of that,

[SPEAKER_02]
but obviously we're having, you you take the Facebook ad boycotts, for example, which seems to, if not explicitly, at least implicitly, suggested that a lot of these companies still aren't doing well enough and that kind of venture capital and tech are mirrors of one another.

[SPEAKER_03]
Yeah, I mean, I think the real issue here, and I started to talk about this with Charles, is the through line that goes from who gets funded to what gets funded to the impact. So I think, you know, one of the biggest racial impacts of tech is the products that they create. And do the products they create further societal racism or do they help break it down? And I

[None]
think that

[SPEAKER_03]
traces all the way back to the venture capital. So I think one of the biggest ways to measure change, too, is the tech industry creating racist products, particularly in areas like facial recognition and algorithms. This is going to be critical and having the right investors early on is a big piece of it. You know, thank you very much. That was

[None]
Ina

[SPEAKER_02]
Fried, Axios Chief Technology Correspondent. And thank all of you for joining us this afternoon for another Axios virtual conversation that has made us all smarter, faster. If you like this conversation and would like more Axios content, please sign up for any one of our newsletters, including mine or Ina's at signup.axios.com. Again, huge thanks to Cooley for sponsoring. And finally, we now at Axios have two podcasts, one in the morning called Axios Today and one in the afternoon hosted by me called Axios Recap. Please go to any podcast platform to check them out

[None]
and

[SPEAKER_00]
we'll see you next time.

[SPEAKER_00]
Hi, I'm Jamie Jeffries and I wanted to speak to you today about the perks of becoming a Scentsy consultant and the awesome potential to have your own business. If you're anything like me, I'm a pretty busy woman. Between a full -time job, my family and their activities, I really have little time for much else. I decided, however, a long time ago that I wanted to go into business for myself but really had no idea how to get started. That's when I ran across Scentsy. I already owned and loved their products and once I learned how easy it was to become a consultant, I was sold. To explain a little bit about Scentsy, the product was created to be a safe and wickless alternative to candles and the system is simple. You purchase the warmer of your choice, plug it in, then you add the scent wax of your choice and you allow the low -watt bulb to melt the wax and release the scent. The warmer is much more attractive and safer than a candle and there are over 40 original scents. When compared to popular Yankee candles, they are more environmentally friendly, safer, and cheaper. The system is even simpler to sell to others. It really sells itself, which makes it that much easier to become a consultant and go into business for yourself. Like I had said before, I was already a Scentsy customer and I had mentioned to my friend and Scentsy consultant that I really didn't know how she had time to work a full -time job, have kids, and sell Scentsy. That's when Heather told me how easy it was. She explained that you make your own hours and you set your own goals. You can host home parties, you can distribute books and take orders, or you can set up your own website through Scentsy for your customer convenience. You decide how many or how few hours you want to work. You really decide your own earning potential. Although you are working through Scentsy's direct selling company, you are your own boss. Hi, I'm David Blaise. I think it's safe to say that just about everyone involved in sales either understands or at least pays lip service to the idea that a well -crafted elevator speech is essential in business. I think it's also safe to say that hardly anyone involved in sales has ever taken the time to compose a really good one. Let's face it, much of what gets said in business is mediocre at best. In fact, some business owners are lucky if the messages that come out of their salespeople's mouths even rise to the level of mediocrity. And in most cases, it's not the salesperson's fault because no one from the business owner all the way down through the janitorial staff has ever once bothered to clearly articulate what sets the business apart. Well, it's our service, they'll say. Our service sets us apart. As if that's enough. Don't you think your competition says exactly the same thing? Remember the old TV show Bewitched with Elizabeth Montgomery and Dick York? Elizabeth Montgomery played Samantha. She was a witch. And her husband Darren was in advertising. Even as a kid, I remember thinking that this guy was a total buffoon. Not just because he could have anything he wanted and refused to take advantage of it, but because he would come up with the worst possible drivel for his advertising clients. He was always looking for the perfect slogan, something he could say about a client that would make people want to buy his clients' products. But he always seemed to be operating in a complete vacuum because he never bothered to take the time to learn what the client was really good at. What the true benefits would be for doing business with that client. Now, in a TV sitcom, this is funny. But the sad fact of the matter is that many people in advertising do exactly the same thing. They focus on creativity over content, design over fundamentals, white space over compelling advertising copy. So what does this have to do with elevator speeches? Everything. Your elevator speech has to be a reflection of you. It can't be just a string of words designed to sell a product. It has to distill down the essence of what makes you, you. What makes you different, unusual, unique, better. If we try to make up a marketing slogan and then gear our business to deliver it, we're doing it backwards. Before you can talk with any level of credibility about what you do, you have to be crystal clear on who you are. In future videos, we'll discuss what a good, solid, credible elevator speech is and what it's not. We'll talk about what it can really do for your business, and it can do a lot. We'll talk about what to say and what not to say, what to start with and what never to start with. It's everything you ever wanted to know about how to make money with an elevator speech. I'm David Blaise, and I help my clients to increase their sales, improve their profit margins, and grow their businesses on a guaranteed basis. Can I help you do that? Maybe. See you next time.

There was plenty of people down this hallway of 20 people dying that no one ever came in those seven days when I was there. There were people like, no, there was one guy that his wife would phone it in. No, I'm kidding. I'm not kidding. My father was wealthy because people were showing up at the end. And the thing I tell you, and the reason I bring up this personal journey, is that at the end of the day, will you truly be wealthy in this journey? I know we talk about building companies, making money, all the success and all the rest of it. But I just ask you a simple question. What is wealth? And who's going to turn up to one of your rooms, one of your 20 rooms? My father died with his three boys over him and his grandkids and everybody else. And I was just looking around the room and I could see all having this conversation over him. But this is his wealth. And I want to impart upon you is that that's a very, very important thing to think of that end game and think of your life. And don't think about the more thing as so much because I think we do that a lot on social media. We do that a lot in this time period. We get addicted to more and what we're seeing and all that kind of stuff. So I wanted to kind of impart a very personal tone to what I think is an important journey. So I'll stop there and I'll take some questions. All right. Stuff about the fire department? At the back, yeah.

[None]
Yeah. All right.

Well, again, one of things I love about what you're doing here is you're highlighting the power of social entrepreneurship. But it's not just about building your own empire. I'm the founder and CEO at Portfolium and we're changing the way college students enter the workforce. Roughly two million students in the US will graduate from college next month and attempt to enter the workforce, but 60 % of employers say they can't find the skills they're looking for in these graduates and this entry -level skills gap results in more than half of all recent graduates being unemployed or underemployed and that is a massive problem. Millennials are falling away from church and have been falling away from church for the past few years due to the big flashy lights, not feeling accepted and loved in the community, and not getting deep enough messages. All of these things are happening, and it's making people not want to come to church. Church is meant and has been built on being a safe place for Christians. It's being an area for us to be able to experience life with one another and be able to have such deep community. This is falling short. We have failed the next generation that is coming up that's supposed to be leading our church right now as it is. Millennials are aged from 22 to 37. We categorize them as the young adults. They're somehow getting lost in the mix from next -gen, which we consider our high school ministry students, and actual adults. They're caught in the crosshairs, thick far in between, and now they're falling away from the church as it is. So to solve this problem, to bring a solution, we have come up with the idea called the point. The point is something that is after a weekend experience service. So this would be on a Sunday night or a Saturday night where people, young adults, can come in and experience Christ in a more deep and intimate setting. It's an area for young adults to be able to have community, and the big flashy lights are stripped back and taken away. It's an intimate setting for everyone to be able to experience Christ in their own unique way. Throughout the point, there will be times for communities and small groups and people to be able just to talk and get to know one another. And then after each service, the point will be providing an after party with events and fun things to do. Ultimately, the point of Christianity is to have fun with each other and make Christ known. We need to have that basic element of community or else simply doing life alone, and that's not the point. And so the point's heart is really based off of community and getting to know one another. There will be food provided, and there will be such a time for everybody to just get to know one another, get to experience Christ in a completely different way, and be so true and so uniquely individually made and getting to know that and know how much Christ loves them.

Hello, I'm Joanne Turner reporting from IP Expo and I'm here for Telecoms Talk and I'm talking to Andrew Workin from Bluecat. Andrew, welcome. Perhaps you can start by telling some other viewers a little bit about Bluecat as a company.

[SPEAKER_01]
Sure, Bluecat is a enterprise DNS company. We're about a 15 year old company that has a great customer base of big, large, complex enterprises around the world. Very, very focused on making DNS a much more capable service within our customers.

[SPEAKER_00]
What are some of the issues you're finding now within the industry for people who are deploying DNS?

[SPEAKER_01]
As our customers are investing more and more in infrastructure that allows them to change and provision to meet their business requirements, DNS and DNS that perhaps has been cobbled together over the years or not necessarily maintained in such a way where we can drive fast change to it becomes actually an impediment for implementing a lot of business strategy because I can't quickly move workloads around or a DNS infrastructure that isn't centrally managed. Oftentimes customers have problems driving automation requirements to, again, quickly provision and create new capabilities in the enterprise. So it's, you know, the challenge though is also mixed with the fact that DNS is such a critical service inside the enterprise that our customers are oftentimes a bit concerned, worried about changing what they have today because of the ramifications of something not working. So, you know, we're very focused on meeting these big, complex needs, but also ensuring that our customers can migrate and migrate confidently without loss of service because usually the SLA is about 100 % for DNS.

[SPEAKER_00]
Absolutely. And one of the biggest things is the security challenge.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, and for sure. And for us, security comes in two flavors. One is protecting the service and ensuring that DNS is up and running, whether there's a denial of service attack or, you know, vulnerabilities sort of inherent in DNS. We take a lot of pride in how we work with our products and customers to ensure that we protect that service and make sure it's up. The other side of it is how DNS can be used to add to the security posture of the enterprise. And there's a whole variety of different ways to do that. But whether it's through DNS tunneling or any other sort of exploit, you know, a lot of companies aren't necessarily 100 % aware of how DNS can be used to take control of local machines. And really almost as, you know, botnet command to control. And so, you we're doing a lot of work on the analytics side as well with our customers to try to drive some really interesting solutions in that space.

[SPEAKER_00]
And you touched briefly on some of the, you know, you work with some of the big names, but what are some of the challenges you see coming out of some of those big enterprise customers that you're working with?

[SPEAKER_01]
Some of those challenges are similar to almost any other type of, you know, software defined infrastructure that they might be deploying in that they can automate these changes and change stuff way more often. But they have a month long change management process for deploying a new network or, you know, they only deploy changes to DNS every 24 hours. Now the business needs to do stuff immediately. And what ends up happening, especially in private and public clouds is the business doesn't wait and they deploy their own DNS service. And they copy, either manually copy over zones that they care about or in other ways actually make the infrastructure even less stable and potentially even hard code and, you know, avoid using DNS altogether. So, you know, part of it's just the same as challenges moving to any world of rapid change and software defined infrastructure. And others are, you know, DNS is rather complex. And, you know, there's always dependency on a few people that really understand the depths and bowels of DNS. And so we really try to help our customers abstract themselves from having to understand, you know, exactly how the technology works, but rather make sure it's available for them. And we take on some of the burden of ensuring that it's optimized.

[SPEAKER_00]
Okay. And what's the future of DNS? What's next going to come out of DNS?

[SPEAKER_01]
We strongly believe that there's a tremendous amount of untapped value in DNS data. And by that, I mean, you know, all of the query information we're seeing going through DNS match that with what we do on the DHCP side and managing the network space in general. And so, you know, from a how do we leverage this data to create visibility to what's happening in the enterprise is a huge area for us. You know, a lot of companies are taking the DNS log data, trying to bring it into Splunk, trying to do things with it. But, you know, there aren't that many DNS experts in the world and we've got a bunch of them and we're doing some really interesting things. And it's actually fun to work with our customers on because of the sort of things we can explore and see both on the security side, but on the employee engagement side on the, you you sort of name it. And DNS is a fairly good proxy for what the user's intending to do and therefore makes it pretty powerful.

[SPEAKER_00]
Brilliant. Thanks for taking the time to talk to us today.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thank you. Good to meet you.
sources.title: BlueCat Networks CTO Talks about the Latest DNS Developments at IP Expo 2016

In today's competitive environment, it's very important to have a refined elevator pitch. Here are 10 tips of what I think is important in an elevator pitch. How do you help? Make sure that you get across in a simple message how you're going to help the potential client. Listen before talking. If you get the opportunity to understand what a prospect is facing and what hurdles they need to get over, you'll be in a more powerful spot to deliver an effective message. Don't be afraid to be a broken record. Even if you have conveyed that same message over and over, that consistency is a good thing. Personalize the message. Make sure that you're talking the prospect's language so that you're both on the same page. Match personalities. You might find that somebody is very energetic or someone is just monotone. You don't have to be a mirror image of them, but they'll feel more comfortable if you're matching how they are. Why are you better than the rest? Know why you differentiate yourself from the competitors. Be engaging. If you find that you're talking to a prospect and you're not getting a lot of dialogue, ask open -ended questions that allows for them to be more forthcoming. And you can then develop your pitch to meet their needs. Make an emotional connection. Look at finding out those benefits of what they really need. Why are you involved? Let the prospect know while you're in this industry. Why are you selling a product or service? What's important to you? The close. In the pitch, make sure that you are trying to get to the next level. Is it asking for the next meeting? Is it asking for a follow -up conversation? That lyric sheet should also be typed and have your contact information so that in case it becomes separated from the CD, they know how to reach out and get to you. You want to make it as easy as possible for them to reach you. Remember, don't send MP3s unless you've been asked to do so. The 1492 Christopher Columbus discovered America, and in 1607 the English established their first permanent colony in the New World at Jamestown, Virginia. Taking these two key dates as my start and end points, my research essentially traces the processes by which the English firstly learned of the New Lands across the Atlantic, and then how they applied this new knowledge to their own colonial enterprise. As you can probably imagine these processes are often very varied and difficult to trace, because Englishmen and women utilize the image of America both consciously and unconsciously, for commercial gain and as a subconscious means of expressing their own specific cultural anxieties. For example an indigenous American could be perceived as barbarous and in dire need of English help and evangelization and thus as a justification for conquest and colonization. But they could equally be seen as the pure innocent alternative to the corruption and decadence of 16th century England. Paradoxically then Amerindians could be both savage and civilized. Because of these complexities, and their seeming contradictions I think that understanding the English reaction to America in the 16th century is crucial to understanding the development of English imperialism in the New World from the 17th century onwards.

TORONTO

,

June 25, 2020

/CNW/ - BMO has today introduced a new podcast dedicated to Canadian businesses. The podcast –

Business Unplanned

– will provide business owners with expert opinions and advice on business resiliency and adaptability during this uncertain time. This announcement builds off of the bank's recently introduced

online resource hub

and will provide Canadian businesses with an additional resource to help their long-term growth.

"We are helping thousands of businesses across geographies and sectors every week and are constantly looking for opportunities to do more," said

Erminia (Ernie) Johannson

, Group Head, North American Personal and Business Banking, BMO Financial Group. "In conversations with our clients, we heard how important and beneficial it is for them to have a community where they can learn from each other. We have now created an additional resource where businesses can come together and learn from entrepreneurs and business owners and apply best practices to their own businesses."

Business Unplanned

will feature six episodes and be available on

bmo.com/BusinessUnplanned

as well as on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and Google Podcasts. Episodes will be released periodically throughout the summer. Entrepreneur, investor, and co-founder of BlueCat,

Michael Hyatt

, has joined as the host of

Business Unplanned

. He will lead listeners on a journey as they dive into stories from leading entrepreneurs and small business owners.

"More than ever before, leaders need to come together to help both small businesses and the wider business community overcome the challenges of this pandemic," said Mr. Hyatt. "Joining BMO as the host of Business Unplanned is a way to do that and provides an outlet where business owners can relate to what we are sharing and take away actionable advice for their business."

The podcast will include guests from a range of sectors and business size and will cover:

Episode 1: The Business Recovery

Episode 2: Making Business Adjustments: How to Plan Post-Pandemic

Episode 3: Getting a Business Loan During Covid-19

Episode 4: Managing Cash Flow Post-Covid-19

Episode 5: How to Stay Motivated in Business

Episode 6: Understanding Customers' Needs

Area of Expertise

Vanessa

is a Senior Counsel at RBC. Prior to joining RBC, Vanessa was a litigation counsel at the Department of Justice Canada, specializing in a broad range of complex legal and policy matters involving social benefits programs and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Vanessa regularly represented the Attorney General of Canada before the Federal Court and the Federal Court of Appeal.

Vanessa is on the Board of Directors of International Planned Parenthood Federation / Western Hemisphere Region and of IPPF Canada. She was a guest speaker on women empowerment at the International Women’s Empowerment and Leadership Conference and at the Women’s Festival Toronto Gala. She has volunteered for the Elizabeth Fry Society of Ottawa, which supports and advocates for young and adult women who are criminalized or may become criminalized. She earned both a JD and a License of Civil Law from the University of Ottawa. Vanessa speaks English, French and Spanish fluently.

Michael

Hyatt is the co-founder of BlueCat, which was sold to Madison Dearborn Partners, of Chicago, IL. He serves as a director of BlueCat, ranks as one of Canada’s top entrepreneurs, and is known as a technology visionary. Michael is also a weekly business commentator on CBC and was a celebrated “Dragon” on CBC’s online Dragons’ Den. He is the Host of BMO’s Unplanned Business podcast to help small businesses and an investor on the hit Spotify podcast “The Pitch”. Michael is a Founding Partner and Fellow at the Rotman School of Management’s prestigious Creative Destruction Lab and sits on the CEO Board of Advisors of Georgian Partners, one of Canada’s leading venture capital firms. He was also recently named Entrepreneur in Residence (EIR) at Blakes, one of the most successful law firms in the country.

Michael was awarded the “Power Partner Award” from the Women of Inspiration Awards for his supportive and innovative work with Women in Canada and the developing world.

Michael and Vanessa

are active investors and philanthropists who are part of the Hyatt Family Foundation. The foundation focuses on women’s health, critical hospital research and sponsorship of underprivileged minorities.

BlueCat Networks, a Toronto-based provider of enterprise-class IP Address Management (IPAM) platforms, has raised a $11m first equity financing.

Successful entrepreneurs often make unsuccessful investors when they sell their companies and become full-time family office chiefs instead, according to a leading family office founder. "It's humbling," said Michael Hyatt, a software entrepreneur and principal of the Hyatt Family Office. "You need to fall on your face and realize that if you're a great entrepreneur, you're likely a pretty bad investor. Start with that, admit you're not good. And you can probably do some good things." Hyatt, 48, co-founded and sold two software companies — Dyadem and BlueCat Networks — before launching the Hyatt Family Office in 2017. A self-made millionaire by the age of 25, Hyatt sold BlueCat for $400 million in 2017. While he declined to comment on the size of the Hyatt Family Office, industry experts estimate its current assets at between $400 million to $600 million. (See the full special interview with Hyatt above.) The rapid growth of family offices — which now number as many as 10,000 worldwide, according to EY — is being driven in large part by entrepreneurs who have sold their companies or taken them public, creating massive liquidity. While older family offices were largely built on inherited wealth and highly conservative investing philosophies, a new generation of family offices is run by born risk-takers who aim for exponential returns -- traits that sometimes also make for costly mistakes. "To be an entrepreneur, you have to be a risk-taker, Machiavellian, damn the torpedoes," Hyatt said. "If you actually calculated the risks of building and exiting a company for, say, over $1 billion, you probably never would have started the company. But when you have money, you have to go from wealth creation to wealth preservation. And that's an entirely different ballgame. It's not sexy. It's boring and you have to save yourself from yourself." Sobering juice bankruptcy Hyatt said that one of his early family office investments was in a juice start-up. He studied the numbers, got to the know the founder and did deep information dives on the juice business before investing. Other sophisticated investors were also buying in. The company went bankrupt less than a year after he invested. Today, the Hyatt Family Office has a diversified portfolio, aiming for a third of its assets to be invested in stocks, a third in real estate and a third in venture capital and private equity. His goal is returns of 8% a year. "We don't push the boundaries," he said. "I've had outcomes where I feel like a genius but I realized I took way too much risk to get that return." Hyatt said he rarely touches his stock portfolio, as tempting as it is with wildly gyrating markets and rising interest rates. He said the family office largely buys Vanguard ETF's, along with a handful of his favorite stocks, which include Google, Microsoft and Apple. With real estate, Hyatt has invested in a fund that buys commercial properties in secondary cities — a trade that's generated strong returns after the pandemic when many residents of big urban hubs moved to smaller cities but still wanted office space. The private equity and venture capital bucket of the portfolio is where Hyatt says he can "scratch his entrepreneurial itch" to find promising start-ups and help them grow. He mainly chooses funds where the founders also have substantial capital at risk and that are largely closed to medium-sized or small investors. The jockey, not the horse When it comes to investing directly in start-ups, Hyatt said he bets on the entrepreneur more than the idea, since every successful company makes big pivots in strategy. "I spend time investing in the jockey not the horse," he said. "And then I help figure it out." Hyatt said the key to a successful family office can be summed up in one word: no. "They don't say no enough," he said. "Just because I made the money doesn't mean I know how to invest it. I'm self aware enough to know that I'm wrong. When you say no to 100 things, there are going to be a couple that you say no to that are just incredible. And that's the point. But on average you really have to be disciplined."

Michael and Richard Hyatt have acquired a majority stake in Mississauga-based DataStealth, an enterprise cybersecurity firm that helps banks and hospitals protect their data.

For the brothers—both successful Canadian tech entrepreneurs-turned-investors who previously built, scaled, sold, and exited Toronto-based Dyadem and BlueCat in deals totalling more than $1 billion—the transaction marks a return to operations.

The Hyatts believe that they could have their “next big thing” with significant ownership of an efficient and fast-growing cybersecurity business at a time when cyber attacks are on the rise.

“We’re back, we’re doing something big, and this is super important to us,” Michael Hyatt told BetaKit in an interview. “We’ve now picked a horse and we’re all in on it.”

The Hyatt brothers’ majority stake investment closed earlier this month. Hyatt declined to disclose the price tag.

Speaking to the appeal of bringing on the Hyatts as investors, DataStealth co-founder and CEO Ed Leavens noted the pair’s experience building large, successful software companies, complementary skill sets, and willingness to “roll up their sleeves.”

“They took BlueCat to $100-million-plus in annual revenue, profitable—everything that we want to do, they just did this, and they did it twice,” Leavens told BetaKit in an interview. “We have a very solid foundation … We decided that we wanted to really grow, and [that] we needed some expertise, and we found our expertise.”

Founded in 2014, DataStealth aims to help large businesses protect their most sensitive data and documents. Built on its patented technology, the company sells a suite of products that tap into organizations’ networks to discover, classify, and protect data by tokenizing, encrypting, or masking it. DataStealth caters to a variety of industries, including telecommunications firms, financial institutions, insurance firms, and healthcare organizations.

According to Leavens, while other firms offer products that look like DataStealth’s offerings, what sets DataStealth apart from other players is its ease-of-use and speed of deployment. “The difference isn’t in what we do necessarily, it’s more about how we do it,” he said.

“It’s very simple—the technology just works,” added Hyatt. “You can install this product with no agent, no code, nothing. It just works.”

Hyatt was first introduced to DataStealth after one of the startup’s senior leaders asked him for advice. When Hyatt lent a hand and peeked under the hood, he said he was shocked at what he found: a profitable company with great technology, solid growth, strong gross margins, no debt, and limited outside capital, that was generating over $10 million in annual revenue.

“The amount of companies that are growing beautifully that have profit and no venture capital [funding] is incredible,” said Hyatt. “It’s very rare.”

Prior to the Hyatt brothers, DataStealth had just one external investor: a majority shareholder named Abe Schwartz. According to Leavens, he and DataStealth co-founder and CIO Marc Carrafiello used a ‘shotgun clause’ to buy out Schwartz for nearly $7 million, or $1.16 per share, and then sold a portion of Schwartz’s stake to the Hyatt brothers in a separate transaction.

Per an Ontario Superior Court of Justice ruling obtained by BetaKit, Schwartz initially took the position that this notice from Leavens and Carrafiello was improper and declined to respond, and pursued other legal action. However, an Ontario judge ruled in May that by not exercising his right to buy out Leavens and Carrafiello at the same price they offered for his stake, Schwartz accepted their offer, enforced the sale, and dismissed other issues brought up by Schwartz.

Speaking to DataStealth’s use of this shotgun clause, Leavens said, “I think that shotgun or buy-sell provisions in shareholder agreements are common, and we had an opportunity to take advantage of ours, so we did. That’s really all it was. And I think that we saw a different future.”

DataStealth has retained its management and roughly 45-person team as part of the deal. Per Leavens, the company’s leadership still holds a “significant piece of equity” in DataStealth.

“We decided that we wanted to really grow, and [that] we needed some expertise, and we found our expertise.”

– Ed Leavens, DataStealth

Hyatt has become executive chairman, and plans to focus his attention on DataStealth’s sales and go-to-market efforts, while Richard, who has also joined the board, is working with the startup’s engineering team.

“This is not a passive investment,” said Hyatt. “We’re working side by side with the executive team to help them grow and scale the business.”

Over the next few years, Hyatt said that their focus will be on scaling DataStealth’s business without taking on additional outside capital. He sees plenty of potential for DataStealth.

“Right now, we have so much runway,” said Hyatt. “Cybersecurity is so big. We think this outcome could be another BlueCat.”

BetaKit on November 1, 2023

and was authored by Josh Scott.

Michael Hyatt is a Canadian entrepreneur and investor recognized for his significant contributions to the technology sector. He co-founded BlueCat Networks, a company specializing in DNS security and management, which was acquired by Madison Dearborn Partners in 2017. Prior to BlueCat, he co-founded Dyadem, a software company that was acquired by IHS in 2011. These ventures have established him as a prominent figure in Canada's tech industry.

In addition to his entrepreneurial endeavors, Michael serves as a Senior Advisor to Northleaf Capital Partners, supporting their venture capital and growth equity investment program. He is also a Founding Partner and Fellow at the Rotman School of Management’s Creative Destruction Lab, a program designed to help early-stage science and technology companies build large, scalable, and impactful businesses. His involvement in these initiatives underscores his commitment to fostering innovation and supporting the growth of emerging companies.

Beyond his business activities, Michael is an active philanthropist, chairing the Hyatt Family Foundation, which focuses on women's health, critical hospital research, and support for underprivileged minorities. He also serves as a weekly business commentator on CBC and has been featured on the cover of Canadian Business Magazine. His diverse roles and contributions highlight his dedication to both business and community development.

Michael's investment philosophy centers on identifying and nurturing high-potential companies across various stages of growth. His strategic approach combines his extensive experience in building and scaling businesses with a keen eye for emerging opportunities, making him a valuable asset to the ventures he supports.

Through his ventures and investments, Michael Hyatt continues to play a pivotal role in shaping the landscape of Canada's technology sector, demonstrating a strong commitment to innovation, entrepreneurship, and social responsibility.

Jan 26, 2022

Northleaf announces appointment of technology entrepreneur Michael Hyatt as a Senior Advisor to its venture capital and growth equity program

News

Private Equity

Northleaf

TORONTO, CANADA (January 26, 2022)

– Northleaf Capital Partners (“Northleaf”), a global private markets investment firm, is pleased to announce the appointment of Michael Hyatt as a Senior Advisor supporting Northleaf’s venture capital and growth equity investment program. Michael will work alongside the Northleaf private equity and venture capital team to source and evaluate investment opportunities. As a serial entrepreneur and active investor, Michael’s knowledge and expertise in the venture capital space complements Northleaf’s longstanding investment approach.

"We are excited to welcome Michael to Northleaf as a Senior Advisor,” said Ian Carew, Managing Director & Venture Partner at Northleaf. “We have invested successfully with Michael in the past and our venture capital and growth equity program will benefit from his deep knowledge and experience and accomplished track record as both an entrepreneur and investor.”

“I am thrilled to act as a Senior Advisor to Northleaf’s successful venture capital and growth equity program and look forward to working with Ian and the team,” said Michael Hyatt. “I’ve had the opportunity to see the Northleaf strategy at work over the years and I’m excited to collaborate with the team on future investments for the program.”

Michael Hyatt is recognized as one of Canada’s leading tech entrepreneurs and an active investor in the technology community. He is the co-founder of BlueCat (in which Northleaf was an early investor and which was acquired by a private equity firm in 2017) and previously co-founded Dyadem (a software company that was sold to IHS in 2011). He currently serves as a Director of BlueCat. Michael is a regular business commentator on the CBC and the host of “Unplanned Business,” a podcast to help small businesses. He is a Founding Partner at the Rotman School of Management’s prestigious Creative Destruction Lab (CDL) and chairs the Hyatt Family Foundation focused on women’s health, critical hospital research and sponsorship of underprivileged minorities.

Northleaf is one of Canada’s most active venture capital investors. Northleaf manages more than US$800 million in venture capital and growth equity commitments on behalf of investors and has played a leadership role in the development of many successful venture capital / growth equity funds. Northleaf has been making direct investments in later-stage and high growth companies since 2008, leveraging its well-established relationships with leading fund managers, institutional investors and entrepreneurs.

About Northleaf Capital Partners

Northleaf Capital Partners is a global private markets investment firm with more than US$19 billion in private equity and venture capital, private credit and infrastructure commitments under management on behalf of public, corporate and multi-employer pension plans, endowments, foundations, financial institutions and family offices. Northleaf’s team of more than 160 professionals, located in Toronto, Chicago, London, Melbourne, Menlo Park, Montreal and New York, is focused exclusively on sourcing, evaluating and managing private markets investments globally. Its portfolio includes over 400 active investments in 40 countries, with a focus on mid-market companies and assets. For more information on Northleaf, please visit

www.northleafcapital.com

On today’s Tank Talk! We welcome our guest

Michael Hyatt

, Co-Founder of Hyatt Family Office.

Michael is well known in the Canadian tech ecosystem as a serial entrepreneur turned angel investor and is regularly seen on TV providing his advice to aspiring entrepreneurs. Before Michael started his first company, he was President & CEO at Dyadem which sold to IHS a US public company in 2011. Michael went on to co-found

BlueCat Networks

with his brother and eventually sold the business to private equity firm Madison Dearborn for a reported $400mm in 2017

On today's Talk, we ask Michael about his family office and their focus on wealth preservation vs wealth creation during the crisis. We also talk to Michael about his operator first approach to investing and what he looks for when backing early-stage founders or fund managers.

BMO Unveils New Podcast for Canadian Businesses
Accessibility Statement
Skip Navigation
BMO reaffirms commitment as the bank for business with content focused on business resiliency and growth to help clients make real financial progress
Well-known entrepreneur and investor Michael Hyatt headlines as the host of the podcast
TORONTO, June 25, 2020 /CNW/ - BMO has today introduced a new podcast dedicated to Canadian businesses. The podcast – Business Unplanned – will provide business owners with expert opinions and advice on business resiliency and adaptability during this uncertain time. This announcement builds off of the bank's recently introduced online resource hub and will provide Canadian businesses with an additional resource to help their long-term growth.
"We are helping thousands of businesses across geographies and sectors every week and are constantly looking for opportunities to do more," said Erminia (Ernie) Johannson, Group Head, North American Personal and Business Banking, BMO Financial Group. "In conversations with our clients, we heard how important and beneficial it is for them to have a community where they can learn from each other. We have now created an additional resource where businesses can come together and learn from entrepreneurs and business owners and apply best practices to their own businesses."
Business Unplanned will feature six episodes and be available on bmo.com/BusinessUnplanned as well as on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and Google Podcasts. Episodes will be released periodically throughout the summer. Entrepreneur, investor, and co-founder of BlueCat, Michael Hyatt, has joined as the host of Business Unplanned. He will lead listeners on a journey as they dive into stories from leading entrepreneurs and small business owners.
"More than ever before, leaders need to come together to help both small businesses and the wider business community overcome the challenges of this pandemic," said Mr. Hyatt. "Joining BMO as the host of Business Unplanned is a way to do that and provides an outlet where business owners can relate to what we are sharing and take away actionable advice for their business."
The podcast will include guests from a range of sectors and business size and will cover:
Episode 1: The Business Recovery
Episode 2: Making Business Adjustments: How to Plan Post-Pandemic
Episode 3: Getting a Business Loan During Covid-19
Episode 4: Managing Cash Flow Post-Covid-19
Episode 5: How to Stay Motivated in Business
Episode 6: Understanding Customers' Needs
To access BMO's Business Resource Hub, visit: https://www.bmo.com/main/business/small-business-resource-hub/.
To stay connected with BMO or to access the bank's new online support tool, visit: bmo.com/covid19.
About BMO Financial Group
Serving customers for 200 years and counting, BMO is a highly diversified financial services provider - the 8th largest bank, by assets, in North America. With total assets of $987 billion as of April 30, 2020, and a team of diverse and highly engaged employees, BMO provides a broad range of personal and commercial banking, wealth management and investment banking products and services to more than 12 million customers and conducts business through three operating groups: Personal and Commercial Banking, BMO Wealth Management and BMO Capital Markets.
Internet: www.bmo.com Twitter: @BMOmedia
SOURCE BMO Financial Group
Media Contact: James DeCosimo, Toronto, [email protected], (416) 867-3996

Michael & Vanessa Hyatt - | DMZ

Michael & Vanessa Hyatt
copied!
Area of Expertise
Vanessa is a Senior Counsel at RBC. Prior to joining RBC, Vanessa was a litigation counsel at the Department of Justice Canada, specializing in a broad range of complex legal and policy matters involving social benefits programs and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Vanessa regularly represented the Attorney General of Canada before the Federal Court and the Federal Court of Appeal.
Vanessa is on the Board of Directors of International Planned Parenthood Federation / Western Hemisphere Region and of IPPF Canada. She was a guest speaker on women empowerment at the International Women’s Empowerment and Leadership Conference and at the Women’s Festival Toronto Gala. She has volunteered for the Elizabeth Fry Society of Ottawa, which supports and advocates for young and adult women who are criminalized or may become criminalized. She earned both a JD and a License of Civil Law from the University of Ottawa. Vanessa speaks English, French and Spanish fluently.
Michael Hyatt is the co-founder of BlueCat, which was sold to Madison Dearborn Partners, of Chicago, IL. He serves as a director of BlueCat, ranks as one of Canada’s top entrepreneurs, and is known as a technology visionary. Michael is also a weekly business commentator on CBC and was a celebrated “Dragon” on CBC’s online Dragons’ Den. He is the Host of BMO’s Unplanned Business podcast to help small businesses and an investor on the hit Spotify podcast “The Pitch”. Michael is a Founding Partner and Fellow at the Rotman School of Management’s prestigious Creative Destruction Lab and sits on the CEO Board of Advisors of Georgian Partners, one of Canada’s leading venture capital firms. He was also recently named Entrepreneur in Residence (EIR) at Blakes, one of the most successful law firms in the country.
Michael was awarded the “Power Partner Award” from the Women of Inspiration Awards for his supportive and innovative work with Women in Canada and the developing world.
Michael and Vanessa are active investors and philanthropists who are part of the Hyatt Family Foundation. The foundation focuses on women’s health, critical hospital research and sponsorship of underprivileged minorities.

BMO Unveils New Podcast for Canadian Businesses
Accessibility Statement
Skip Navigation
BMO reaffirms commitment as the bank for business with content focused on business resiliency and growth to help clients make real financial progress
Well-known entrepreneur and investor Michael Hyatt headlines as the host of the podcast
TORONTO, June 25, 2020 /CNW/ - BMO has today introduced a new podcast dedicated to Canadian businesses. The podcast – Business Unplanned – will provide business owners with expert opinions and advice on business resiliency and adaptability during this uncertain time. This announcement builds off of the bank's recently introduced online resource hub and will provide Canadian businesses with an additional resource to help their long-term growth.
"We are helping thousands of businesses across geographies and sectors every week and are constantly looking for opportunities to do more," said Erminia (Ernie) Johannson, Group Head, North American Personal and Business Banking, BMO Financial Group. "In conversations with our clients, we heard how important and beneficial it is for them to have a community where they can learn from each other. We have now created an additional resource where businesses can come together and learn from entrepreneurs and business owners and apply best practices to their own businesses."
Business Unplanned will feature six episodes and be available on bmo.com/BusinessUnplanned as well as on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and Google Podcasts. Episodes will be released periodically throughout the summer. Entrepreneur, investor, and co-founder of BlueCat, Michael Hyatt, has joined as the host of Business Unplanned. He will lead listeners on a journey as they dive into stories from leading entrepreneurs and small business owners.
"More than ever before, leaders need to come together to help both small businesses and the wider business community overcome the challenges of this pandemic," said Mr. Hyatt. "Joining BMO as the host of Business Unplanned is a way to do that and provides an outlet where business owners can relate to what we are sharing and take away actionable advice for their business."
The podcast will include guests from a range of sectors and business size and will cover:
Episode 1: The Business Recovery
Episode 2: Making Business Adjustments: How to Plan Post-Pandemic
Episode 3: Getting a Business Loan During Covid-19
Episode 4: Managing Cash Flow Post-Covid-19
Episode 5: How to Stay Motivated in Business
Episode 6: Understanding Customers' Needs
To access BMO's Business Resource Hub, visit: https://www.bmo.com/main/business/small-business-resource-hub/.
To stay connected with BMO or to access the bank's new online support tool, visit: bmo.com/covid19.
About BMO Financial Group
Serving customers for 200 years and counting, BMO is a highly diversified financial services provider - the 8th largest bank, by assets, in North America. With total assets of $987 billion as of April 30, 2020, and a team of diverse and highly engaged employees, BMO provides a broad range of personal and commercial banking, wealth management and investment banking products and services to more than 12 million customers and conducts business through three operating groups: Personal and Commercial Banking, BMO Wealth Management and BMO Capital Markets.
Internet: www.bmo.com Twitter: @BMOmedia

Media Contact: James DeCosimo, Toronto, [email protected], (416) 867-3996

She has volunteered for the Elizabeth Fry Society of Ottawa, which supports and advocates for young and adult women who are criminalized or may become criminalized. She earned both a JD and a License of Civil Law from the University of Ottawa. Vanessa speaks English, French and Spanish fluently.
Michael Hyatt is the co-founder of BlueCat, which was sold to Madison Dearborn Partners, of Chicago, IL. He serves as a director of BlueCat, ranks as one of Canada’s top entrepreneurs, and is known as a technology visionary. Michael is also a weekly business commentator on CBC and was a celebrated “Dragon” on CBC’s online Dragons’ Den. He is the Host of BMO’s Unplanned Business podcast to help small businesses and an investor on the hit Spotify podcast “The Pitch”. Michael is a Founding Partner and Fellow at the Rotman School of Management’s prestigious Creative Destruction Lab and sits on the CEO Board of Advisors of Georgian Partners, one of Canada’s leading venture capital firms. He was also recently named Entrepreneur in Residence (EIR) at Blakes, one of the most successful law firms in the country.
Michael was awarded the “Power Partner Award” from the Women of Inspiration Awards for his supportive and innovative work with Women in Canada and the developing world.
Michael and Vanessa are active investors and philanthropists who are part of the Hyatt Family Foundation. The foundation focuses on women’s health, critical hospital research and sponsorship of underprivileged minorities.

It is with pleasure and gratitude that I welcome you to

From our long standing position as a neutral industry
