Hyatt Brothers Acquire Majority Stake in DataStealth
Michael and Richard Hyatt have acquired a majority stake in Mississauga-based DataStealth, an enterprise cybersecurity firm that helps banks and hospitals protect their data.
For the brothers—both successful Canadian tech entrepreneurs-turned-investors who previously built, scaled, sold, and exited Toronto-based Dyadem and BlueCat in deals totalling more than $1 billion—the transaction marks a return to operations.
The Hyatts believe that they could have their “next big thing” with significant ownership of an efficient and fast-growing cybersecurity business at a time when cyber attacks are on the rise.
“We’re back, we’re doing something big, and this is super important to us,” Michael Hyatt told BetaKit in an interview. “We’ve now picked a horse and we’re all in on it.”
The Hyatt brothers’ majority stake investment closed earlier this month. Hyatt declined to disclose the price tag.
Speaking to the appeal of bringing on the Hyatts as investors, DataStealth co-founder and CEO Ed Leavens noted the pair’s experience building large, successful software companies, complementary skill sets, and willingness to “roll up their sleeves.”
“They took BlueCat to $100-million-plus in annual revenue, profitable—everything that we want to do, they just did this, and they did it twice,” Leavens told BetaKit in an interview. “We have a very solid foundation … We decided that we wanted to really grow, and [that] we needed some expertise, and we found our expertise.”
Founded in 2014, DataStealth aims to help large businesses protect their most sensitive data and documents. Built on its patented technology, the company sells a suite of products that tap into organizations’ networks to discover, classify, and protect data by tokenizing, encrypting, or masking it. DataStealth caters to a variety of industries, including telecommunications firms, financial institutions, insurance firms, and healthcare organizations.
According to Leavens, while other firms offer products that look like DataStealth’s offerings, what sets DataStealth apart from other players is its ease-of-use and speed of deployment. “The difference isn’t in what we do necessarily, it’s more about how we do it,” he said.
“It’s very simple—the technology just works,” added Hyatt. “You can install this product with no agent, no code, nothing. It just works.”
Hyatt was first introduced to DataStealth after one of the startup’s senior leaders asked him for advice. When Hyatt lent a hand and peeked under the hood, he said he was shocked at what he found: a profitable company with great technology, solid growth, strong gross margins, no debt, and limited outside capital, that was generating over $10 million in annual revenue.
“The amount of companies that are growing beautifully that have profit and no venture capital [funding] is incredible,” said Hyatt. “It’s very rare.”
Prior to the Hyatt brothers, DataStealth had just one external investor: a majority shareholder named Abe Schwartz. According to Leavens, he and DataStealth co-founder and CIO Marc Carrafiello used a ‘shotgun clause’ to buy out Schwartz for nearly $7 million, or $1.16 per share, and then sold a portion of Schwartz’s stake to the Hyatt brothers in a separate transaction.
Per an Ontario Superior Court of Justice ruling obtained by BetaKit, Schwartz initially took the position that this notice from Leavens and Carrafiello was improper and declined to respond, and pursued other legal action. However, an Ontario judge ruled in May that by not exercising his right to buy out Leavens and Carrafiello at the same price they offered for his stake, Schwartz accepted their offer, enforced the sale, and dismissed other issues brought up by Schwartz.
Speaking to DataStealth’s use of this shotgun clause, Leavens said, “I think that shotgun or buy-sell provisions in shareholder agreements are common, and we had an opportunity to take advantage of ours, so we did. That’s really all it was. And I think that we saw a different future.”
DataStealth has retained its management and roughly 45-person team as part of the deal. Per Leavens, the company’s leadership still holds a “significant piece of equity” in DataStealth.
“We decided that we wanted to really grow, and [that] we needed some expertise, and we found our expertise.”
– Ed Leavens, DataStealth
Hyatt has become executive chairman, and plans to focus his attention on DataStealth’s sales and go-to-market efforts, while Richard, who has also joined the board, is working with the startup’s engineering team.
“This is not a passive investment,” said Hyatt. “We’re working side by side with the executive team to help them grow and scale the business.”
Over the next few years, Hyatt said that their focus will be on scaling DataStealth’s business without taking on additional outside capital. He sees plenty of potential for DataStealth.
“Right now, we have so much runway,” said Hyatt. “Cybersecurity is so big. We think this outcome could be another BlueCat.”
--
This article originally appeared on BetaKit on November 1, 2023 and was authored by Josh Scott.

The Most Underrated Canadian Founder You’ve Probably Never Heard Of
If Michael Hyatt were American, he’d have 500,000 LinkedIn followers, a book deal, and a Netflix documentary called “How to Print Money Legally.”
But he’s Canadian…
So nobody talks about him.
Let’s fix that.
Meet Michael Hyatt: the quiet Canadian who sold not one, but TWO huge companies before he turned 30.
Everyone knows Shopify.
Everyone knows Lululemon.
But almost nobody knows the guy who built one of Canada’s most valuable cybersecurity firms and sold it for $400M+, and then just kept going.
This is why I love studying founders like Hyatt:
They aren’t loud.
They aren’t flashy.
They just win.
The Story
At 17, he’s playing with servers while the rest of us were trying to get a date to grad.
At 25, he starts his first tech company, Dyadem.
At 29, he sells it.
Then he does the most un-Canadian thing ever:
He starts another one.
That company?
BlueCat.
The invisible plumbing behind the internet that no one thinks about until it breaks.
Think cybersecurity meets infrastructure meets “oh God don’t let this fail.”
Everyone said building it in Canada was impossible.
Hyatt built it anyway.
Scaled it.
Then sold it for hundreds of millions.
Instead of buying a yacht and disappearing to Anguilla, he becomes an angel investor, backs dozens of companies, becomes a CBC Dragon, gives straight-talk business advice, and mentors founders across the country.
No ego.
No influencer vibes.
Just results.
Why I’m Obsessed With His Playbook
Here’s the thing about Hyatt:
He didn’t build a social app.
He didn’t build a marketplace.
He built boring infrastructure that powers the internet.
And boring infrastructure is where the money is.
His lessons hit hard:
Solve real problems, “not founder feelings.”
Ignore hype, focus on customers who pay.
Build discipline, not dopamine.
Be relentless, even when nobody sees you.
Think decades, not quarters.
Canada desperately needs more founders like him, quiet killers who build important things instead of shiny things.
The Takeaway
Canada has a lot of amazing founders building amazing things.
They’re the ones who don’t go viral.
They don’t chase clout.
They build internet plumbing, cybersecurity rails, utilities, enterprise tools, the stuff billion-dollar companies rely on.
Hyatt is the blueprint:
Start small
Build something real
Sell it
Do it again
Help others
Simple.
Not easy.
If you’re building something in Canada, study this man.
He’s one of our country’s best founders.
We just haven’t built him a statue yet.

Every conversation about AI eventually circles back to the same question.
If AI can answer, advise, act, and coordinate, what is left for the human?
The answer is the entire reason Level 6 exists.
Levels 1 through 5 of the AI Ascension Model describe what AI does. Level 6 describes what you do.
The Visionary sets the mission. Defines the values. Holds final accountability for what the operation produces. The AI runs the operation. The human decides what it’s all for.
This is the only level that cannot be outsourced.
AI can climb the first five with you, for you, around you. AI cannot replace you here. The Visionary is the keeper of intent. The one who says why the business exists, who it serves, and what it must never become.
For executives, this is not philosophy. It is the operating model of the next decade.
In an AI-saturated industry, the differentiator is no longer what your business can do. The capability surface flattens. The differentiator becomes who you serve, what you stand for, and which lines you will not cross. Even when AI makes it cheap to cross them.
Boards and leadership teams that treat Level 6 as a strategic discipline, rather than a soft cultural exercise, will outperform peers that delegate the question to the AI itself. This is the conversation that should occupy the next strategic offsite. Not which model to standardize on. Not which vendor to consolidate. The mission, the values, and the lines you will not cross. Everything else cascades from there.

The channels everyone's betting on are collapsing

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗜𝗱𝗲𝗮: Cello, a referral platform that turns users into acquisition engines
𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱: $5.8M total raised
𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆 #𝟭: 𝗢𝘄𝗻 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Monday.com lost 50% of market cap from SEO over-reliance.
The #1 Google result just hemorrhaged 79% of traffic.
Cold calling pickup rates are tanking because Apple made screening the default.
Stefan's fix: make the product the distribution.
Every Cello integration becomes free advertising. The loop compounds without depending on channels you don't control.
𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆 #𝟮: 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗟𝗼𝗼𝗽𝘀, 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀els
Funnels leak at every stage. Loops compound.
Users engage → users share → new users discover → repeat.
Each cycle makes the next easier.
Stefan stacks multiple loops (referrals, integrations, brand plays) so when one channel wobbles, the system stays alive.
𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆 #𝟯: 𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗮𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝘀 𝗔𝗰𝗾𝘂𝗶𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Stefan skipped cold email and paid ads at launch. Just founder-led sales through his network.
He brought on investors who delivered portfolio companies as design partners. Used fundraising itself as customer acquisition.
Later ran GTM 10 Awards that went viral and accelerated every loop without creating new dependencies.
𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆 #𝟰: 𝗗𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗳𝘆 𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗬𝗼𝘂'𝗿𝗲 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲𝗱
Referrals drive 10-50% additional revenue for B2B. Not a silver bullet, but part of a system.
Founders betting 70% on one channel get blindsided when it collapses.

Everyone told her to go bigger, faster.
She shrank her company instead. That's when everything changed.
Anya remembered the sleepless nights, staring at spreadsheets, chasing metrics she barely understood. The startup world screamed "scale, scale, scale!" and she listened.
Her team was exhausted. The work felt rushed, shallow. They were hitting numbers, yes, but losing their soul. And her own peace of mind was long gone.
One Tuesday, after a particularly draining meeting where a new investor pushed for an impossible 300% Q3 growth, she walked out.
She needed air. And a radical idea.
What if growth wasn't just about *more*?
What if it was about *better*?
Anya gathered her small, weary team. "We're stopping," she announced. The silence was deafening. "We're not chasing volume anymore. We're chasing excellence."
She let go of half their client roster – the high-maintenance, low-profit ones. She cut projects that didn't align with their true passion.
It felt like jumping off a cliff. Every fiber of her entrepreneurial being screamed "wrong move!"
But a strange calm settled over them. They focused on their best clients, poured every ounce of their talent into a few key projects. The quality skyrocketed.
Their small team, no longer stretched thin, started innovating again. They felt proud of their work, genuinely connected to their clients' success.
Word spread. Not about their massive numbers, but about their incredible *results*. Clients started seeking *them* out, willing to pay premium for the dedicated, high-quality output.
Their revenue dipped initially, then stabilized. Then, quietly, it began to climb. Not a hockey stick curve, but a steady, sustainable, joyful ascent.
They discovered true growth wasn't in the size of the operation, but in the depth of its impact.
Sometimes, the bravest move isn't to expand, but to refine.
What would you have done in their place?

Our NYC panel proved that scale and impact can (and should!) grow together.
We gathered 70 founders and investors to talk about one question: how do you build unicorns without losing your purpose?

→ EVERYONE in a company should talk to customers. If you can’t hear them, you can’t build for them.
→ Purpose scales only when it’s built into how you operate.
→ Fundraising bias is real: women get asked about risks, men about opportunities. Best approach: acknowledge the risk, then pivot to opportunity.
I have a love-hate relationship with organizing events: I’m obsessed with audience quality and depth of conversation, and while striving for that excellence exhausts me, I left feeling we truly leveled up.

He publicly shut down his most profitable product line.
Everyone called him crazy.
But what happened next shocked the entire industry.
Mark had this product, "QuickFix," that was bringing in good money. Steady income, kept the lights on.
But it was a soul-suck.
Every customer call was a complaint. Every new feature request felt like patching a leaking boat.
His team was burnt out, constantly firefighting. Morale was in the basement, even with the decent revenue.
One Tuesday morning, looking at the Q4 projections – all green, all soul-crushing – he made a call.
He pulled the plug. On QuickFix. The company's cash cow.
Silence in the boardroom. Then panic. "Are you serious? We'll go bankrupt!"
Mark just nodded. "We're already bankrupting our spirit. We're building something we hate."
He laid off a small part of the team, the ones exclusively on QuickFix. Toughest day of his life, but he knew this wasn't sustainable for anyone.
For months, the company bled cash. Investors were calling, worried. His wife was worried. He himself stared at the ceiling at 3 AM, wondering if he'd just destroyed everything.
But with QuickFix gone, a weird thing happened.
His remaining team, smaller but committed, started breathing again.
They started talking about *the other idea*. The one they always pushed aside because QuickFix demanded all their attention.
This new idea was risky. It was niche. It was *hard*.
But it excited them. It lit a fire.
Late nights shifted from despair to pure creative energy. They were building something they actually believed in.
He remembered his mentor once saying, "Sometimes, you have to burn the bridge to build a rocket."
It wasn't easy. They almost didn't make it.
But twelve months later, that 'risky, niche, hard' idea launched.
It didn't just succeed. It revolutionized a small but crucial corner of the market.
The revenue? Surpassed QuickFix within 18 months, with happier customers, a passionate team, and zero soul-suck.
Mark realized then: Profit isn't just a number. It's the byproduct of passion and purpose.
Sometimes, sacrificing good for great isn't a gamble. It's a strategy.
Drop a 💪 if you’ve ever rebuilt from scratch.

Flaherty urges G7 countries to tackle debt
Finance Minister Jim Flaherty is urging his fellow G7 finance ministers who gathered in France this weekend to "stay the course" on deficit and debt reduction and is calling on the eurozone to increase its bailout fund.
CBC News · Posted: Sep 10, 2011 5:50 PM EDT | Last Updated: September 11, 2011
Listen to this article
Estimated 4 minutes
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.
Finance Minister Jim Flaherty remains confident about the Canadian economy despite troubles in the U.S. and Europe.
Social Sharing
Finance Minister Jim Flaherty is urging his fellow G7 finance ministers who gathered in France this weekend to "stay the course" on deficit and debt reduction and is calling on the eurozone to increase its bailout fund.
The danger "is that we have countries slip into deficit and debt situations that put them in peril, quite frankly, and that markets lose confidence in the economy," Flaherty told CBC News from Marseille. "We don't want any more of that. We've seen some of that already in certain peripheral European countries."
Those domestic problems can, and have, spread beyond their borders, Flaherty said.
Flaherty called on the eurozone Friday to increase its bailout fund beyond the current $440 billion, an unusually concrete demand from a non-European politician.
Flaherty optimistic about Canada's outlook
Flaherty said he expects to be able to "stay on plan" in Canada, but would be flexible if the economic system received a "shock, particularly from Europe."
"If the European situation got out of control, and then if that affected our economy dramatically, of course we'd be pragmatic and we'd take the necessary actions. We've done it before and we would do it again. But I don't anticipate that will happen. Our revenues this year are good. We had a weak second quarter, but I expect the rest of the year will be good."
Christine Lagarde, the head of the International Monetary Fund, urged policymakers to take concerted action quickly. The so-called Group of Seven economies comprise the U.S., Canada, Japan, Britain, France, Italy and Germany.
"The key… is for policymakers to act with conviction and urgency in tackling today's challenges, while at the same time being nimble, should circumstances change," Lagarde said in London before travelling to the G7 meeting.
But big new measures and strong unity in the face of a threatening economic slowdown were elusive among finance ministers and central bankers gathering there, with different countries touting divergent solutions to the crisis.
"I don't think you should expect from this meeting any dramatic change in signals," U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said in an interview on Bloomberg TV.
With little prospect for united action on economic stimulus, the three eurozone countries in the G7— Germany, France and Italy — were facing pressure from the other members to find a lasting solution to the debt crisis that has dragged on for nearly two years.
Global outlook downbeat
The talks came on the back of a downbeat assessment of the global outlook by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. The watchdog for the world's most developed economies slashed its forecast for growth in the U.S. and the eurozone this year due to government belt-tightening and falling consumer and business confidence.
The meeting also came after Canada lost a total of 5,500 jobs in August — the second consecutive month that employment picture was little changed.
"It's not a good sign," said Elmer Kim, general manager of the Ontario investment firm Roynat Capital. "What's clear is that the Canadian economy is catching the tailwind of the U.S. economy, and it really is slowing down. The U.S. hasn't added a job in 15 years... and the jobs Canadians are adding are low-quality, low-paying jobs."
Michael Hyatt, CEO of BlueCat Networks, said there's a misconception among Canadians that they are protected from the vagaries of the U.S. economy.
"We don't have a broken political system and we probably can balance our deficits, but there's never been a time where the U.S. goes into recession or has a really dark hour that we don't at least follow or come near to it," he said.

You can love each other deeply and still struggle to see what the other person is carrying.
Especially when you are both tired. Both stretched thin. Both trying to keep the business, the family, and everything in between moving.
It is easy to start interpreting exhaustion as indifference. A short response as a lack of care. A missed detail as proof that you are carrying this alone.
And before you know it, you are defending your side instead of trying to understand theirs.
But your spouse is not the opposition.
You may be looking at the same life from two different places, each carrying responsibilities, worries, and pressures the other person has not fully seen.
The goal is not to prove who is carrying more. It is to make enough room to understand what you are both carrying.
Sometimes, the most important conversation starts with a different question:
“What has been feeling heavy for you lately?”
Send this to your spouse as a reminder that you are on the same team.

Your husband may know everything about your life and very little about what it feels like to be you right now.
And I don’t mean that as an indictment of your husband.
Think about it.
He probably knows your schedule. He knows the kids. He knows what’s going on with the business. He knows what you’re worried about this weekend.
You two may talk all day.
But when was the last time he asked you something that made you stop and think before answering?
That is what a lot of long-married women are actually missing.
Not communication.
Discovery.
You can know somebody incredibly well and still stop being curious about them.
And sometimes “I miss us” really means:
I miss finding out who you are now.
And I miss you wanting to find out who I am now too.
Send this to the woman who has a good marriage and still knows exactly what I mean.

Apparently there was a whole generational meeting and I missed it.
I had to Google what ages are Gen X, Gen Y, and Gen Z just to figure out where I belonged.
Turns out... Gen X.
Great.
Glad we cleared that up. 😂
I also learned that Gen Y became Millennials, there are apparently Xennials AND Zillennials, and Gen Alpha showed up sounding like they had already been promoted to management.
Meanwhile, I’m just trying to understand when our socks, jeans, and hair parts became evidence in determining our age.
I was not briefed on any of this.
And apparently being slightly skeptical of the entire conversation only makes me MORE Gen X.
Which feels suspiciously convenient.
Will I remember the exact birth years for each generation after posting this?
No.
Will I Google it again the next time someone mentions it?
Absolutely.
Will I suddenly develop strong feelings about which generation is superior?
Also no.
I have enough things to think about.
But now that I had to Google it...
I feel morally obligated to make this someone else’s problem.
SEND this to a woman your age.
Not because she needs to know which generation she belongs to.
Because it will irritate her that now she has to Google it too.
And if you already knew exactly which generation you were without Googling... please identify yourself in the comments. Some of us have questions. 😂

What if you’re not the only one paying the price for your success?
That’s the part we don’t put on the spreadsheet.
You can measure revenue.
Growth.
Clients.
Team size.
Opportunities.
Hours worked.
But it’s harder to measure what success costs the people waiting for you at home.
The dinner where you were physically there but mentally somewhere else.
The conversation you half-heard because you were thinking about tomorrow.
The “give me five minutes” that turned into forty-five.
The date night interrupted by “one quick thing.”
The kid who stopped asking because the answer was usually, “Not right now.”
The spouse who doesn’t necessarily need more hours with you... they just want access to the version of you everyone else seems to get.
None of this means ambition is bad.
Building something meaningful matters.
But there’s a difference between your family benefiting from what you’re building... and your family continually paying for it.
Success gets expensive when the people you love keep covering the bill with your absence.
And absence isn’t always an empty chair.
Sometimes you’re sitting right there.
So here’s a question worth sitting with:
What is your success costing the people you love right now?
And is that a price you actually intended for them to pay?
SHARE this with someone who is building something big and needs the reminder that the people they’re building it for still need them along the way.

You left work hours ago... but did work actually leave you?
Because closing the laptop doesn’t always mean you’re done working.
Sometimes you’re sitting next to your spouse while your brain is still:
Replaying the meeting.
Solving the problem.
Planning tomorrow.
Thinking about the client.
Running through the numbers.
Mentally answering an email you haven’t even opened yet.
You’re home... but you haven’t fully arrived.
And for entrepreneurs, business owners, and people carrying a lot of responsibility, this can become so normal that you don’t even notice it anymore.
But your spouse might.
The problem isn’t always how many hours you work.
Sometimes it’s how much mental and emotional space work continues to occupy after those hours are over.
Your marriage doesn’t necessarily need more hours on the calendar.
Sometimes it needs more of YOU in the hours you already have.
Your attention.
Your curiosity.
Your laughter.
Your presence.
The part of you that isn’t trying to solve the next problem.
So here’s the question:
When you come home... what percentage of you actually comes with you?
👇 Drop your percentage in the comments. No judgment... just awareness.

You might be saying yes before anyone else even realizes there was a question.
You see what needs to be done.
So you handle it.
The appointment.
The email.
The kids.
The problem nobody has noticed yet.
The thing that will become a bigger problem if someone doesn’t take care of it now.
And because you’re capable... you do.
Again.
Then one day you’re standing there thinking:
“WHY am I the only person who notices anything around here?”
Here’s the uncomfortable part...
Sometimes nobody asked you to take it on.
You noticed.
You anticipated.
You decided.
You handled it.
Before anyone else had the opportunity to respond.
That doesn’t mean the people around you shouldn’t step up.
And it doesn’t mean your resentment isn’t real.
It means there may be something underneath it worth noticing.
An automatic yes.
The yes that happens so quickly you don’t even experience it as a decision anymore.
“Yes, I’ll handle it.”
“Yes, I’ll figure it out.”
“Yes, I’ll make sure it gets done.”
“Yes, I’ll carry this too.”
But every yes has a no attached to it.
And when the “no” is repeatedly your own rest, needs, time, boundaries, or capacity...
resentment starts keeping the receipts.
This is where capability can quietly become self-abandonment.
Not because caring for people is wrong.
But because constantly volunteering yourself before checking your own capacity eventually costs you something.
So the next time you notice something that “needs” to be handled, try not to immediately fix it.
Pause.
Ask:
“Did someone actually ask me to carry this?”
“Does this have to be mine?”
“What am I saying no to if I say yes?”
That tiny pause might be where resentment starts losing some of its power.
SAVE this for the next time your automatic yes wants to answer before you do.

You can run a business, manage a family, solve problems all day long... and still forget to actually date your spouse.
Not because your marriage is falling apart.
Not because you don’t love each other.
But because somewhere between the kids, work, appointments, bills, responsibilities, and the 47 things that apparently needed to happen yesterday...
your marriage became another thing you assumed you’d “get to.”
You still talk.
A lot, actually.
But the conversations sound more like:
“What time will you be home?”
“Did you call them?”
“Can you pick that up?”
“What are we doing about the kids?”
“Did you see that email?”
You become really good at running a life together... while having fewer conversations about the two people actually living it.
And that’s the sneaky part.
Nothing has to be terribly wrong for connection to start slipping.
Sometimes your marriage doesn’t need a huge intervention.
It needs your attention.
It needs time that doesn’t have an agenda.
It needs conversations that aren’t about solving a problem.
It needs moments where you remember you’re not just business partners, parents, chauffeurs, household managers, and calendar coordinators.
You’re husband and wife.
And “sometime” is probably not going to magically appear on the calendar.
So maybe it’s time to actually schedule it. 😉
Send this to your husband with three available dates.
No agenda allowed.
The first person to say,
“While we’re here, we should probably talk about...” buys dessert.

Your spouse can miss you while you’re sitting three feet away.
That’s the part successful people don’t always notice.
You came home.
Your phone is down.
You’re sitting at the same table.
But your best thinking never left the business.
So when your spouse says, “I miss you,” your first thought is:
“I’m right here.”
And technically, you are.
But part of your brain is still replaying the meeting, solving tomorrow’s problem, thinking through the decision, or remembering the email you forgot to send.
At work, people got your curiosity.
Your sharpest thinking.
Your patience.
Your ability to notice what everyone else missed.
Then you came home with six percent battery and tried very hard to be pleasant.
That’s one of the invisible costs of success nobody talks about.
Sometimes the business doesn’t take more of your time.
It just gets first access to your attention.
And nothing has to be “wrong” with your marriage for this to happen.
You can love each other deeply.
You can be committed.
You can have a good marriage.
And slowly become really efficient roommates.
Because physical presence and emotional presence are not the same thing.
The question isn’t only:
“How much time am I giving my marriage?”
It’s:
“Who gets the most alive version of me?”
That answer might reveal a cost of success you haven’t been measuring.
SAVE this for the next time your body makes it home before your attention does.
And SEND it to your spouse or a friend who’s building something big without wanting to lose what matters at home.

My husband and I have the same toothbrush.
I don't mean that we have matching toothbrushes.
I mean that there is a blue toothbrush in the bathroom and we both think it belongs to us.
We discovered this last weekend.
I went away and packed "my" toothbrush.
Nathan stayed home and discovered "his" toothbrush was missing.
(We've since bought a green one. We decided not to talk about how long either of us has been using the blue one.)
There’s a link to marketing here, it won’t take me long to find it 😉
I’ve got it.
A lot of the posts I read are blue toothbrushes.
"I help ambitious professionals step into their power."
"Your mindset is the key to your success."
"It's time to show up as your authentic self."
Any coach could pick those up and think they were theirs. And that's the problem. If your posts could have been written by anyone, it doesn't really belong to you.
Your reader can't tell whose it is either. So they scroll past.
The answer isnt AI posts. And it’s not MORE content.
It's your words. Your personality. Your stories.
The phrase only you would actually say out loud to clients. (Mine is “I’d rather shit in my shoes and go for a walk”) The opinion you hold that someone in your niche would disagree with.
Write the green toothbrush.
The one nobody could mistake for anyone else's.

Tuesday, November 06, 2007
Success without Distress
My Financial Post column today focuses on an interview with Toronto technology entrepreneur Mchael Hyatt of BlueCat Networks. I met him at the dinner for the Deloitte Fast 50 a few weeks ago, where he challenged me to write a story about how he and his brother built two multi-million dollar companies without relying on venture capital.
As he complained in the interview, many company founders today are just "buying an employer... They give everything away because they don't have any money themselves. They give the reins of control to an investor that doesn't love the company, may not even understand the market space -- and will fire the founders as soon as the numbers aren't realized."
Hyatt's formula for success without bosses:
* Focus on the U.S. market from the start.
* Start cheap.
* Begin selling fast.
* Put your money into marketing: "Focus on doing fewer sales calls and more sales."

Michael Hyatt
Michael Hyatt became a self-made millionaire when he was just 25, by building two highly successful tech firms valued in the hundreds of millions. Today, he ranks as one of Canada’s top entrepreneurs, is a celebrated “Dragon” on CBC’s new online sensation Next Gen Den, and is a weekly Business Commentator on CBC News Network. Hyatt is also an active investor and philanthropist. Speaking on leadership, entrepreneurship, the future of tech, and managing change, he underscores all his talks with the message that to achieve success you need to prepare for a marathon, not a sprint.
Hyatt sees tremendous disruptive change coming to all businesses, and believes that the Golden Age is ahead. He feels that computing power is set to become exponentially stronger (as it has been for many years), but that this time artificial intelligence (AI) will step out—Siri is just the start. In his view, AI is coming to everything we do, and, combined with the massive Internet of Things wave, we will see huge changes to just about every profession including medicine, law, banking, and energy.
Hyatt is the co-founder and executive chairman of BlueCat, one of the leading growth companies in the country, focused on the internet of things. Prior to his current role, he led the company since its inception as CEO, where his leadership philosophy was to focus on strategy and empower his employees to execute. Intentionally hiring people “smarter than him”, Hyatt looked for team players that could help make the big decisions as a group. Always keeping an eye on the big picture, Hyatt led—and leads—with the idea that the constant and consistent march toward the strategic goal wins the day.
Before co-founding BlueCat, Hyatt also co-founded (and was the initial CEO of) Dyadem, which provided software and services that improved the ability of large industrial, energy, manufacturing and chemical companies to manage quality, mitigate risk, achieve regulatory compliance, plan for business continuity, and improve profitability. The highly successful engineering software company was acquired by IHS in a great eight-figure deal.
A “G7 Fellow” at the Rotman School of Management’s prestigious Creative Destruction Lab, Hyatt acts as a coach for venture founders to set business and technical milestones to increase the ventures’ chances of success. He is also on the CEO Board of Advisors at Georgian Partners, one of Canada’s leading venture capital firms; was a finalist in Ernst & Young’s Entrepreneur of the Year Award; and was a recipient of the Top 40 Under 40™ Award.
An active investor, Hyatt is driven by his core principals which focus most significantly on people and companies that are trying to make a huge impact (and have the ability to disrupt). Additionally, Hyatt helps and mentors youth to succeed and become contributing citizens in their communities. He is the chair of his family’s charitable foundation, The Hyatt Family Foundation, which donates and invests in a number of important projects including women’s health and employment, biomedical research, and international water programs. He is also an active lender with Kiva.org, a non-profit organization with a mission to connect people through lending to alleviate poverty.

Research from MIT Sloan published in March 2026 found that generative AI doesn’t just accelerate individual tasks — it draws workers into a broader range of tasks than they handled before.
For senior leaders, this has a specific consequence I’ve been calling the DIY Trap.
The economics of delegation rest on a simple calculation: is the cost of doing it yourself higher than the cost of handing it off and waiting? For most strategic work, the answer has historically been yes — which is why effective executives build teams and delegate freely.
AI changes that calculation. When AI can produce in two hours what used to take a specialist a week, the logic of handing off breaks down. Why wait two weeks when you and AI can get most of the way there by Thursday?
So the work that used to leave your plate stays on it. You become both the leader and the contractor. Strategic thinking time gets consumed by execution — because AI made execution fast enough to feel worth your time.
I confessed this pattern to a room of CEOs in my AI Business Lab mastermind in April. The room recognized itself immediately.
The DIY Trap doesn’t target low performers. It finds the most capable leaders — the ones whose judgment adds genuine value to every project they touch.

We talk a lot about how AI will change sales.
We don’t talk enough about how it should change leadership.
AI is brilliant at pattern recognition. It can tell you where deals stall and who is at risk. It cannot sit with a human being and have the uncomfortable, career-defining conversation that actually changes behavior.
That’s the real leadership gap.
Too many teams are adding AI on top of old habits: more dashboards, more “coaching” that is really pipeline inspection.
If we want AI to matter, we need a different standard for managers:
• From scorekeepers to real coaches who build capability
• Use AI to prepare better conversations, not replace them
• Treat insights as a starting point for curiosity, not the end of the discussion
The future is not “AI versus managers.”
It’s AI-augmented leaders versus everyone else.

I've seen AI programs with world-class models fail. And I've seen programs with average models succeed.
The difference was almost never the technology.
The single biggest predictor of whether an AI transformation delivers real results: whether senior leadership treats it as their program or someone else's. Not in name. In time, attention, decisions, ownership, and action.
Here's what I mean by that. The leaders whose programs actually land aren't just sponsoring AI. They're living it first.
They use the tools before they ask their teams to. They've personally felt where AI accelerates and where it still frustrates. They come to the room with real experience, not a briefing deck.
They don't patch AI into their existing schedule and call it transformation. They've actually asked themselves: how does my week need to look different? What decisions should I be making faster? What am I still doing manually that I shouldn't be? They redesigned their own operating rhythm, then asked the organization to follow.
And when they're in a review, they're not approving output. They're interrogating it. Because they understand it well enough to ask the question that matters.
What I see more often: leadership delegates AI to a talented team, gets regular updates, sponsors the initiative on paper, and wonders why adoption is slow and ROI is missing. The team was great. The tools were real. But the org around them never moved.
AI transformation doesn't stall at the model level. It stalls when the people asking others to change haven't changed themselves.
You can't lead an AI transformation you haven't been through.
#AITransformation #Leadership #GenAI

Stop asking if AI will replace your team. Ask this instead.
They're asking: What AI can do?
The more consequential question is: What does it reveal about you?
Because here's what Pivut observed working with senior leaders navigating transformation AI doesn't replace human capacity.
→It amplifies what's already there.
→The clarity you have.
→The blind spots you carry.
→The quality of your thinking.
→The depth of your self-awareness.
The leaders who are thriving right now aren’t the ones with the most sophisticated AI stock. They’re the ones who’ve done the harder work understanding how they make decisions, where they default to control, and why they sometimes confuse being busy with leading well.
There's a quiet discomfort settling into many leadership teams. Not about technology but about identity.
When a machine can analyse faster, synthesise better, and never burn out; what does a leader actually stand for?
The answer isn't a job description. It's not a title. And it definitely isn't a list of competencies.
It's the quality of your presence. Your judgment under complexity. Your ability to hold tension, carry ambiguity, and still create direction for others. These aren't soft skills. They're the hardest skills and they've always separated good leaders from genuinely great ones.
AI just made them impossible to ignore.
So before you rush to become more efficient, more automated, more optimised ask yourself what kind of leader you're actually becoming in this period. Not what you're doing with AI but who they are while doing it.
The organisations that will matter the most in the next decade won't be the ones that deployed AI the fastest. They'll be the ones that used this moment to build something rarer: leadership is more human, not less.
That's the evolution worth leading.

Coffee Thoughts ☕️ AI transformation gets real when leaders change their own habits
One of the most impactful actions a leader can take to transform their business with GenAI is simultaneously one of the simplest and hardest — personally using the tools, reflecting on what worked, and then changing how they operate.
What I've seen after a year of recurring 1:1s with senior leaders is that you can't just sponsor AI from a distance. The ones transforming their businesses are actually using it, 3-5 times per day, building daily habits that compound.
Learning to ask better questions. Bringing rough thinking into a model and iterating. Testing new ways to prepare for meetings, synthesize inputs, coach teams, or make decisions. Then sharing the messy middle with their teams — showing how the next prompt got closer to what they needed.
That behavior matters because teams watch what leaders actually do. If AI is framed as "something the org should adopt," it stays abstract. When leaders visibly use it to improve their own work, it becomes permission for others to experiment.
I've learned a lot from leaders who carved out time, built their own habits, and thought through how those habits could scale into team and org-level change. I'd like to thank them for wading into the ambiguity, being uncomfortable, and leading this transformation in their own work. They made the time, and helped pave the way for so many others.
Tagging a few people whose openness, curiosity, and leadership have helped me better understand and facilitate real behavior change at scale: Christie Feraudo, Mamar Gelaye, Beth Galetti, J. Ofori Agboka, Raoul Sreenivasan, Adam Baker, David Cardadeiro, Stephanie Collett, John Tagawa, Robert Kowalik, Sandy G., Chris Turner, Scott Dresser, Steve Walter, and Catherine Furlani.
The more I work in this space, the more convinced I am that transformation is not driven by slogans. It is driven by repeated behaviors that make better work easier to do.

Podcast, Private Wealth
How the Hyatt Family Office approaches VC opportunities
January 7, 2026
By
Lauren Bailey
Listen on
YouTube
Join us for the Annual Private Wealth Canada West Forum
Michael Hyatt, principal of the Toronto-based Hyatt Family Office, discusses what he looks for in the ideal venture capital investment, rapid transformation through artificial intelligence, and leaving a lasting family legacy.
Lauren Bailey:
Your path has been nothing but traditional. So why don’t you walk me through how you got where you are today and how that grassroots type of beginnings of your family business sort of shaped your approach to investing?
Michael Hyatt:
Yeah. Look, my story is I went to University of Western and I graduated with a science degree and it was a recession at that time when I graduated. This is in the 90s. And my brother Richard had dropped out of UFT who was a brilliant programmer and we really didn’t have anything. My dad had an idea of developing some software for his industry. So my brother would code that software and then I would sell it and that’s what happened in the 90s. And really we just came out of pretty much nowhere with no money, no financing, no background. And I could sell, my brother could code and my dad understood the industry. And my mom kind of held it all together and we just kind of got it going. And if you said you were an entrepreneur in the 90s, it was probably another word for unemployed or jobless or something like that.
Or you just kind of threw that down. And it seemed very differently today, but back then it was kind of this you looked as like you had horns on your head or something like that. And then we slowly but surely built up that company and that engineering software company. Then we started BlueCat in the early 2000s. We built up that company and we sold all our companies, we had all these transactions which went extremely well. But I would say that I’m a kind of a 25-year overnight success. That’s probably the best way to aptly put where we’ve come from to where we are. And we started a family office in 2017, and then we started investing in other businesses and other entrepreneurs. And it’s a very interesting thing, transforming your life from being an entrepreneur where essentially you take risk for a living to then running a family office where you’re an investor and you learn very quickly that being a pretty good entrepreneur doesn’t mean you’re going to be a pretty good investor.
They’re very, very different things. Good investing is a lot slower, a lot more boring, a lot less sexy than building a company, and it takes a lot of patience and I don’t have much of that. And it is just a slow and steady wins the race in investing. And so you have to have almost like a diametrically opposite personality to be a good investor than you are a good entrepreneur. So I’ve been learning over the years of how to slow down and get the right people in my family office to help us make the right investments.
Lauren Bailey:
So you’ve taken a value-driven approach to building this foundation, this office. I wonder, besides the obvious wealth management, wealth preservation, what is your mandate for your family office and where are you focusing?
Michael Hyatt:
So the way I looked at it is I have parents and I have two brothers and we all have children. So there’s a new generation of the three of us brothers and there’s 10 children. And when you look at it, you wonder, the first thing somebody tells you at a bank once you’ve sold your company, you’ve made some money is there’s a saying called shirt sleeves to shirt sleeves in three generations. And that’s kind of an old school way of saying that my grandkids will basically become penniless because there is never really a good intergenerational understanding of money and wealth and how to live. And so what I wanted to do is set up a family office that railed against that and created a platform for our larger extended family to live by. And I tried to make it so it didn’t counter just on me, meaning that if something ever happened to me, we just can’t be at peril.
We have to be an organization that can go on. And I wanted to create something that would last the test of time. And so in the coming years, how do we get the next generation involved appropriately? Because if my brother Richard and I were kind of like nine out of 10 and making money kind of guys, and our kids are a six, and their kids are going to be a three out of 10, and then the old adage is correct, nothing really stays on. And also, I find that the scary thing about having a family office is that I didn’t grow up, for example, having a swimming pool or an elevator in my house or going to a private school or ever flying private. And it is a terrifying idea that my kids think having an elevator in their house is normal or having a pool is normal.
It’s not normal. And I’m most worried about how do you create a family office that works intergenerationally where they don’t see those things as normal, which is a very hard thing to run from. And so you have to create this kind of institution that works and gets them to work in that institution properly and understand risk and money and that relatively life is quite hard and getting ahead in life is actually a pretty cold and hard thing and nothing is given to you. And so the family office was created to fight against this idea that anything is automatic, that any money passing on is just simple. And my children will just get money and just go on with their day because I think that would mean that I’m stealing their journey. And that’s a terrifying thought because that’s real theft. That’s real theft. So there’s a lot to consider.
So there’s two things. I wanted to, one, get it away from just pinpointing on me as the money maker, and I wanted to make it so that we democratize the idea that people have to, all our children and grandchildren have to work incredibly hard to get somewhere in life because the world is a hard place.
Lauren Bailey:
You come from a private equity sort of background, right? That’s sort of your thing. You started you and your family . . . you, your brother, and your father started your company from scratch. I read that it was in the back of, was it a print shop or. . . .
Michael Hyatt:
A photography studio.
Lauren Bailey:

Michael Hyatt:
We try to do three buckets and we never get to the split that we get to. If you look at our asset allocation, we always try to do a third or more in the stock market, a third in private equity, big P, small VC, as in we do more in private equity than doing venture. And then our last bucket is that we’re always trying to acquire a company and use our operational excellence to do something. And we don’t try to time the markets, we just try to back great entrepreneurs and a great market, and we know that markets will ebb and flow, but anytime we invest in a company, our minimum hold time in our head has to be 10 years.
So we don’t do quick trades, we don’t get caught up in . . . I love CNBC, but I don’t get caught up into this trade this, trade that, buy this, buy that. It’s like this constant churning wheel. It would drive me crazy to do that. I’m not trying to do that. And look, some people are incredibly successful at it. We’re not. I mean, there’s something very nice about being a family office and no matter what happens, making 10% a year. Sometimes we make 30%, but sometimes . . . But I mean, it’s something that’s very nice just being very predictable.
Lauren Bailey:
Well, it seems as though what you’ve just described as being there to pick up the phone when things go wrong and you have to really talk it through with the CEO of a company that you’ve invested in. That kind of gradual growth can’t be done under 10 years, which is a very long-term view that you need to really realize . . . Go ahead.
Michael Hyatt:
Yeah. If you want to make it asymmetrical return though, you have to do that. I mean, look, absolutely some people buy a stock and buy Nvidia or Shopify early and they get that kind of return. That happens every once in a while. Sure it does. And then if we knew what we was going to do, we’d all have piled in earlier. But the truth is that you have to be there for the ride with the entrepreneur if you’re going to do the private markets. It’s not for the fainted heart. I’ll say that. It’s certainly a tough path.
Lauren Bailey:
I mean, I know we just had this long conversation about AI and a lot of people would say that that’s where they’re pivoting, that’s where they’re really looking for growth companies that are doing something different. Where are you seeing private equity? What sectors are you really seeing potential for that growth in the five, 10, 15, 20 years?
Michael Hyatt:
Yeah. So do you want to actually name funds or. . . .
Lauren Bailey:
Sectors. Is it just AI that’s intriguing? Is it sustainability within that clean tech?
Michael Hyatt:
Listen, I don’t fully understand clean tech, so I stay out of it. I don’t quite understand health tech because I stay out of it. We just backed a very large private equity firm’s fund who does a lot of automation. They’ll be buying into companies that are doing robotics that have a minimum of 50 to 75 million of EBITDA per company. So this is not like startups. We buy into a lot of companies, businesses out of New York that do distressed debt very well, come in and do turnarounds. That has been very successful for us. We do companies that do massive roll-ups. One in Toronto in particular, we back a fund that way. I sold my company to Madison Dearborn, so I stay invested with them because I really like them.
But pretty much I stick to things that I understand. I stick to things that I feel that are probably going to do well in the future. And listen, we’re not always right, but typically we don’t chase fads, so we never chased blockchain, which if we had this conversation five years ago, that’s all we would talk about. Today, all we talk about is AI, and I feel that there’s a lot of good stuff, but there’s also equally a lot of bad stuff in that. So AI to me is just a means to an end. And I don’t want to hear about AI. What I want to hear about what is what you’re doing for the customer and how you’re delighting them. And by the way, you happen to be using AI as part of your story. That’s kind of what I want to hear.
Lauren Bailey:
That’s very interesting. I mean, you’re right. There’s going to be AI winners and AI losers and-
Michael Hyatt:
More losers than winners because whenever the crowd runs after something, you know what happens, right? It’s a pretty tough haul when . . . it’s a pretty crowded trade when everybody’s in AI.
Lauren Bailey:
Yeah. I mean, that said, my daughter using it in school, they’re making them adopt it within their schoolwork in some ways . . . well before we were using them regularly in the workforce.
Michael Hyatt:
So you bring up a really important point. Let me just give everybody a little bit of a piece of advice. And you’re probably going to think that I’m nuts for telling you this. If you’re in a company right now, you desperately need to go hire two students. And you’re like, Michael, what are you talking about? What do I want a student? They know nothing. I guarantee the student knows more than you. I have now hired five or six students at one of my companies, and the way they come in using AI is not like we understand it. And I’m hugely appreciative of their intelligence. So for example, I want a new product coded. They use Cursor, they use Devon, they use PICA, they use all these different products, Copilot, they use all this stuff, and they’re doing stuff that we wouldn’t naturally do. We’d code this, we’d use a little AI.
The way they are so naturalized to it, a 20-year-old today, I believe some of those valuable people right now in the workplace are 20-year-olds. I can guarantee it because I’ve seen it and I’m hugely appreciative of students. And a lot of these students can’t get jobs right now. I’m like, people don’t know what they’re missing.

Northleaf annonce la nomination de l'entrepreneur en technologie Michael Hyatt comme conseiller principal de son programme de capital-risque et de capital de croissance
Nouvelles
Placements privés
Northleaf
TORONTO, CANADA (January 26, 2022) – Northleaf Capital Partners (« Northleaf »), une société mondiale de placement sur les marchés privés, a le plaisir d'annoncer la nomination de Michael Hyatt comme conseiller principal pour soutenir le programme de placement en capital-risque et en capital de croissance de Northleaf. Michael travaillera aux côtés de l'équipe de Northleaf chargée du capital-investissement et du capital-risque pour détecter et évaluer les possibilités d'investissement. En tant qu'entrepreneur en série et investisseur actif, les connaissances et l'expertise de Michael dans la sphère du capital-risque complètent l'approche de placement de Northleaf établie de longue date.
« Nous sommes très heureux d'accueillir Michael chez Northleaf comme conseiller principal », a déclaré Ian Carew, directeur général et partenaire associé du capital-risque chez Northleaf. « Nous avons investi auparavant de manière fructueuse grâce à Michael et notre programme de capital-risque et de capital de croissance pourra bénéficier de ses connaissances et expérience solides ainsi que de ses antécédents irréprochables comme entrepreneur et investisseur ».
« Je suis très heureux d'agir à titre de conseiller principal du programme de capital de risque et de capital de croissance de Northleaf, qui est en pleine apogée, et je me réjouis de travailler avec Ian et son équipe », a déclaré Michael Hyatt. « J'ai eu l'occasion de voir la stratégie de Northleaf à l'œuvre au fil des ans et je suis enthousiasmé à l'idée de collaborer avec l'équipe sur les futurs investissements du programme ».
Michael Hyatt est réputé comme étant l'un des principaux entrepreneurs technologiques du Canada et un investisseur actif dans la communauté technologique. Il est le cofondateur de BlueCat (société dans laquelle Northleaf a participé comme l'un des premiers investisseurs et qui a été acquise par une société d'investissement privée en 2017) et a précédemment cofondé Dyadem (une société de logiciels qui a été vendue à IHS en 2011). Il occupe actuellement le poste de directeur de BlueCat. Michael fait régulièrement des chroniques économiques sur la CBC et est l'hôte de « Unplanned Business », un podcast destiné à aider les petites entreprises. C'est un partenaire fondateur du prestigieux Creative Destruction Lab (CDL) de la Rotman School of Management et il préside la Hyatt Family Foundation orientée sur la santé des femmes, la recherche hospitalière essentielle et le parrainage des minorités défavorisées.
Northleaf est l'un des investisseurs en capital de risque les plus actifs au Canada. Northleaf gère plus de 800 millions de dollars américains d'affectations de capital de risque et d'actions de croissance au nom des investisseurs et a joué un rôle de premier plan dans le développement de nombreux fonds de capital de risque et d'actions de croissance. Depuis 2008, Northleaf effectue des placements directs dans des entreprises later stage et à forte croissance, en exploitant ses relations bien établies avec des gestionnaires de fonds, des investisseurs institutionnels et des entrepreneurs de premier plan.
À propos de Northleaf Capital Partners
Northleaf Capital Partners est une société internationale de placement sur les marchés privés gérant plus de 19 milliards de dollars américains d'affectations en matière de capital-investissement et de capital-risque, de crédit privé et d'infrastructure pour le compte de régimes de retraite publics, d'entreprises et inter-entreprises, de fonds de dotation, de fondations, d'institutions financières et de family offices. L'équipe de Northleaf, qui compte plus de 160 professionnels répartis entre Toronto, Chicago, Londres, Melbourne, Menlo Park, Montréal et New York, est exclusivement dédiée à la recherche, à l'évaluation et à la gestion de placements sur les marchés privés à l'échelle mondiale. Son portefeuille comprend plus de 400 investissements actifs dans 40 pays, en se focalisant sur les entreprises et les actifs du marché intermédiaire. Pour de plus amples informations sur Northleaf, veuillez consulter le site à l'adresse www.northleafcapital.com.

It is with deep sorrow that we share the passing of Petrisa Pecnik, our esteemed Chief Customer Officer. Petrisa's unwavering dedication to our Customer Success organization spanned over a decade, where she instilled a customer-centric approach as the foundation of our team's vision. Her profound impact on our company's culture, prioritizing customer satisfaction above all else, will forever resonate within our organization.
One of Petrisa’s enduring legacies is our Serbian office. As BlueCat grew, more than doubling in revenue over the last 3 years, we needed to expand our Customer Success team to ensure we could continue to support our customers throughout our tremendous growth.
I had the great pleasure of being able to stand, side by side with Petrisa, in Serbia as we celebrated the opening of the office with the Canadian Serbian Embassy and our employees. It meant so much to her and her family to see BlueCat invest in her homeland. The Serbian office began with just 14 people. It has grown now to be 200 strong, thanks to her passion and commitment to the health of our customers. Our customer satisfaction metrics have never been higher.
Petrisa's legacy extends beyond borders, shaping a world-class organization in Toronto and globally. We will continue to support our customers with the same level of care that she showed them each and every day.
In this time of profound loss, we remember Petrisa not only as a dedicated professional but also as a cherished sister, daughter, and Aunt to the Pecnik family. Her absence leaves a void in our hearts, a testament to the impact she had on all who knew her. She was more than a colleague to many of us, she was a loving and caring friend.
As we reflect on Petrisa's life and legacy, let us hold our loved ones close and embrace each day with gratitude and purpose.

Every business owner testing AI independently pays an invisible tax: the cost of redundant experimentation.
They evaluate tools that peers have already vetted. They make mistakes others have already made. They spend weeks discovering what a well-connected room could reveal in minutes.
Conservative estimates suggest solo AI experimentation takes 3–5x longer to produce equivalent outcomes compared to structured peer learning environments. The opportunity cost compounds with every month.
I experienced this firsthand. My first two years of AI implementation were marked by expensive dead ends, overhyped tools, and slow iteration cycles. What ultimately accelerated everything was surrounding myself with peers who were running parallel experiments and sharing results openly.
The AI Business Lab® Mastermind was built to eliminate this experimentation tax. Twelve to fourteen established business owners, each testing different tools across different business functions, sharing wins and failures in real time.
Three annual in-person intensives in Nashville. Monthly virtual sessions. Continuous collaboration via private Slack. The result: implementation timelines compressed from years to months.
A few spots remain for business owners generating $1M+ annually.

Your 2026 AI budget is being spent on the wrong work.
Gartner: 40%+ of agentic AI projects canceled by 2027.
Composio: 88% fail before production.
MIT Sloan: 8% success rate at scale.
Three walls everyone is hitting:
Scale. One agent cannot maintain thousands of repos. You need systems of specialized agents.
Accuracy. Nondeterministic outputs compound. A 2% hallucination rate in a demo is catastrophic across thousands of PRs.
Cost. Agents burn millions of tokens rebuilding context on every call, grepping code they grepped yesterday, reasoning through mechanical work a program could execute in seconds.
The winners in 2026 will not have the biggest budgets. They will have programs instead of prompts for work that never needed a reasoning model, and pre-resolved context so agents stop paying retail to rediscover the same facts.
If you need proof the bill comes due fast: Uber's CTO admitted they are back to the drawing board after burning through their AI budget, despite $3.4B in R&D.

Pasar al contenido principal
Michael Hyatt recently sold his company BlueCat Networks Inc. to Madison Dearborn Partners LLC for approximately $400-million.
To most of his followers, Michael Hyatt is a business expert, investor, and a dragon on CBC’s Dragons Den (Next Gen Den) and weekly business commentator on CBC news. However, there is more to this man than his incredible accolades and achievements. Despite only spending just around two hours with him, I was able to pick up on a few lessons that he was trying to convey to me not only through words but his actions. So not only would I like to share my experience meeting him, but also the lessons I learnt while we walked down Bloor Street in Toronto a few months ago.
Four months ago, I reached out to Michael introducing myself as a young entrepreneur that wanted to learn more about how he became successful. Given how successful he is, it was no surprise to me that he didn’t reply immediately. However, Michael eventually did reply a month later when I sent him a follow-up message. We tried setting up times to meet for about a week and then finally, we decided on November 7, 2016, at 3:15PM outside the Jack Astors. We both arrived on time, and when we met, Michael immediately led with a kind compliment that broke the ice. We decided to go for a walk to various places with his very opinionated dog (9 year old Chihuahua named Chiquita). We first went to a second hand game store, where Michael gave me his first lesson: money has no value compared to relationships. Michael, despite being a wealthy, successful man lived below his means, and spoke passionately about his network. He said he meticulously picks who he wants to associate with, and constantly reflects on the relationships he has made. He wants to be strategic that he is not affiliated to someone who is harming his brand inadvertently. Also, he spoke highly of valuing friends and family above the prospect of making more money. That being said, Michael values money but he believes you can make more if you spend time around people who will challenge you to think harder, and if you constantly give back to your network. My experience with him at the games store proved this. He had a nine year relationship with the store owner, and he was able to get a better discount for a game he wanted. This isn’t to say that Michael only strikes relationships with others to get things in return (it’s quite the opposite actually), but he does believe that one can live a happier and more fruitful life by caring more about others.
As we were walking down Bloor Street and about to enter a high end clothing and accessories store, Michael told me something I won’t forget. He told me he believed he was a 20-year overnight success. This especially resonated with me as it’s aligned with a lesson I have learnt from other notable entrepreneurs like Gary Vaynerchuk. Michael like Gary believe that there is no shortcut to success and that the road to success is determined by the level of hardwork and patience a person puts in. Michael also believes that most people when they view success underestimate how much they can do in the long term and overestimate how much they can do in the short term. His advice for making money is to work hard in an occupation you are passionate about, and while you are doing that, invest resources into passive income streams because within ten to twenty years, the dividend drip will be substantial.
After exiting the clothing store due to our inability to get any discounts or holiday deals, Michael and I continued down Bloor Street and we went to a store selling cashmere. It was definitely an expensive store, and we ended up not buying anything, but Michael gave me an insight on his view on money and its utility on the way there. He told me his love was investing in deals (making cash flow), and that beyond that, he viewed money as not necessarily needed for happiness. He wants to have enough money that he does not have to be concerned about money (ie. paying bills). Michael alluded to his childhood and his experience growing up not wealthy as a contributing factor in shaping his mentality.
Michael and I left the cashmere store after spending about five minutes in there. We began to head to Michael’s house, and this part of our walk is probably the most useful advice I have been given; partly because it was aimed at millennials like myself. I asked Michael what he thought about young people like myself believing that sleep needs to be sacrificed in order to become successful. Michael rejected the claim immediately on face value and said that the three aspects of life that he continuously prioritizes are diet, sleep, and exercise. He continued this discussion by pointing out that millennials tend to put too much pressure on themselves to become successful at a very early age. He stated that many people in my generation tend to have an expectation of becoming like Mark Zuckerberg; a 20 year old billionaire that owns a tech company and philanthropic initiatives. I added to this discussion by discussing depression among young CEOs and how over time it’s only gotten worse. Michael believes that if you are 30 years old, that is actually a young age to become a millionaire at.
At Michael’s house, I realized why I wanted to write this article. I picked up on a few lessons along the way, but the biggest lesson was in front of me: Michael himself. Michael truly walks his talk (no pun intended), and his optimistic and long-sighted view towards business is undoubtedly one of the biggest reasons for his growing success. If someone wants to learn how to be a perfect millionaire, learn from Michael. He is humble, excited to give back to his community, and thus, lives a fulfilling life. Today, I am proud to call him my mentor and if you think he’s done after his recent deal, think twice. He loves the process and the game too much, just like any true entrepreneur.
“The rich stay rich because they live like they’re poor, the poor stay poor because they live like they’re rich.” – Anonymous

Two years from now, the most consequential platforms in AI will not be the foundation models.
They will be the orchestration layers that coordinate Agents into operations.
Hermes Agent from Nous Research spawns and coordinates specialist agents from a single hierarchy. Paperclip wraps your agents in an org chart with budgets, goals, and approval gates. Neither is finished. Both are public signals that Level 5 of the AI Ascension Model is forming as we speak.
Level 5 is the Orchestrator. The maturity stage where multiple Agents are sequenced toward a larger goal. The owner is no longer running tasks or managing Agents. They are choosing what gets built.
Salesforce’s 2026 Connectivity Report shows the average organization now deploys twelve AI agents, with deployment projected to surge sixty-seven percent in two years. Twelve agents do not coordinate themselves.
The companies that build orchestration capability first will operate at a structural advantage. They will deploy new functions with weeks of latency, not quarters. They will reshape their cost base without proportional headcount. They will scale the operation without scaling the leadership team.
This is the most architecturally demanding move on the curve. It asks you to treat the business as a system, not a job. And it sets up Level 6. The only level no one can outsource, where the human sets the mission and AI runs the operation. The boards and leadership teams that name this climb now will set the architectural standards their industries are still arguing about in 2028.

Architecting to Win the Agent Age
This morning, DigiLive Events had the pleasure of organising an executive virtual roundtable that brought together senior technology, AI, data, and transformation leaders to discuss: "How do we successfully govern, orchestrate, and scale AI agents across an increasingly complex enterprise ecosystem?"
As organisations move beyond experimentation and into deployment, the conversation has shifted from simply adopting AI to creating the architecture, governance, and operational foundations required to deliver measurable business value.
Key Discussion Points
🔹 Multi-Agent Orchestration is the Next Challenge
Many organisations already have AI agents in production, but the next stage of maturity requires agents, applications, and systems to communicate and collaborate seamlessly across business processes. Success depends on combining rules-based orchestration with more adaptive approaches that can operate effectively in increasingly complex environments.
🔹 Shadow AI Requires Balance, Not Just Control
As AI adoption accelerates, organisations must strike the right balance between innovation and governance. Creating safe environments for experimentation, supported by appropriate oversight, security, compliance, and cross-functional collaboration, is becoming essential for sustainable growth.
🔹 Cost Management Must Be Built In From Day One
The true cost of AI often emerges at scale rather than during pilot programmes. Visibility into spending, strong governance, optimisation strategies, and clear business cases are critical to ensuring AI investments deliver long-term value.
🔹 Data Readiness Remains the Foundation
The effectiveness of AI is directly linked to the quality, accessibility, and reliability of the underlying data. Connected and trusted data enables better decision-making, more accurate outputs, and stronger business outcomes.
🔹 Business Outcomes Must Lead Technology Decisions
The most successful AI initiatives begin with clearly defined business objectives rather than technology adoption alone. Establishing measurable success criteria, expected outcomes, and ROI from the outset creates a stronger foundation for long-term success.
The Agent Age is no longer a future concept; it's already here.
However, successful AI adoption isn't simply about deploying more agents. It's about creating the governance, architecture, integration, and operational frameworks that allow organisations to scale AI responsibly and effectively.
The organisations seeing the greatest success are those treating AI as a business transformation initiative rather than a technology project.
A huge thank you to everyone who joined the discussion.

ChatGPT is a calculator. A custom AI solution is a calculator built into your specific workflow, connected to your data, and configured to do exactly one job really well.
People often think they're the same thing.
They're not.
ChatGPT is a general-purpose tool. It's impressive, it's useful, and for a lot of tasks it's genuinely good enough. I use it myself.
But when a client tells me they tried AI and it didn't stick, nine times out of ten they were using a general tool and expecting specific results.
Here's the gap:
ChatGPT doesn't know your service offerings. It doesn't know how you qualify leads. It doesn't know that you always follow up on day three, or that certain clients need a softer touch.
A custom solution does. Because you built it that way.
That could mean a trained assistant that drafts responses in your voice. A workflow that pulls from your own client data. An intake form that automatically categorizes and routes inquiries without you touching it.
The difference isn't the AI. It's the fit.
Off-the-shelf tools are a starting point. Custom builds are where they start paying for themselves.
If you've played around with ChatGPT and thought "this is fine but not quite right for what I do" -- that instinct is correct. That gap is exactly what I help close.
What's a task in your business you'd want AI to handle if it actually understood your context?

On November 30, 2022, ChatGPT launched and the conversation about Artificial Intelligence moved from research labs and tech conferences into every boardroom, break room, and LinkedIn feed on the planet.

The hard things were never the 'what' of business — they were always the 'how'. Sifting through contracts and documents to find what matters. Drafting proposals, emails, and follow-ups that actually get read. Capturing the knowledge that lives in one person's head and making it available to the whole team. Responding to customers and prospects quickly enough that they don't move on.
These tasks didn't disappear. But the effort required to handle them well has dropped considerably.
We're seeing it firsthand. Businesses we work with — sales organizations, operations teams, and growing mid-market companies — are beginning to explore where AI fits, not as a transformation initiative, but as a practical question: where are we spending time and attention on things a well-designed Generative AI system could handle?
That's the right question. Not "how do we become an AI company" — but "where is the friction, and do better tools now exist to reduce it?"
For most businesses, better tools do exist. The work is in knowing where to look.

ChatGPT might already be recommending your business, and still getting your offer wrong.
I saw an agency get inbound leads because ChatGPT mentioned them by name.
Sounds great, until you hear what happened next.
The model was recommending them for legacy software setups, not for the AI service they actually wanted to sell.
Why?
Because AI does not read between the lines.
It looks for:
- Explicit entity signals.
- Clear statements.
- Repeated language.
- Structured context.
So if your website hints at your core offer, but an old blog post explains an older service more clearly, AI can pitch the old service instead.
That is the risk most companies miss.
They assume their positioning is obvious because it is obvious to them.
- But AI is not reading intent.
- It is matching the clearest signal it can find.
If your primary offer is not stated plainly in the first 200 words of every important page, you are leaving your positioning up to the model.
And models are very confident guessers.
My view:
- This is one of the simplest AI visibility fixes a B2B company can make, and one of the most ignored.

Your business isn't AI-powered just because you use ChatGPT.
That's a tool. Not a system.
Real estate development demands systemized decision-making. Especially with AI.
Here's the "AI-Accelerated Go/No-Go Screen."
It's a 3-step framework to get clarity on any deal in under 2 hours.
It's not about complex models. It's about rapid, disciplined evaluation.
Step 1: Hard Constraints Sweep (30 min)
Zoning, environmental, utility access, easements. The absolute deal breakers.
If one fails, you kill it. No emotion.
Step 2: Market Reality Check (45 min)
Local comps, absorption rates, demographic shifts. Is there *actual* demand for your product?
This isn't about what you *hope* the market will do. It's about what it *is* doing.
Step 3: Quick Financial Screen (45 min)
Back-of-napkin proforma. Revenue potential vs. all-in costs.
**If the initial DCR or profit margin doesn't scream "YES," it's a "NO."**
This isn't about finding a reason to say yes. It's about finding reasons to say no, fast.

This screen gives you the conviction to kill bad deals or pivot to a viable strategy.
