The AI tool marketplace has a signal-to-noise problem.
Thousands of products. Every vendor claiming transformative results. Marketing optimized for urgency rather than accuracy. For a busy CEO without a technical evaluation team, distinguishing genuine capability from sophisticated marketing is nearly impossible.
The most reliable filter isn’t product reviews or analyst reports. It’s peer testing in comparable business contexts.
The AI Business Lab® Mastermind functions as exactly this kind of filter. When a member discovers a tool that genuinely delivers, the entire group knows within days. When something proves overhyped, that intelligence spreads equally fast—before others waste time and budget.
Over twelve months, a mastermind of 12–14 members evaluates more tools across more business functions than any individual could in three years. The collective evaluation creates an intelligence advantage that compounds over time.
For business owners who can’t afford to evaluate every AI tool independently—which is every business owner—this peer filter may be the mastermind’s most immediately practical benefit.

Quiet but significant news for every local business: the dominant search platform has built its AI directly into business listings. It now drafts the answers customers get: pulling from your profile, your site, and your reviews, and the stated direction is an assistant that acts “on your behalf.”
On its face, it’s a time-saver, and plenty of owners will welcome it. But look at what’s actually happening. When a customer reaches out to a local business now, the thing that answers is increasingly not the business. It’s a model trained to sound like it.
Here’s why that matters more for local than for anyone else. A chain has nothing to lose from an automated voice since it never had a human one. But a great local place is made of its voice: the owner who remembers your order, the specific, slightly weird personality that made it yours in the first place. Smooth that into a competent AI reply and you’ve quietly deleted the exact thing that made it worth choosing.
The trend is clear: platforms are inserting themselves deeper into the space between a business and its customers, and calling it convenience. We think that space is sacred. It’s where a business becomes a place people love.
We’re building the opposite — discovery that connects people to a local business, not to a layer standing in front of it.

Will AI kill certain businesses?
The honest answer is that nobody truly knows everything AI will change six months, one year, or five years from now.
But Dan’s message helped me realize that we may be asking the wrong question.
Instead of asking, “What is AI going to do to my business?” we should ask:
“What is the one thing my business depends on so heavily that, if it disappeared tomorrow, I would be in serious trouble?”
It could be:
• One client producing most of the revenue
• One employee who knows how everything operates
• One platform generating nearly all the leads
• One product or service paying the bills
• One business owner trying to manage everything alone
That is a single point of failure.
AI did not create that weakness. It is simply causing business owners to recognize it.
The answer is not to panic or chase every new AI tool. The answer is to strengthen the business.
First, identify what your business cannot afford to lose.
Then, create another way.
If one platform brings your leads, begin developing a second channel.
If only one person understands the operations, document the process and train someone else.
If one service produces all the revenue, develop another offer that solves a related problem.
If you are doing everything alone, begin building systems and using the right technology to support you.
We do not need to predict the future perfectly. We need to build businesses strong enough to operate through more than one possible future.
This is part of what I want to help business owners accomplish through Superb Living LLC: identify the gaps, strengthen their systems, and use AI with purpose—not because it is popular, but because it can help create a business that does not depend on one person doing everything.

What is the one thing that, if it disappeared on Monday morning, would put your business in trouble?

Northleaf Announces Appointment of Technology Entrepreneur Michael Hyatt as a Senior Advisor to Its Venture Capital and Growth Equity Program
January 27, 2022
Source: Businesswire
TORONTO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Northleaf Capital Partners (“Northleaf”), a global private markets investment firm, is pleased to announce the appointment of Michael Hyatt as a Senior Advisor supporting Northleaf’s venture capital and growth equity investment program. Michael will work alongside the Northleaf private equity and venture capital team to source and evaluate investment opportunities. As a serial entrepreneur and active investor, Michael’s knowledge and expertise in the venture capital space complements Northleaf’s longstanding investment approach.
"We are excited to welcome Michael to Northleaf as a Senior Advisor,” said Ian Carew, Managing Director & Venture Partner at Northleaf. “We have invested successfully with Michael in the past and our venture capital and growth equity program will benefit from his deep knowledge and experience and accomplished track record as both an entrepreneur and investor.”
“I am thrilled to act as a Senior Advisor to Northleaf’s successful venture capital and growth equity program and look forward to working with Ian and the team,” said Michael Hyatt. “I’ve had the opportunity to see the Northleaf strategy at work over the years and I’m excited to collaborate with the team on future investments for the program.”
Michael Hyatt is recognized as one of Canada’s leading tech entrepreneurs and an active investor in the technology community. He is the co-founder of BlueCat (in which Northleaf was an early investor and which was acquired by a private equity firm in 2017) and previously co-founded Dyadem (a software company that was sold to IHS in 2011). He currently serves as a Director of BlueCat. Michael is a regular business commentator on the CBC and the host of “Unplanned Business,” a podcast to help small businesses. He is a Founding Partner at the Rotman School of Management’s prestigious Creative Destruction Lab (CDL) and chairs the Hyatt Family Foundation focused on women’s health, critical hospital research and sponsorship of underprivileged minorities.
Northleaf is one of Canada’s most active venture capital investors. Northleaf manages more than US$800 million in venture capital and growth equity commitments on behalf of investors and has played a leadership role in the development of many successful venture capital / growth equity funds. Northleaf has been making direct investments in later-stage and high growth companies since 2008, leveraging its well-established relationships with leading fund managers, institutional investors and entrepreneurs.
About Northleaf Capital Partners
Northleaf Capital Partners is a global private markets investment firm with more than US$19 billion in private equity and venture capital, private credit and infrastructure commitments under management on behalf of public, corporate and multi-employer pension plans, endowments, foundations, financial institutions and family offices. Northleaf’s team of more than 160 professionals, located in Toronto, Chicago, London, Melbourne, Menlo Park, Montreal and New York, is focused exclusively on sourcing, evaluating and managing private markets investments globally. Its portfolio includes over 400 active investments in 40 countries, with a focus on mid-market companies and assets. For more information on Northleaf, please visit www.northleafcapital.com.

For the AI economy to thrive, the return on investment (ROI) often takes a backseat.
The tech industry excels at developing technology, but it truly shines in marketing it. Here’s a snapshot of the current AI economy:

Tech vendors benefit from subscription revenue. Startups gain valuation from pilot projects that often don’t reach production. Consulting firms earn advisory fees. Public companies see stock increases from announcements about "leveraging AI." Careers are built on the momentum of this trend.
The one group left with uncertain returns? The enterprise customers footing the bill.

Posted: October 28, 2020
Tune in to Mount Saint Vincent University’s Business & Tourism Department’s new (virtual) Fireside Chats series to hear personal stories, perspectives and interesting anecdotes from top business and tourism leaders.
The next event in the series is coming up at 12 p.m. AT on Tuesday, November 3, 2020 and will feature entrepreneur, mentor and investor Michael Hyatt.
The event will be broadcast live on Zoom. Advance registration is required; anyone interested in taking part can register here. Questions can be submitted to business@msvu.ca in advance for inclusion in the conversation.
About Michael Hyatt
“A self-made millionaire by age 25, Michael is a mentor and investor in many start-ups, including the Rotman School of Business Creative Destruction Lab and The Founders Institute. He has built two highly successful tech firms valued at hundreds of millions of dollars, and is a recipient of the Top 40 Under 40™ award. He chairs his family’s charitable foundation, and is the executive chair of BlueCat, one of Canada’s leading growth companies. Michael is a weekly business commentator on CBC News.” (Source: CBC)
At the fireside chat on November 3, Michael will provide his perspective on the entrepreneurial ecosystem in Canada and how we can be better positioned for growth.
About the Fireside Chats Series
Launched in September 2020, the Fireside Chats series features online addresses by high-profile entrepreneurs, managers, government officials and CEOs working in business and tourism in Canada. Presented by MSVU’s Business Administration and Tourism & Hospitality Management Department, the webinars are open to all and also designed to provide exceptional additional learning opportunity for MSVU Business & Tourism students.
The series will continue in 2021 with several excellent speakers lined-up, including Christine Halef, President of AtlantiCann Medical, a cannabis producer based in Nova Scotia. Stay tuned for updates

I want to tell you something I wish someone had told me twenty years ago.
The higher you climb as a leader, the fewer people you can talk to honestly.
Your team looks to you for certainty. Your spouse wants you to leave work at the door. Your friends don’t fully understand the weight of making payroll every two weeks.
So you end up making the biggest decisions of your career—the ones that affect your family, your team, your future—essentially alone.
I know because I’ve lived it. As CEO of Thomas Nelson Publishers, I had 700 employees depending on me and exactly zero peers I could be fully transparent with.
That isolation cost me. In time, money, relationships, and nearly my health.
Here’s what changed everything: I found a small group of leaders who were playing at my level, facing similar challenges, and willing to be radically honest.
That’s exactly what I’ve built with the AI Business Lab Mastermind—a brain trust of established business owners implementing AI together. Real conversations. Real solutions. Real results.
We have just a few spots remaining. If you’re running a $1M+ business and tired of navigating this alone, I’d love to hear from you.

Building Custom Software Without Coding Expertise
This title was summarized by AI from the post below.
Michael Hyatt
7mo
Report this post
Three years ago, my team spent over $1 million and a full year trying to build a Full Focus app. After 12 months of iteration with an outside development team, we pulled the plug.
It just wasn't worth it.
But here's what haunts me: With the AI coding tools available today, I literally could have built that app myself in 1-2 weeks. Maybe 40 hours of my time and a few hundred dollars.
That's not an exaggeration. That's the reality of what's now possible with vibe coding.
If you're a business leader with specialized expertise you want to monetize through software, you're probably facing the same challenge we did: You have the vision and the knowledge, but you lack the coding skills or the budget to execute.
The barrier to building custom software isn't technical anymore—it's psychological.
According to recent research, 80% of companies now offer AI-enabled products or features. The no-code market is projected to reach $187 billion by 2030. And 70% of new enterprise applications in 2025 use low-code or no-code technologies, up from less than 25% in 2020.
Here's what this means for you: Your domain expertise can now be packaged as software that works 24/7, without requiring a development team or a six-figure budget.
I've personally built three full-stack applications using AI tools. One is Promptlee—a prompt management tool I use daily and couldn't work without.
The question isn't whether this is possible. The question is: what will you build first?

Architecture is the only moat. If you don't understand the underlying systems, you aren't an architect, you're just an intern supervising an AI that’s hallucinating your business logic.
Build for the shadows. The real winners aren't building pretty destinations; they’re building the reliable, headless infrastructure that agents actually call.
If you think you can "vibe-check" your way to a working startup without understanding the plumbing, you’re just building a faster way to fail.

On today’s Tank Talk! We welcome our guest Michael Hyatt, Co-Founder of Hyatt Family Office.
Michael is well known in the Canadian tech ecosystem as a serial entrepreneur turned angel investor and is regularly seen on TV providing his advice to aspiring entrepreneurs. Before Michael started his first company, he was President & CEO at Dyadem which sold to IHS a US public company in 2011. Michael went on to co-found BlueCat Networks with his brother and eventually sold the business to private equity firm Madison Dearborn for a reported $400mm in 2017
On today's Talk, we ask Michael about his family office and their focus on wealth preservation vs wealth creation during the crisis. We also talk to Michael about his operator first approach to investing and what he looks for when backing early-stage founders or fund managers.

AI is dismantling the traditional leadership pyramid - and creating capacity at scale.
For decades, organizations were built on layers:
Analysts → Managers → Directors → MDs → Executives.
AI is collapsing that chain.
What once required multiple reporting lines, status meetings, management checkpoints, and manual reporting cycles can now be coordinated, synthesized, and escalated in real time.
The consequence is clear:
fewer layers, faster decisions, greater accountability.
But the real leadership question is this:
What do organizations do with the capacity AI creates?
This is where the winners will separate themselves.
The capacity released from repetitive coordination, reporting, and manual oversight should not sit idle.
It must be repurposed.
Efficiency without redeployment is wasted enterprise value.
Repurposed into:
• faster client response and revenue generation
• deeper innovation and product development
• stronger risk and control environments
• sharper customer experience execution
• more strategic leadership bandwidth
In simple terms:
do more in less time, with greater precision.
Projects that took 12 weeks should now take 4.
Board decisions that took a month should now move in days.
Leadership teams should spend less time managing process and more time driving outcomes.
This is no longer an IT transformation.
It is an organizational productivity and growth agenda.
AI is not just flattening the pyramid.
It is giving organizations the ability to redeploy talent toward higher-value work at scale.
The real question for boards is no longer whether AI creates efficiency.
It is whether leadership can convert efficiency into growth.
That is where competitive advantage will be built.
How is your organization redeploying the capacity AI is creating?

Every executive I meet tells me the same thing. They’re being sold “AI ROI” on the back of better models. Behind closed doors, they admit it’s not the model they worry about. It’s whether they trust the data that feeds it.
I’ve seen projects come to a halt because leaders felt uneasy with answer quality. Sometimes the numbers looked off. Sometimes the story didn’t match experience. Rarely was the problem the model – it was data coming from too many places, with no common rules or reliable history.
This trust gap slows everything. I’ve watched teams spend twice as long building proofs of concept because no one agrees on which figures are real. I’ve seen steering committees go silent when an AI-generated insight doesn’t align with the business’s lived reality.
The winning projects always shared one trait: disciplined, visible data lineage. Someone owned the source. Someone checked what went in. Teams stopped arguing when everyone could see exactly where the numbers came from, and why they moved.
Before you expand your AI rollout, ask yourself: If five senior leaders challenged an AI result tomorrow, would your team have the data trail to answer them?
**How much trust does your data process deserve today?**
Agree? Share your take.

The founder's office is one of the biggest beneficiaries of AI right now.
In a typical week, someone in this role used to spend significant time on research. Competitive analysis. Building briefing documents. Summarising what different stakeholders had said over the last month before a big decision.
AI handles all of that in a fraction of the time.
What it cannot handle is the things that actually make someone in this role valuable. Knowing which way the wind is blowing before anyone else does. Understanding the dynamics between two leaders who are technically aligned but actually in tension. Recognising when the founder needs to hear something uncomfortable and choosing the right moment to say it.
The information layer is faster now. The relationship and judgment layer has not changed.
The risk is that people in this seat spend the time AI freed up on more information gathering rather than more judgment. More decks rather than more conversations. More outputs rather than more presence.
AI gave the founder's office more leverage. How you spend that leverage is still the job.

At 1ArtificialIntelligence, Sonita Lontoh, Partner at Alpha and Board Member of Sunrun and TrueBlue, joins Glenn Tyranski, Partner at 1BusinessWorld, for Boards and AI: Balancing Risks and Opportunities for Long-term Value Creation, a presentation and conversation focused on one of the most consequential governance questions facing business today. The session examines how boards can approach artificial intelligence not only through the lens of risk, but through a broader and more strategic understanding of value creation, organizational readiness, and long-term competitiveness.
Lontoh brings a clear boardroom perspective to the conversation. She emphasizes that companies are at very different stages in their AI journeys, and that no single framework fits every organization. What distinguishes the stronger approaches, she argues, is a high level of intentionality around AI ambition, a disciplined focus on the use cases that are most material to the business, and a commitment to integrating AI into business strategy rather than treating it as a siloed technology initiative. She also outlines the three dimensions boards should oversee closely, value creation, organizational readiness, and risk mitigation with ethical alignment, while highlighting the need for governance structures, committee design, and incentives that reflect the growing strategic weight of AI.
Lontoh makes clear that effective board oversight in the age of AI requires more than caution. It requires the ability to ask sharper questions, shape stronger governance, and help organizations pursue innovation with both ambition and responsibility. Boards that do that well will be better positioned to guide companies toward stronger resilience, stronger competitiveness, and stronger long-term value creation.

1KHO 797: Win at Work and Life | Michael Hyatt, Free to Focus
From The 1000 Hours Outside Podcast
Episode Description
He built a wildly successful career and nearly lost everything that mattered most along the way. In this powerful conversation, Michael Hyatt shares the moment his wife told him she felt like a single mom, the wake-up call that changed everything, and the framework he’s spent decades refining to help people succeed without sacrificing their health, their families, or their souls. From the “rule of 50” to time boundaries, from the myth of having enough hours to the truth about what actually moves life forward, this episode is full of hard-won wisdom and practical shifts you can start today. It’s about reclaiming your time, remembering your why, and building a life where your best energy goes to the people who matter most.
Check out all that Michael has to offer at https://fullfocus.co/

Yeah. And so the first one is on productivity. The second one is on goal achievement. And by the way, I make a difference between goal setting and goal achievement because it's one thing to set goals. It's another thing to achieve your goals. And so I'm all about the achievement of the goals. So Joel Miller, who is married to my oldest daughter, Megan, who's the CEO of Full Focus. He's our chief content officer. It's really designed to help people get greater productivity so that they can really do less of what they don't want to do and more of what they do best so that they create margin

for those other eight domains of life. Yeah. And all the things that you mentioned. Yeah. So you told me this story last time, and I hope that you're OK to share it again because nobody heard it. It disappeared into the wind. But I am super impressed with Thomas Nelson. I think it's a really cool book publisher. And I love how their books are always in the store and several of my friends have published with them. And so I always think they're like the premier. When I talk in my friend circles with people who have published books, I'm always like, oh, we talk about Thomas Nelson.

And I learned through reading All About You that you were the CEO of Thomas Nelson Publishers, but you started off where they gave you this division that's like sinking. It's like a sinking ship. It's doing the worst of all because a publisher will have all these different divisions. They give you this one. It's doing the worst. They're actually losing money. And they put you in this position like, can you turn this around?
00:07:23
So can you talk about that story about what you did and then the response from your wife? Sure. Okay. So that's kind of become a signature story because it was such a defining moment for me. But I was initially flattered that they asked me to take over this division as a general manager. And at the time, Thomas Nelson had 14 different book publishing divisions. We had a children's book division. We had a Bible publishing division. We had gift books. We had all different kinds of books.

And so the CEO said to me, he said, how long do you think this will take to turn this around? Well, I never turned around anything. You know, I had never done anything like this. Interview: Michael Hyatt | Ivey Business Review
0
Interview: Michael Hyatt
Interview
Dec 31
Written By Ivey Business Review
The Ivey Business Review is a student publication conceived, designed and managed by Honors Business Administration students at the Ivey Business School.
IBR: Your transition into entrepreneurship came after four years of studying science at Western University. What motivated you to make such a bold decision?
MH: I did a four-year Biochemistry degree at Western and I remember giving my fourth-year thesis presentation to my professors. At the end of it, they looked at me, stunned, and said, “Mr. Hyatt, you should go sell cars.” I realized at that point that continuing with sciences just wasn’t for me. More than that, it was a recession, so getting a job wasn’t going to be easy.
My motivation was simple — I just wanted to have my own money, my own independence. I wanted to make it in life. There was no technology community at that time, or proven methodologies on how to create a start-up. Entrepreneurship was a journey that wasn’t well accepted as a career path. I thought that if I could remotely make it as an entrepreneur, that would be more meaningful to me than working a day job.
IBR: How do you think university plays a role in the development of an entrepreneur?
MH: I think the most important thing about university is that it’s the first time in your life where you have to live on your own and make something of yourself. You learn to build relationships with other students and professors, run on a schedule, and deliver on time. I don’t believe that specific majors matter as much as the university experience at large. For many, it’s the first time you’re really an adult.
When I went to school from 1992-96, there was no Internet. From an information perspective, there was almost a bubble around the campus, and you lived in this bubble. This relative isolation prepares you because it’s your first time away from you parents. But the real world is tougher. In the real world— you sleep in, you get fired. You don’t deliver, you get fired. There’s no makeup exam in the real world. It’s just not as protected. University’s a great stepping stone, but not entirely reflective of reality.
IBR: Was there a time when you thought that you might lose it all? If so, was there anything that kept you going?
MH: There are so many times in business when things go bad. Your ability to absorb a punch is very important. When you watch the best poker players in the world, you’ll notice that they don’t get too excited when they win, but they also don’t get too disappointed when they lose. In business, you sometimes have to divorce emotion from what’s happening and just stick to the facts.
There is no problem I haven’t overcome because I’m still here and the business is still growing. However, I’d be lying to say that we haven’t had tremendous challenges over the years. That’s part of it. You get a company the size of BlueCat and you’ll realize there are not many software companies like us in Canada. That’s because it’s that hard to get here.
IBR: IHS Markit acquired your first business Dyadem in 2011. Not many people get to say that they were able to scale up a company and subsequently sell it. How did you feel about this whole experience?
MH: I felt great. I felt it was the right time. It was a terrific business, and it allowed me to build an even bigger business called BlueCat. It felt great to be able to share successes with the employees, investors, and management team that supported me throughout this journey. We were able to collectively share the returns of this sale, and that meant a lot to me.
I think there’s a misconception that entrepreneurs should stay with their businesses at all costs. Sometimes you run your course in your business and then transact it. Then, you’re enabled to start something new. That’s a very natural and even important process, because sometimes someone can take your business and move it to a place better than you can yourself. Taking some profit for yourself and leaving some profit for the next person isn’t a bad thing.
IBR: Do you think that interdependence is important in the business world?
MH: It takes a village to build a company. BlueCat, as good as it is, is not solely the product of mine and Richard Hyatt’s goals. If you look at BlueCat today, you’d say that Michael and Richard founded something wonderful, but that’s not entirely true. You’d have to acknowledge the tremendous efforts made by the current executive team that took BlueCat to the next level. I’m also very grateful for the efforts of our employees – many outwork me, which is humbling.
Another example of this dependence is when I decided to hire an external CEO to run my first company, Dyadem. I left it to him to decide what’s best for the company, and in the end, he decided that selling it was the best path.
Often times, it becomes difficult when the outgoing and current CEO have differing opinions. But, good leaders understand that when you hire others, you have to trust them to be effective. At the time, I was already building BlueCat with my brother, so I wasn’t operationally involved in Dyadem. In the end, I trusted his decision to sell and it was a fantastic move for the company. He was right.
IBR: What are some key changes you expect to see in the technology industry in the near future?
MH: We’re living in a world where exponential change is the soup du jour. I expect there to be radical change in just about everything simply because Moore’s law still applies. Computing power is still doubling every 18 months and getting a lot cheaper. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is stepping up for the first time. AI is moving from narrow intelligence towards something more general.
Our future is changing exponentially due to rapid innovation in computing power. The average person thinks that we’re seven to 10 years away from having autonomous cars. But we’re not. We’re actually a few years away, since technology is moving exponentially and not in a linear fashion. As Ray Kurzweil at Google says, and I’m paraphrasing, we think our future is like our linear past – and it’s not.
Rapid innovation will also bring about the ability to make smarter decisions. We are going to add billions of people to the Internet for the first time in the near future. There are going to be hundreds of billions of connected devices all doing something for us. This creates a tremendous amount of data, all of which will go to engines that will carve out logic and decision-making effectiveness from the vast data pool.
The core message here is that our lives are going to get much better. We’re going to get healthier, we’re going to live longer, things are going to cost a lot less. For example, if I start making trucks autonomously driven, it’s going to make things a lot cheaper, and that passes on to you, the consumer. That’s a small example, but the supply chain is going to get dramatically cheaper. The same applies to the energy needed to transport those goods. Life is going to get a lot cheaper as we bring in more intelligence. Your children are going to be doing jobs that you can’t imagine today – we simply do not know maybe even understand their job titles – yet.
I truly believe that the future is amazing, and that will be due to technology. I am very much an optimist about humankind. It’s going to be shockingly different. In 1912, we’d look at the Titanic and say that’s the world’s biggest ship, no one could ever build a ship bigger than that. That’s simply wrong, because the average cruise ship today is many times that size, but in 1912 you couldn’t have imagined it.
We have a hard time imagining the exponential future. But it’s always happened that way. You can imagine technology as evolving in an S curve. You will see innovation plateau as you reach top of the S. Then, something radical is developed and suddenly you’re on top of another S curve that you did not know existed. We’re about to undergo that massive shift in terms of AI and leveraging data through the Internet of Things. The future will be an exciting time.
IBR: There are many Ivey students who wish to start a business one day. What advice would you give them? What are some of the ways that they can better prepare for the world of entrepreneurship?
MH: First off, my most important piece of advice is to slow down and don’t feel pressured. I feel bad for this generation because there’s a tremendous and undue amount of pressure that the youth feels. You must have a very successful business by age 19 and maybe a non-profit on the side. I don’t even know how they do it. What’s funny, is that if you look at the most successful people in the world like Mark Zuckerberg, Bill Gates, and Elon Musk, they don’t get up every day to do all those things. They do one thing very well. Mark Zuckerberg clearly does one thing well — Facebook. For a very long time, Bill Gates did one thing well — Microsoft. The same goes for Elon Musk and Tesla.
The pressure that I see young students put on themselves to be successful by doing multiple things as early as possible is a recipe for disaster. I think they need to slow down, finish their education, and work at a company for a couple of years. This way, they would meet people and make relationships.
Eventually, they’ll find a real problem they want to solve. Once they find that problem, then they should start their own business.
My second piece of advice is that the most important thing you can do right now is spend an enormous amount of time building relationships. You are worth as much as your relationships. You should give, you should donate, you should push, you should console, you should get involved with your relationships. You should pay for lunch, pay for coffee, connect people, give into your relationships. Invest time and money into the people you want to spend time with. That is the most important thing you can do when you’re young.
IBR: How do you personally define success, in your personal careers and the entrepreneurial ventures you have taken part in?
MH: I think success should have very individual definitions based on the person you ask this question to. Money is only one dimension. I was a millionaire by 25, I lived in Richmond Hill, I had my own house, but I was unhappy. For a long time, I couldn’t find my way out of this unhappiness. Money doesn’t buy you happiness, but it does make life a lot easier. Money helps you out tremendously, but only in some respects.
Here’s my advice: make money, but don’t value it. The minute you start placing substantial value on accumulating money, you’re in the wrong place psychologically. Success shouldn’t be about the money you gain, but the problems you’re able to solve and the personal goals you’re able to achieve.
IBR: Being involved with both the Next Gen Den, and Rotman’s Creative Destruction Lab, it seems like you judge a lot of promising ventures. What do you typically look for in a venture that you’ve typically seen results and success?
MH: I look for people who I can work with. Typically, that comes down to finding the entrepreneurs who have ambition, but also flexibility. Most of the time, the company that they’re starting out with is not going to be the company they’re ending with. All I’m doing is looking very carefully and asking myself, can I work with this person? Are they ambitious? Can they pivot if they have to? I have to like the general direction of the company, but the real question I have to ask when partnering with new ventures is whether or not I can work with them.
IBR: What would you like your career legacy to ultimately be?
MH: I just want to be known as the guy who built something from nothing and made a difference for our country. I truly believe that Canada is the greatest place in the world to live in and I care very much about our country and building companies here. That’s why I spend a lot of time speaking across the country about entrepreneurship. I believe that we need to think very carefully about being more than just an oil and manufacturing country. We need to think about shifting our focus to becoming more involved with building technology companies that support all industries. Those new jobs will have high wages and that helps everyone. We’re a relatively small population on a very big landmass and we’re very spread out. That’s a big disadvantage, but our advantage could come from leveraging the technology culture that has developed to create value for our country.

We've spent a lot of time asking "should we use AI agents?" — and not nearly enough asking "who owns them once they're running?"
Here's the thing about agents: they're not like buying software. You don't sign a contract, flip a switch, and move on. Most businesses wonder why their AI is not working. Here is the answer.
They buy the tools first. They automate the chaos. Then they are surprised when output is inconsistent, hallucinations slip through, and the whole thing feels brittle six months in.
The debate is not AI FIRST vs. DATA FIRST as a philosophical preference. It is a sequencing question, and the sequencing has real consequences.
Here is what actually happens on each path:
AI FIRST means your tools are running on top of undefined processes, dirty data, and tribal knowledge no one has written down. The demo looks sharp. Production is a different story.
FOUNDATION FIRST means you map the workflow before you touch the tooling. You clean the data before you automate the decisions. You build something that compounds instead of something that cracks.
The underrated risk of Foundation First is moving so slowly that competitors build momentum while you are still in prep mode. The underrated risk of AI First is that you have now automated the very dysfunction you needed to fix.
The answer is not binary. The question worth asking is: which layer are you skipping, and do you know it?
Most founders do not know. That is the problem.
What layer is your team skipping right now?

I've been tracking how business leaders adopt AI, and one finding stands out: the gap between AI investment and operational change is almost entirely explained by the absence of a delegation plan.
Leaders who see measurable results share a common approach. They started by building a list: a complete inventory of the routine tasks in their week that don't require executive judgment. Then they systematically delegated those tasks to AI, three at a time, over the course of a quarter.
Leaders who see no meaningful change are doing something different: experimenting. New tools, new prompts, no list, no commitment to hand anything off permanently.
The operational math is straightforward. If the typical CEO's week contains twelve routine tasks consuming 10–15 hours, and those tasks can be delegated to AI running on a schedule, then three months of systematic delegation recovers roughly half a working week—permanently. That's not a productivity gain. It's a structural change in how the executive role operates.
The framework: list, sort, delegate three a week, consolidate on one platform. It's in this week's newsletter, along with the complete twelve-task list and step-by-step implementation guidance.
The executives who establish their AI delegation practice in the next six months will have a compounding operational advantage over those who continue experimenting.
Here's the framework:

A leader I coach told me, with real pride, that her team's dashboards had never looked better.
Every objective tracked. Every score current. Reports that used to eat a full day now took AI eleven minutes.
Six months later, two of her best people quit. Neither one mentioned the dashboards on the way out.
That gap, dashboards getting sharper while people quietly walk out the door, is the whole story of what AI is doing to leadership right now, and most organizations haven't noticed yet.
Here's the confusion at the root of it: we promote people into "leadership" and then evaluate them almost entirely on management. Management is the tactical work: tracking progress, organizing resources, keeping the machine on schedule. AI is exceptional at that job. It sorts information fast, drafts the first version of the report, and tells you what to do next.
Leadership is a different job entirely. It's the judgment call about which objectives actually matter this year. It's telling someone the truth about their trajectory while there's still time to change course. None of that shows up on a dashboard, and none of it can be automated, because it isn't a process. It's accumulated judgment.
"AI can hand someone an analysis. It can't hand them the years of context that tell them which analysis to trust."
Here's what worries me: researchers at MIT's Media Lab found that brain connectivity dropped by as much as 55 percent when people leaned on AI to do tasks they'd normally reason through themselves. Judgment is a muscle, and muscles that stop working start to atrophy.
The fix isn't slowing down AI adoption. It's deciding what you think before you ask a machine what it thinks. That single ordering choice does more to keep a leader's judgment intact than any policy ever could.
Where is your organization letting AI make the judgment calls that should still belong to a person? I'd like to hear about it in the comments.
If you're not sure where that line sits inside your own organization, I offer a complimentary session to work through it together. Reach out at bradhenderson@me.com to set one up.

The next management challenge isn't managing people.
It's managing AI-assisted work.
For decades, managers were responsible for people.
Today, they're becoming responsible for something new.
Work that is created, reviewed, influenced, or accelerated by AI.
And that changes the management challenge entirely.
Recent findings from Microsoft, Deloitte, and McKinsey all point in the same direction.
Organizations are adopting AI faster than they are redesigning how work is managed.
That is why many leaders are starting to ask different questions.
Not:
"How do we get people to use AI?"
But:
"How do we know AI is improving the work?"
"How do we stay accountable?"
"How do we manage quality when part of the work is no longer entirely human?"
At Plan AB Global Holding , we believe this is the next management discipline. Not AI adoption.
It's 𝐌𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐀𝐈-𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤.
Because in the AI era, success will not belong to the organizations using AI the most.
It will belong to those that know how to manage work after AI becomes part of it.
That is 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝 𝐏𝐚𝐭𝐡.

There is a useful distinction in the skill-acquisition literature between declarative and procedural knowledge, knowing about something versus knowing how to do it, and they develop through entirely different mechanisms.
Sitting in strategy meetings builds declarative knowledge, a CEO can describe AI's capabilities and risks fluently without ever having built the procedural fluency that only comes from repeated, hands-on use. Procedural knowledge is what produces the fast, largely unconscious pattern recognition experts rely on, the sense of when something is off before you can articulate why. BCG's finding that personal hours predict value is consistent with this: governance produces people who can talk accurately about AI. Only direct use produces people who can feel when it is wrong.

⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯
BCG's 2026 research surfaced a quiet finding alongside the headline numbers. CEOs who spend at least eight hours a week building their own AI capabilities are significantly more likely to generate meaningful value from the technology. Eight hours. Not on roadmaps. Not on governance. On using it themselves.
That is the part I see most often missed in coaching.
The CEOs leaning into the AI program of record are running rooms. Steering committees. Vendor reviews. Strategy offsites. The dashboard shows AI ownership going up. The clock shows zero hours of the leader actually thinking with the tool.
The leaders quietly getting the most are different. They are working alongside it. Drafting and arguing with it before a board call. Stress-testing their own assumptions in a Sunday-night chat window. Letting it surface the question they were too tired to find on their own.
They are not using AI to scale the org's productivity yet. They are using it to upgrade their own thinking first.
You can see it in the body. The leaders running the AI strategy room carry it as another file on the stack, shoulders inching toward their ears across the quarter. The leaders thinking with it have something looser in the chest. They are working harder than ever, and the work feels like it is theirs.
The difference is not about who is more into AI. It is about whether the leader has actually let the tool change how they think, before deciding how it changes the org.
If you have not yet sat with it for eight hours of your own real questions, the AI strategy your team is debugging is downstream of an upgrade that has not happened yet.

Start with your own questions. The org strategy follows.

Not because agreement is bad.
But because sometimes “yes” simply means,
“I don’t feel safe enough to say what I’m really thinking.”
Recently, I asked a room full of leaders a simple question:
“When you announce your AI strategy, who feels comfortable disagreeing with you?”
The room became noticeably quieter.
One executive smiled and admitted,
“We keep asking whether our people are AI-ready… but we’ve never asked whether they feel safe enough to tell us they aren’t.”
That stayed with me.
Across the Middle East, organisations are investing heavily in AI, and many are now moving from experimentation to enterprise-wide deployment. Yet workforce readiness, trust and human-centred leadership remain among the biggest challenges to successful transformation.
Technology doesn’t fail because it’s intelligent.
Transformation fails when people stop telling the truth.
The best leaders I know don’t create rooms where everyone agrees.
They create rooms where people feel safe enough to disagree.
Because that’s where innovation begins.
And that’s where trust grows.
As AI becomes more capable…
our greatest competitive advantage won’t be the quality of our algorithms.
It will be the quality of our conversations.
Before your next AI meeting, ask one question:
“What concerns haven’t been voiced yet?”
Then listen without interrupting.
You may learn more in five minutes than you would from fifty slides.
What is one question every leader should ask before introducing AI into their organisation?

There's a specific kind of dread going round at the moment. It usually shows up around eleven at night, scrolling launch announcements, working out how far behind you've fallen.
92% of leaders say they're building a class of AI elite employees. 60% plan to cut the people who haven't adopted. Fine, brutal, believable.
But 75% of those same leaders admit their AI strategy is mostly for show.
Read that twice. The list is real. The standard you're being measured against isn't. Nobody defined the workflow, nobody owned it, and most people's manager isn't modelling any of it either.
Which means the people getting praised right now mostly aren't more talented than you. They stumbled into one task where the tool happened to fit, usually in their own time, usually without being asked.
You can stop trying to be across everything. Genuinely. Pick one repetitive part of your week, rebuild it properly, and write down what it cost before and what it costs now.
That's the whole move. One workflow with a number attached beats a year of tool fluency nobody can see.
What would you rebuild first, if you only got one?

𝗖𝗘𝗢𝘀 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝟯𝟯% 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲
That’s not opinion. That’s Gallup research from a study of 143 Inc. 500 CEOs.
Those with high delegator talent posted an average three-year growth rate of 1,751% — 112 percentage points higher than low-delegator CEOs. They also created more jobs at a faster rate.
Yet 75% of the entrepreneurs Gallup studied had limited-to-low delegation talent. The skill that generates the most revenue is the one most leaders lack.
Here’s why: delegation feels slower than doing it yourself. And in the moment, it is. But every task you refuse to hand off is a task that holds you hostage. It keeps you in the weeds instead of leading the business.
AI changes the delegation equation. When I triaged my calendar last week using AI, it didn’t just flag items to delegate. It suggested who could take each one and drafted handoff messages with full context — ready to review and send.
That eliminates the two biggest barriers: figuring out who should do it and writing the communication. The AI handles both in seconds.
For any leader who has said “it’s faster if I just do it myself,” I’d challenge you to test that assumption with this framework. The 30 minutes you invest may return 10+ hours this week.

My last two posts were about a blind spot most performance systems share. This one is about you.
𝗜𝗳 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗻, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗮𝗺 𝗜 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿?
(Links to both posts that led here are in the comments 👇)
───
Over the last two posts, I wrote about why 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼 𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 and about where that contribution has actually moved in the AI era.
Many leaders are carrying a quiet question they rarely say out loud.
This is not a question born from weakness.
It is born from 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗵𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘆. And it deserves an honest answer.
Leadership authority has historically rested on two things.
🔹 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲
🔹 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆
AI has disrupted both.
But here is what that disruption is actually revealing.
The years spent building deep expertise have given leaders something AI cannot replicate.
Not the expertise itself as a static body of knowledge.
The 𝗷𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 that expertise has cultivated.
The ability to know 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁.
The pattern recognition to sense when a recommendation is 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴.
The understanding of organizational dynamics that exists only inside a specific culture.
𝗔𝗜 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀.
It has removed the transactional layers that were always, in a sense, in the way of them.
𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗱.
𝗜𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱.
The question is: are our organizations designed to support that clarity?
Next: why 𝗰𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 are the real foundation of human contribution in an AI-integrated world.

Tuesday’s Experience
The Credential That Holds
For most of the last century, a leader's track record was the primary evidence of their future value.
It was a reasonable assumption. If someone had navigated complexity before, built something before, delivered results in demanding conditions, the probability was high they could do it again. Experience was the credential that carried the most weight because it was the hardest to replicate quickly.
That assumption is under pressure.
AI is compressing the half-life of technical expertise. What a leader mastered in their last role may already be automated or restructured by tools that did not exist when they were hired. The pace at which roles evolve has outrun what most organizations anticipated. In many domains, past performance is no longer a reliable predictor of future value.
This is not a threat to experienced leaders. It is a clarifying force.
The qualities that have always separated leaders who endure from those who plateau are not technical. They are dispositional. The capacity to reason clearly under uncertainty. The willingness to adapt without losing coherence. The discipline to build judgment over time rather than rely on the repetition of what previously worked.
These qualities were valuable before AI. They are more valuable now because AI can replicate output but cannot replicate the judgment behind it. The leaders who remain effective when the domain shifts are not those with the deepest expertise in any single area. They are those whose judgment is transferable — built on character and clarity rather than on the specific conditions that produced their last success.
That is not a new requirement. It is an old one that the current environment has made impossible to defer.
The credential that holds is not what you have done. It is the quality of judgment you have built in doing it — and whether that judgment travels with you when the work itself changes.
What endures is rarely what moves fastest, but what remains coherent when everything else changes.
#Leadership #ALifeThatMatters

AI changes every single day. The pressure on leaders is real. But the answer isn’t to move faster.
It’s to get more grounded.
Here are 5 practices I keep coming back to for senior leaders navigating this moment:
1. Separate signal from noise, deliberately. Build a small, trusted group that helps you filter what actually matters for your context. Not what’s trending. What’s relevant to your strategy.
2. Make your purpose operational, not decorative. If it only shows up in annual reports, it won’t hold under pressure. Use it as an active filter for every major decision.
3. Give your team clarity, even when you don’t have certainty. Leaders who go quiet in uncertainty destabilize their organizations. Name what you know, what you’re watching, what you’re not chasing.
4. Protect time to think. Not a luxury, a requirement. Even one hour a week to step back and ask whether the direction still holds.
5. Ask: who can help? A mentor. An advisor. A team member closer to the ground. You don’t have to figure this out alone. Leadership means knowing who to bring in, and being willing to do it.
Which of these is hardest for you right now?

Because not seeing problems does not make you conscious.
Transforming how you see them does.

A “problem” is often:
A misalignment not yet understood
A system not yet redesigned
A capability not yet developed
A conversation not yet had
In that sense, every problem carries information.
And every piece of information carries possibility.
The difference between reactive leadership and conscious leadership is simple:
Reactive leaders try to fix symptoms.
Conscious leaders decode systems.

It reveals them faster.

In culture.
In decision-making.
In clarity.

Are you being asked to transform, reduce cost, move faster with fewer resources, and redesign operating models, while also navigating rising levels of uncertainty and anxiety across your teams?
You’re not alone. This is one of the most consistent themes emerging across the C suite conversations I’m having right now.
In consumer markets, I’m seeing this driven largely by ongoing margin pressure, the pace of AI adoption, and increasing competitive intensity.
A recent HBR article, “To Lead Through Uncertainty, Unlearn Your Assumptions” (Peshkam, Feb 2026), offers a number of practical ideas that feel highly relevant:
Pause instead of rushing to resolution:
The instinct to move quickly can mask the real issue. Naming the tension and sitting with it, even briefly, often surfaces what actually needs to be solved.
Name what is hard (don’t smooth it over):
Reassurance can push anxiety underground. Leaders who explicitly acknowledge what’s difficult create space for teams to process and move forward.
Share the burden of uncertainty:
Many leaders still feel they need to “hold it all together.” In reality, progress accelerates when teams are invited into the ambiguity, not shielded from it.
Stay with tension rather than closing it down:
Conflict and hesitation often contain useful signal. Moving too quickly to alignment can lead to rework and poorer decisions.
Trade polish for presence:
Teams don’t need a perfectly composed leader, they need a grounded one. Being clear on what you know, don’t know, and are working through builds trust.
What I’m seeing is that the leaders who handle this best maintain pace, but are more deliberate about where they create space so issues don’t resurface later.
Interested to hear how others are approaching this, particularly the balance between pace and presence.

Decision Making in the Age of Noise
In a world of constant input, how are you sharpening your judgment before you make the call?
Leaders today are drowning in information but starving for insight.
The challenge isn’t access to data. It’s clarity of thought.
The strongest executives I coach use AI to organize perspectives, surface trade-offs, and challenge their own assumptions. Not to decide for them — but to think more completely before they do.
They remain decisive. But they get there with better questions and fewer blind spots. They consistently ask: What might I be missing? Who else sees this differently? Where could this go wrong?
AI doesn’t replace judgment. It refines it.

In October 2025, Anthropic released Claude Skills.
By December, OpenAI had adopted the same SKILL.md format for ChatGPT and Codex CLI.
By March 2026, 16+ major AI tools supported the specification—including Perplexity, Google’s Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor.
This is the fastest cross-platform AI standard adoption we’ve seen.
Why does this matter for business leaders?
Because every Skill you build today is portable. It’s not locked into one vendor. A Skill you create for Claude works in ChatGPT, Gemini, and a growing ecosystem of tools—without modification.
This changes the ROI calculation entirely. You’re not investing in a platform-specific customization. You’re building reusable intellectual property that compounds across every AI tool your organization uses.
The Agent Skills marketplace already lists 500,000+ Skills. Anthropic’s repository has 87,000+ GitHub stars.
The infrastructure is here. The question is whether your organization is building on it.

A notable shift is happening in AI infrastructure that most business leaders haven’t noticed.
Anthropic published Claude Skills as an open standard in late 2025. Within months, OpenAI adopted the same format for ChatGPT. Google’s Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and a dozen other platforms followed.
Today, 16+ AI tools support the same SKILL.md specification.
This means the expertise you encode isn’t platform-dependent. A financial analysis Skill built for Claude works in ChatGPT. A document formatting Skill works in Gemini.
For enterprise decision-makers, this shifts the strategic question from “which AI platform should we standardize on?” to “what organizational knowledge should we encode first?”
The Skills you build become a form of institutional knowledge that persists regardless of which model or platform you use.
Companies that start building their Skill libraries now will have a meaningful operational advantage as AI tools continue to evolve.

Built a small open-source CLI tool called ctxport for devs using AI tools on free tiers.
If you use Cursor, Claude, or ChatGPT, you know the pain: you hit the limit, switch tools, and lose all your context back to square one.
ctxport fixes that.
Run ctxport watch while you work in Cursor. It silently tracks your session in the background. When you need to switch tools, run ctxport export it copies your full context as a ready-to-paste prompt. Pick up exactly where you left off.
It's fully open source PRs and contributions are welcome. If you find ituseful

Most AI agents forget everything the moment you close the chat window. Hermes Agent was built to fix exactly that.
And honestly, once you understand how it works, it is hard to go back to thinking about agents the old way.
Most agent frameworks follow the same basic loop. You give it a task, it executes, it returns a result, and the session ends. Next time you open it, it has no idea who you are, what you prefer, or how it solved something similar last week. You start from zero every single time.
Hermes Agent, built by Nous Research, is designed around a completely different idea.
So how does it actually work?
Traditional agent:
User input ➡️ Plan ➡️ Execute ➡️ Return result ➡️ Session ends ➡️ Memory wiped
Hermes agent:
User input ➡️ Load memory + skills ➡️ Plan + retrieve ➡️ Execute ➡️ Evaluate + extract ➡️ Save skills + session log + user model ➡️ Feeds back into next session
After completing a complex task, the agent does not just return the result and move on. It evaluates what it did, extracts the reasoning pattern, and saves it as a reusable skill. Next time a similar task comes up, it loads that skill and applies it. And if a better approach comes along, the skill gets updated automatically.
The memory system is just as thoughtful. It maintains two persistent files: one for environment facts, conventions, and lessons learned, and one for your preferences and communication style. Both get injected into the system prompt at the start of every session. It also has full-text search over all past conversations stored in SQLite, so it can pull up how it handled something three weeks ago.
Here is what makes this genuinely interesting.
It is not tied to a single LLM provider or a single platform. You can run it on a $5 VPS, plug in OpenAI, Anthropic, or a local model via Ollama, and chat with it over Telegram, Slack, Discord, or your terminal. The conversation continues across all of them.
The agent you are using in month three is measurably more capable than the one you started with, because it has been learning from your actual workflows the entire time.

The Most Underrated Canadian Founder You’ve Probably Never Heard Of
If Michael Hyatt were American, he’d have 500,000 LinkedIn followers, a book deal, and a Netflix documentary called “How to Print Money Legally.”
But he’s Canadian…
So nobody talks about him.
Let’s fix that.
Meet Michael Hyatt: the quiet Canadian who sold not one, but TWO huge companies before he turned 30.
Everyone knows Shopify.
Everyone knows Lululemon.
But almost nobody knows the guy who built one of Canada’s most valuable cybersecurity firms and sold it for $400M+, and then just kept going.
This is why I love studying founders like Hyatt:
They aren’t loud.
They aren’t flashy.
They just win.
The Story
At 17, he’s playing with servers while the rest of us were trying to get a date to grad.
At 25, he starts his first tech company, Dyadem.
At 29, he sells it.
Then he does the most un-Canadian thing ever:
He starts another one.
That company?
BlueCat.
The invisible plumbing behind the internet that no one thinks about until it breaks.
Think cybersecurity meets infrastructure meets “oh God don’t let this fail.”
Everyone said building it in Canada was impossible.
Hyatt built it anyway.
Scaled it.
Then sold it for hundreds of millions.
Instead of buying a yacht and disappearing to Anguilla, he becomes an angel investor, backs dozens of companies, becomes a CBC Dragon, gives straight-talk business advice, and mentors founders across the country.
No ego.
No influencer vibes.
Just results.
Why I’m Obsessed With His Playbook
Here’s the thing about Hyatt:
He didn’t build a social app.
He didn’t build a marketplace.
He built boring infrastructure that powers the internet.
And boring infrastructure is where the money is.
His lessons hit hard:
Solve real problems, “not founder feelings.”
Ignore hype, focus on customers who pay.
Build discipline, not dopamine.
Be relentless, even when nobody sees you.
Think decades, not quarters.
Canada desperately needs more founders like him, quiet killers who build important things instead of shiny things.
The Takeaway
Canada has a lot of amazing founders building amazing things.
They’re the ones who don’t go viral.
They don’t chase clout.
They build internet plumbing, cybersecurity rails, utilities, enterprise tools, the stuff billion-dollar companies rely on.
Hyatt is the blueprint:
Start small
Build something real
Sell it
Do it again
Help others
Simple.
Not easy.
If you’re building something in Canada, study this man.
He’s one of our country’s best founders.
We just haven’t built him a statue yet.

T — Teamwork
Cybersecurity is a team sport. Hyatt built a team of experts capable of addressing complex enterprise challenges, ensuring that innovation and protection evolve together.

Michael Hyatt’s greatness lies in seeing what others overlooked—the data itself—and building systems to control, monitor, and protect it at the highest level. Through clarity of focus and disciplined execution, he transformed cybersecurity from reactive defense into proactive data intelligence.

There is a pattern I have watched repeat itself across more than 15 years working in information security, data protection, and enterprise risk. Every few years, a new term rises to the top of every conference agenda, every board deck, every vendor pitch. Right now, that term is AI governance. Before that, it was Zero Trust. Before that, compliance frameworks. Before that, GDPR.
Each wave arrives with a sense of urgency — as if the industry has discovered something entirely new. Each wave attracts enormous attention, investment, and debate. And each time, the same foundational question goes quietly unanswered: have we actually built the thing that makes all of this work?
Because here is what I have observed, consistently and across many organisations: the buzzword changes. The underlying principle does not.
It Started With a Simple Idea — Protect the Environment
Cast your mind back to the early days of information security. The model was straightforward. Organisations operated within sealed network perimeters. If you were inside the boundary, you were trusted. If you were outside, you were not. Security meant building a strong enough wall.
That worked for a while. Then digitalisation arrived, and with it, the imperative to connect. Being able to operate across systems, grant access to clients and third parties, and develop as a business online stopped being optional. The perimeter dissolved. And the model had to change.
From my own experience, that shift accelerated significantly around 2010. The focus moved from protecting networks to protecting data — wherever it lived, wherever it travelled, whoever touched it.
The Standard That Changed the Conversation
In this context, the information security industry began to formalise its thinking. The roots go back to 1995, when the British Standards Institution published BS 7799, an early code of best practices for information security management. The concept of the Information Security Management System (ISMS) was introduced in BS 7799-2 in 1998, and in 2005, it became the first internationally recognised standard: ISO/IEC 27001:2005. [1]
The most recent version, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, updated the standard further to address cloud computing, remote work, and modern threat landscapes. [3]
ISO 27001 introduced more than just a checklist. It was a system — built on a deceptively simple principle: that protecting data is not an IT function. It is a business function. And for it to work, it must be embedded across the entire organisation, aligned with business goals and objectives, and brought to every level of the enterprise.
That was the foundation. That was the holistic approach. Strategy first. Alignment second. Controls third — not the other way around.
Then the Cycles Began
What followed was a series of waves, each one picking up one thread from that foundational model and pulling it to the front.....

Step 3: Define a High-Value Strategy
With a clear picture of current strengths and gaps, the cyber leader must develop a multi-year security strategy aligned to organizational objectives. This means building a three-year roadmap with defined priorities, actions, outcomes, and accountabilities — one that addresses the most critical risks first, delivers early wins, and meets regulatory and customer requirements.
The primary goal should be to build security capabilities the organization can sustain, rather than acquiring additional tools for their own sake. Implementing robust threat detection and response — with defined processes, skilled people, and appropriate technology — often reduces risk more effectively than investing in the latest tools. Focusing on capabilities over features is the surest way to ensure security investments deliver meaningful, long-term improvement.
Step 4: Build the Business Case and Secure Funding
With a clear plan in hand, the cyber leader must develop a compelling business case that articulates the problem or opportunity, the proposed solution, expected benefits, cost, and resource requirements, risk analysis, and a return on investment. Each initiative should be linked to measurable outcomes — reduced risk, improved compliance, or increased operational efficiency.
To gain approval, funding, and executive support, present a phased plan that balances long-term ambition with near-term delivery. Highlighting quick wins within the first 90 days — such as closing critical control gaps or strengthening oversight of high-risk assets — builds momentum and earns the confidence of key stakeholders.

🌫️ Organizations often believe they are resilient when systems remain available, processes continue, and dashboards stay green. Yet an enterprise can appear stable while quietly weakening at its seams. A public platform may remain online even as sensitive data is exposed. A trusted outsourcing workflow may continue operating while HR records slip into unsafe hands. A finance process may complete as designed while funds are diverted to an attacker. An AI coding tool may increase productivity while also expanding the reach of privileged software and fueling malware campaigns driven by curiosity and urgency. What looks like resilience can be a carefully maintained illusion of control.
🧩 The common lesson across these cases is that cyber risk rarely collapses an enterprise in one dramatic moment. More often, it accumulates in areas leaders are most likely to treat as secondary: workforce readiness, cloud-facing services, third-party transfer points, payment verification routines, release engineering, telemetry boundaries, and developer behavior during moments of intense attention. NIST’s emphasis on aligning cyber risk, enterprise priorities, and workforce capability fits this reality closely, because gaps in skills, accountability, and governance do not remain administrative for long. They become operational exposure. The deeper weakness is not simply inadequate security tooling. It is the separation of business continuity from confidentiality, compliance from maturity, outsourcing from ownership, and AI productivity from software governance.
🛡️ One of the most dangerous signals in modern cybersecurity is a process that is still functioning. Operations may continue even as loss is spreading through the workflows the business trusts most. Resilience, therefore, cannot be defined by uptime alone. It must also include the ability to preserve trust, data integrity, decision quality, and institutional credibility under pressure. In practice, that requires tighter governance over third-party handoffs, stronger validation for financially sensitive changes, clearer control over AI agent permissions, disciplined software release pipelines, restrained telemetry practices, and executive ownership of workforce capability as a risk issue rather than merely a staffing concern. The organizations most likely to succeed in this environment will not be those that simply keep operating. They will be the ones that can prove they are operating safely, deliberately, and with trust still intact.
💬 Where in your environment does resilience look strongest on the surface, yet depend most on fragile trust underneath? Have you seen continuity metrics create a false sense of security while confidentiality, governance, or accountability were quietly weakening?

🛡️📁 Cybersecurity maturity is not built only with tools — it is built with structure, templates, and repeatable dashboards.
A lot of teams invest in platforms, scanners, and alerts.
But the part they often underestimate is this:
Security operations become scalable only when the work is documented, tracked, and repeatable.
That is why collections like this are so useful.
They show cybersecurity not just as a set of technologies, but as an operating system of templates, logs, trackers, matrices, dashboards, and response documents.
What stands out to me:
🔹 Information security needs documentation discipline
Things like a Data Breach Notification Log, Encryption Key Management Sheet, Security KPI Dashboard, and Data Classification Register turn policies into operational control.
🔹 Application security needs tracking, not just testing
A Patch & Update Tracker, Threat Modeling template, and Application Data Encryption Checklist help teams move from ad hoc reviews to structured AppSec processes.
🔹 Cloud security depends on visibility
Without tools like a Cloud Access Control Matrix, Cloud Asset Inventory Tracker, and Cloud Incident Response Log, cloud security becomes fragmented very quickly.
🔹 Network security benefits from operational dashboards
A Network Traffic Monitoring Dashboard, Security Event Correlation Tracker, VPN Usage Log, and DDoS Mitigation Plan Tracker are examples of how teams make monitoring more actionable.
🔹 Security management needs governance artifacts
Checklists, backup and recovery plans, bug tracking templates, and disposal/destruction policies are often what connect daily operations to compliance and audit readiness.
🔹 Incident management lives or dies on process clarity
Templates like IT Security Incident Reports, Major Incident Reports, and a clear Security Incident Management Process help teams respond consistently under pressure.
My biggest takeaway:
Cybersecurity does not become stronger just because you add more tools.
It becomes stronger when you can answer:
What are we tracking?
How are we documenting it?
Who owns the process?
How do we measure progress?
And how do we respond consistently?
Because mature security teams do not rely on memory.
They rely on systems.

The blog /Link post by Adaptive Information Systems explores a critical business scenario — what happens when an organization loses all its data, including files, customer records, invoices, and operational data. It highlights that the consequences can be devastating, ranging from downtime and lost revenue to compliance violations and even permanent business closure. The article covers the common causes of data loss — cyberattacks, hardware failures, and accidental deletions — and focuses on prevention strategies.
💥 Impact of Business Data Loss
Downtime alone can cost small businesses thousands of dollars per hour, and recovering lost data — if even possible — is expensive and time-consuming.
Around 43% of all cyberattacks target smaller companies because they are easier to break into, and an estimated 60% of these small businesses shut down within six months of a major attack. Additionally, 40% of businesses hit by ransomware lost important data, and 51% of those affected paid the criminals.
🔑 Key Prevention Strategies
1. Backup & Disaster Recovery (BDR) A BDR plan works in the background, making copies of important business data and storing them in a separate, secure location. If main systems are compromised, it enables rapid restoration and minimizes downtime.
2. Recovery Objectives Two critical metrics guide any recovery plan — Recovery Time Objective (RTO), which defines how fast systems must be restored, and Recovery Point Objective (RPO), which defines how much recent data loss is acceptable. These two goals form the foundation of a business continuity strategy.
3. Ransomware Defense When ransomware locks your files, having a clean backup is often the only way to get back to business without paying the criminals.
4. Human Firewall — Employee Training Cybercriminals often bypass tough firewalls by sending convincing emails to employees. Building a human firewall through security awareness training makes employees the first line of defense rather than the weakest link.
5. Proactive Monitoring Infrastructure monitoring acts as a 24/7 health checkup for all business technology — catching small issues before they escalate into major failures that can shut operations down entirely.
6. Access Controls & MFA The biggest threat to personal data is unauthorized access. Storing sensitive information on a robust cloud platform with correct permission settings, multi-factor authentication (MFA), and restricted user access is essential to preventing breaches.

1.Perform a cybersecurity risk assessment
Enterprises must ensure regular evaluation of the impact of any crisis on their digital and operational systems. At the outset, it is important to take inventory of all digital assets and evaluate if all security controls, such as access controls and encryption, are in place. Simulate real-world attacks and conduct penetration testing to assess the defenses. This exercise helps in identifying, analyzing, and prioritizing critical risks caused by common security threats and the presence of vulnerabilities such as weak passwords or outdated software.
2.Implement Zero Trust Architecture
Traditional perimeter-based security models fail in today’s digital age,where hybrid and remote work cultures and cloud adoption are prevalent. Zero-trust architecture addresses this challenge by following the principle of ‘never trust, always verify’. This model performs continuous verification, enforces least privilege access, and constantly monitors all user activities.
3.Build cyber resilient supply chain and operations
Emergencies often disrupt global supply chains and expose vulnerabilities within partner ecosystems. Several organizations share sensitive data with suppliers, which is stored with them. If the vendors do not follow strong cybersecurity practices, in the event of a security breach, attackers gain access to data that is now with the suppliers.
When such incidents are not reported, organizations are not even aware of the security breaches
4.Implement advanced threat detection and security operations frameworks
With advanced technologies such as AI and machine learning, organizations are able to automate detection while identifying threats at scale. AI-driven Agentic Security Operations Centers (SOCs) can analyze huge volumes of data to detect anomalies and low-noise intrusions in real-time. Behavioral biometrics analyzes user behavior and detects patterns to identify potential threats
5.Business continuity and disaster recovery planning
Cyber incidents, data breaches, and AI-driven deep fakes and frauds are pervasive and evolving, impacting organizations and individuals. Organizations have to ensure operational resilience even during cybersecurity incidents or any crisis by implementing comprehensive business continuity and disaster recovery strategies. High-risk digital assets and services are to be identified, and mission-critical data documented. Having a response plan for incidents and ensuring they align with the organization’s business continuity strategy is key. Rapid system recovery mechanisms should be in place with organizations following the 3-2-1 backup rule. Backup recovery must be evaluated regularly. The aim is to recover the data and restore the business function with minimum disruption.
