5 Principles for Achieving Sustainable Work-Life Balance with Michael & Megan Hyatt
November 4, 2024
Michael Hyatt is the Founder and Chairman of Full Focus. He has scaled multiple companies over the years, including a $250M publishing company with 700+ employees and his own goal-achievement company. Michael is also the author of several New York Times, Wall Street Journal, and USA Today bestselling books. He has been married for over 45 years to his wife Gail, has five daughters, and ten grandchildren.
Megan Hyatt Miller is the President and Chief Executive Officer of Full Focus, co-host of the popular Double Win podcast, and Wall Street Journal bestselling author of Mind Your Mindset and Win at Work & Succeed at Life. All of this while finishing every day by 3 pm, so she and her husband, Joel, can be fully present with their five kids when they get home from school.
This content contains affiliate links. If you use these links to purchase something, we may earn a commission. Thanks.
Is achieving a work-life balance a realistic goal in today’s modern age?
It can often feel like there is no winning when it comes to balancing all areas of your life. Working long hours usually results in less sleep. You have more time for meetings, but less time for friends and family. But there’s good news. It’s possible to give every area of your life the attention it needs so you can thrive.
Our guests today are more than familiar with this dilemma and they’ve found a way around it. Michael and Megan Hyatt are a father-daughter team who run Full Focus, a company dedicated to helping high achievers live their best lives. They’re here to talk about their book, Win at Work and Succeed at Life: 5 Principles to Free Yourself from the Cult of Overwork.
All areas of your life are interconnected. That’s why balance comes down to energy management—not time management. By focusing on the right things, you can get more done in less time. If you’ve been looking for a way to stay ambitious without sacrificing your happiness, this episode is for you.

Most businesses don't fail at AI because the technology is too complex. They fail because they skip the strategy.
Before you buy another tool or run another ChatGPT experiment, it helps to have a clear framework. Here's a simple 4-step AI strategy blueprint that actually works for small and mid-sized businesses.
🔍 Step 1: Audit your operations. Identify the repetitive, time-consuming tasks that drain your team every week. These are your highest-value automation targets.
Step 2: Set clear goals. AI works best when it's solving a specific problem, not just "doing AI things." Tie every initiative to a measurable outcome, whether that's reducing response time, cutting costs, or improving lead quality.
Step 3: Start with one workflow. Pick the single highest-impact process and build there first. A focused pilot gives you proof of ROI before you scale, and keeps your team from getting overwhelmed.
⚙️ Step 4: Measure, learn, expand. Track what changes after implementation. Use those insights to refine your approach and roll out automation across more areas of the business.
This is exactly how businesses go from curious about AI to genuinely competitive with it. No hype, no expensive overhauls. Just a clear, repeatable process that builds real momentum over time.

Customers never see the puzzle, only the finished answer
Artificial intelligence assembles your business the way someone assembles a jigsaw puzzle. It gathers pieces from your website, directories, review sites, news articles, social profiles, and partner pages, then fits them together into one description.
Some pieces fit perfectly. Some overlap. Some belong to an older version of your business. A few may not belong to your business at all.
Your customer never sees any of that.
They ask ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude a question and receive one confident answer. They have no way to know whether that answer came from a puzzle that was assembled correctly or one that left out the wrong pieces.
That is the part most business owners never think about. You are not just being described. You are being assembled, piece by piece, from sources you may not even remember publishing.
Two businesses with nearly identical websites can receive completely different AI descriptions if one has years of consistent sources and the other has scattered, conflicting ones. The website looks the same to a person reading it. It does not look the same to AI trying to build a picture from every source it can find.
The only way to know what picture AI actually assembled is to see it laid out plainly instead of guessing from the finished answer.
The Frank Masotti AI Business Understanding Report shows you exactly how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude currently describe your business, what pieces they used, and where the picture comes apart. Frank personally puts the puzzle back together so you can see it, not just the answer it produced.

Over lunch last week, an old friend told me the formula had changed.
He has spent more than a decade in outsourcing. Helping companies move work offshore in the name of efficiency and cost reduction. The maths used to be simple, he said.
Revenue = "Number of people × billing rate."
That equation shaped a generation of global work. Optimising labour. Distributing talent across continents. Squeezing inefficiency out of systems that ran on human input.
"Today," he continued, "it's outcome × AI leverage."
That shift says everything.
We are no longer just rethinking where work gets done. We are rethinking how it gets done. And increasingly, who or what does it.
The unit of value has changed. Human effort alone no longer carries the price. It is now human judgement combined with machine capability. The two together. Or in some cases, the machine on its own.
What happens to the role of people when outcomes can scale without scaling the humans behind them?
This question cuts into how we define contribution, purpose, and the dignity of work itself.
In Leading in the Age of AI, one of the threads I keep returning to is this. The hardest questions of this decade will not be technical. They will be moral. The Stoics understood that what you do with power matters far more than what power you hold. We are about to find out whether modern leadership has the same nerve.
That conversation over lunch is exactly why I wrote the book.

Way longer than I expected.
But then I considered how long it would take to define, recruit, interview, hire, and onboard a human chief of staff.
Thirty hours suddenly didn’t seem so unreasonable.
My chief of staff will be the first member of the digital team I’m building for my AI consulting business—and eventually, the agent responsible for helping orchestrate the others.
Its job is to help me:
* Keep priorities from getting buried
* Track projects, decisions, and follow-ups
* Reduce the mental load of holding everything in my head
* Turn the way I work into repeatable processes
* Coordinate the specialized agents I’ll add to the fleet
I’m building the operational foundation that will help future humans—and agents—do their best work.
What surprised me was how much “hiring” an AI agent resembles hiring a person.
I had to define the role, establish responsibilities, determine what context it needed, create guardrails, and decide what success should look like.
The technology was only part of the work.

"The best people in a company are often trapped by the worst workflows"
I didn't realize this at first.
For years, I thought great companies were built by great people.
And that is true.
But after working closely with different teams, I noticed something strange.
The people with the most experience were often spending the most time doing things that didn't require their experience.
They were not solving difficult problems.
They were searching for information,
Copying data,
Checking documents,
Following up on approvals,
Updating reports,
Connecting systems that were never designed to work together.
What surprised me was this:
These people were not inefficient.
They were doing exactly what the system around them required.
The problem was not the people.
The problem was the way work was designed.
Every company has invisible workflows.
The email thread that contains the real decision.
The Excel file that everyone depends on.
The employee who remembers how things actually work.
The process that exists only because "this is how we have always done it."
And I started asking myself:
What happens when the person who knows everything leaves?
What happens when the company grows faster than its processes?
What happens when talented people spend more time managing information than creating value?
That question became the beginning of anchor.
I didn't want to build another tool that companies have to learn.
I wanted to help companies rethink how work happens.
Because the future of work is not about asking people to work harder.
It is about removing the unnecessary friction that prevents them from doing their best work.
At Anchor, we believe:
Better businesses are built on better workflows.
We study how teams actually work, identify where friction exists, and redesign the processes behind the work.
Not more complexity.
Not more tools.
Just better ways of working.
This is the beginning of our journey.
I’m excited to share what we learn along the way.
What is one process in your company that feels harder than it should be?

The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
Stephen R Covey
This book, first published in 1989, outlines seven habits that are designed to help individuals become more effective in their personal and professional lives.
The habits are grouped into three categories: Private Victory (habits 1-3), Public Victory (habits 4-6), and Renewal (habit 7).
The habits include being proactive, beginning with the end in mind, putting first things first, thinking win-win, seeking first to understand and then to be understood, synergizing, and sharpening the saw.
Covey emphasizes the importance of personal integrity, effective time management, empathetic communication, and continuous self-improvement.
If your business is taking over your life, it’s time to step back and rethink the playbook. Success shouldn’t come at the cost of everything else. The good news is, it doesn’t have to—and I’m the living proof.
In this episode, the tables are turned as I take the guest seat on Michael Hyatt and Megan Hyatt-Miller’s podcast, The Double Win. We dive into my journey of building Triad Partners—the company I co-founded to help independent financial advisors grow their businesses without losing sight of what really matters.
We cover everything from transitioning from a sales-driven mindset to a CEO role, to the importance of therapy for high-achieving entrepreneurs, to why business culture will make or break your success.
I hope this conversation gives you practical insights and fresh perspectives to help you break free from the hustle trap.
3 of the biggest insights from Brad Johnson & Michael Hyatt …
#1.) Breaking Free from the Hustle Hamster Wheel
Many financial advisors build a business only to find themselves working more hours than ever. We talk about the common cycle of “market, sell, repeat” and how to escape it by structuring your business to scale beyond you.
#2.) The Mindset Shift from Salesperson to CEO
Scaling a business isn’t just about bringing in more clients—it’s about shifting from a doer to a leader. I share the biggest leadership lessons I’ve learned while growing Triad from the ground up and building a 100-person team in just four years.
#3.) Culture Is Everything
Hiring the best talent is important, but if they’re not a culture fit, they’ll do more harm than good. We break down how Triad built a movement around Do Business, Do Life and why culture is the ultimate competitive advantage.

AI’s greatest value isn’t making you busier. It’s creating margin. Time margin. Strategic margin. Personal margin. What I call the Double Win: better business results achieved with less personal sacrifice.
I’ve recovered 10+ hours per week through systematic AI implementation. My businesses are more profitable and more efficient. And I have more presence for the relationships and activities that define a well-lived life.
The AI Business Lab® Mastermind is built around this philosophy. We don’t celebrate overwork. We celebrate leaders who build businesses that serve their lives rather than consume them.

BlueCat - About the company
BlueCat is an acquired company based in Toronto (Canada), founded in 2001 by Richard Hyatt. It operates as a Cloud-based DNS and DHCP appliance and security solutions provider. BlueCat has raised $27.8M in funding from Trident Capital and Bridgescale. The company has 144 active competitors, including 2 funded and 20 that have exited. Its top competitors include companies like Vonage, Infoblox and Whalebone.
Company Details
Cloud-based DNS and DHCP appliance and security solutions provider. It offers features such as integration points, robust API library, SSO, DNSSEC development, IPv6 support, threat protection, direct internet access, and automated management. The company also provides technical education, services for DNS, DHCP administrators, network professionals, and security professionals. Its customers span across government, military, financial services, retail, enterprise, and manufacturing sectors.

The most dangerous word in AI right now: “free.”
OpenClaw is open source. Free to download. But every action it takes burns API tokens—and the costs are staggering.

For most SMB leaders, the math doesn’t work. Not yet.

This week, I asked an LLM to multiply two large numbers: 2837 × 4853. It gave me an answer: confident, and incorrect.
So I followed up. “Are you sure?” I asked. It responded again, equally confident, and this time, thankfully also correct.
That exchange explains more about AI systems than most product demos.
Traditional software is deterministic. The same set of inputs produces the identical output, every single time. LLMs are probabilistic. They do not calculate in the way a calculator does. They predict the most likely sequence of tokens based on training data.
Change the phrasing slightly, and you can change the outcome. That flexibility is what makes them powerful. It is also what makes them unreliable in contexts where precision is non-negotiable.
For investors, the real question is not whether a company is “AI native,” it is understanding how reliability is engineered into the system. Where are errors caught? Which parts of the solution are deterministic, which are probabilistic? What happens when the model is wrong?
I explore this in depth in my latest blog - follow the link in the comments.

#Why_Adding_More_Tools_Make_Your_Agent_Worse?
Unbelievable fact about AI agents:
Adding more tools makes them worse.
Here's why.
Every tool definition consumes context window space.
Each tool needs a description, input schema, output schema,
and usage guidance. That's stable, predictable space,
but it adds up fast.
Give an agent 50 tools and you've burned thousands of tokens
before a single user message arrives.
But the real problem isn't space. It's decision quality.
The more tools an agent has, the harder it is to choose
the right one. Vague tool descriptions lead to wrong invocations.
Overlapping tools create ambiguity. The LLM starts guessing.
The engineering principle:
→ Every tool description should answer 4 questions:
What does it do?
What inputs does it require, in what format?
What does it return?
When should the agent prefer this tool over alternatives?
If you can't answer all four clearly,
the tool isn't ready for production.
Fewer tools, better described, beat
many tools, poorly documented. Every time.

The question I ask before any AI tool conversation gets serious: who owns the decision that this tool is supposed to support, and what happens today when that decision is wrong?
If the answer is vague, the workflow underneath is broken. And buying a tool with a human-in-the-loop feature does not fix a process where nobody has agreed who the human is, what they are reviewing, or what they do when the output looks wrong.
The checkpoint I would put in is not technical. It is before procurement. Map the exception first. Find the moment where the current process stalls, gets escalated to the wrong person, or quietly disappears. If you cannot describe that moment clearly without the tool in the picture, the tool will inherit the ambiguity and automate it at speed.

Everyone is asking how the AI model was breached.
But that’s not the real question.
The more important detail:
The access didn’t come through the core system — it came through a third-party environment.
Which means:
* The model was restricted
* Access was controlled
* And still, it was used outside its intended boundary
This is not just a security issue.
It’s a system design problem.
We’ve spent years securing:
* models
* APIs
* infrastructure
But real-world failures don’t happen at the center.
They happen at the edges.
Where?
* systems integrate
* environments vary
* and actions actually get executed
AI changes the scale of this problem.
A small gap is no longer small.
Because once something gets through:
* it can adapt
* it can execute
* it can scale
So the question is shifting:
Not “Who has access?”
But “What is allowed to happen after access?”
Because in the end:
Systems don’t fail where they are designed.
They fail where they are used.

Most AI systems assume that once an action is “approved,” it stays approved.
That assumption breaks the moment the system becomes distributed.
A workflow starts.
An agent proposes an action.
Upstream checks pass.
But before execution:
• permissions change
• state shifts
• another action commits first
• a dependency moves
Now the question isn’t:
“Was this allowed?”
It’s:
“Is this still allowed right now?”
Most systems don’t answer that.
They carry forward earlier decisions and treat them as authority.
That works in static systems.
It fails in real ones.
Because authorization is not authority at execution.
Authority has to be re-derived against the state that actually exists when the system attempts to act.
If it isn’t, you get:
• time-of-check vs time-of-use gaps
• race-condition-driven behavior
• actions executing against invalid assumptions
The system didn’t “fail policy.”
It executed without re-validating reality.
If your system proposes state transitions:
Where is that re-validation happening?
And what prevents a previously valid action from becoming invalid before it commits?

The evolution of LLMs is pushing a new way of building software. We’ll increasingly see models generating a large portion of the code, while humans move into roles more focused on reviewing, guiding, and deciding.
That’s exactly where human skills become even more valuable as a critical factor of quality.
These models can produce functional solutions at impressive speed, but they still don’t have real judgment, contextual reasoning, or genuine critical thinking as an experienced professional does.
When we challenge their responses and ask for alternatives, better options often emerge. And in that exchange, something interesting happens. The model improves the proposal, but it also gives the human new inputs to think more clearly. That is where real value is created.
There’s also a tradeoff. More critical thinking from the human side, usually means more iterations, and more iterations mean more consumption. When token cost starts driving the conversation, the risk is sacrificing depth for efficiency.
As with almost everything in technology, this is not about choosing speed or judgment, but about balancing both. Because even if AI builds more of the software of the future, its quality will still depend deeply on human capabilities such as judgment, curiosity, and critical thinking.

A quiet truth about today's AI tools: your memory doesn't travel.
What you teach ChatGPT stays in OpenAI's ecosystem. What you build in Claude stays with Anthropic. Gemini operates apart from both. There is no clean way to move your accumulated context between them.
For an individual, that's friction. For a business, it's a strategic liability. Data portability determines whether you can access, export, and reuse the knowledge that powers your operation, outside any single vendor's system. It is the most fundamental dimension of AI risk, and it's the one most leaders overlook.
The fix isn't to bet on the "right" platform. It's to stop depending on any one of them.
Keep your core knowledge, your context, your processes, your reference material, in an open, portable format that you own. Then let whichever model you prefer read from it. The model becomes a tool you can replace. The knowledge remains an asset you keep.
This is the difference between building on rented land and building on ground you own. One leaves you exposed to someone else's roadmap. The other puts you in control.
As AI becomes central to how your organization runs, portability stops being a technical detail and becomes a board-level question.

"Use AI" is the emptiest instruction in corporate right now.
It sounds like direction. What it actually does is hand someone a logo and a deadline, then walk away from every hard decision — which tool, which task, where the risk sits, how the work itself has to change.
The guy in that photo isn't behind on his tasks. He was set up to freeze.
I watch it in kickoffs constantly. A team gets access to ten tools and a line about "being more efficient with AI." Nobody tells them which of the ten touches their actual job. So they open ChatGPT, paste in a task, get a flat answer, and quietly decide the whole thing was hype.
What they were missing was a starting point, and starting points are specific. Not "learn AI." More like: this is the one report in your week it rewrites, this is the tool that does it, this is the line you don't cross with client data. Give people that and the panic in the photo turns into a Monday habit inside a week.
If your AI rollout is a tool list and a pep talk, you've recreated the photo.

Eliminate Developer Dependency Tax with Vibe Coding
This title was summarized by AI from the post below.
Michael Hyatt
7mo
Report this post
Let's talk about what I call the developer dependency tax—the hidden costs of relying on outside development teams.
The financial cost is obvious. Even modest projects typically require $50,000-$200,000 in development fees, with ongoing maintenance costs that never stop.
But the real tax isn't financial. It's operational:
• Every change requires explaining your vision to someone who doesn't live in your business
• Every iteration takes weeks instead of hours
• Every pivot means renegotiating scope and budget
• You're constrained by someone else's availability and understanding
According to McKinsey research, 46% of companies now report significant productivity impact from AI implementation, with many specifically citing reduced dependency on traditional development resources.
Vibe coding eliminates this tax entirely.
You describe what you want. AI builds it. Something doesn't work? You adjust your description and regenerate. No tickets, no sprints, no waiting for the next build cycle.
This shift represents more than cost savings. It's about strategic agility. The ability to move at the speed of your vision rather than your development team's schedule creates a fundamental competitive advantage.
I've experienced both sides: the frustration of waiting weeks for changes that should take hours, and the freedom of iterating on applications in real time.
For business leaders building software-enabled services, this transition from dependency to self-reliance changes everything.
The question is: are you ready to make that shift?
Learn how to eliminate your developer dependency tax: https://lnkd.in/e8p9A35R

Tax planning is one of the highest value services a financial advisor can offer. It is also the most operationally painful.
Usually, it involves requesting PDF tax returns, manually keying data into planning software, and cross referencing paystubs against custodial data. It is slow, mentally draining, and prone to error.
This week, Altruist flipped this dynamic with their new AI platform, Hazel.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺: 𝗜𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹. Hazel does not just calculate numbers. It reads the unstructured mess of a client’s financial life. It ingests 1040 forms, paystubs, account statements, and even meeting notes and emails.
It applies deep tax logic to this unstructured data in minutes, eliminating the manual data entry that typically bottlenecks firms during tax season.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗛𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗟𝗼𝗼𝗽: 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴. The real innovation here isn't the speed; it is the interactivity.
Instead of an advisor taking a week to generate a static report, they can now sit with a client and run live "what if" scenarios.
- What happens if we sell the vacation home?
- What is the tax impact of this year's bonus?
- How does a retirement transition change the liability?
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝘂𝗽𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗮𝘅 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲.
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: This keeps the human advisor in the loop but shifts their role. They stop being a data entry clerk and start being a true strategist. As Altruist CEO Jason Wenk noted, this technology "makes average advice a lot harder to justify."
𝗔 𝗡𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗰𝘆: For the Human Loop to work in finance, trust is non negotiable. Hazel operates on a zero data retention agreement. The model providers are prohibited from retaining client data or using it to train their models.
This is the blueprint for vertical AI: Automate the reading, accelerate the math, and let the human handle the judgment.

There’s a behavioral reality few transformation programs truly address:
“Spreadsheets feel safe.”
They are:
🔹flexible when last-minute changes hit
🔹transparent to the person who built them
🔹familiar after years of close cycles and audits
Under tight reporting timelines, leaders hesitate to disrupt a model that “works.”
But here’s the irony. Manual spreadsheet environments are exactly where financial reporting and SOX risk concentrates, relying heavily on human judgment, offline evidence, version control, and compensating controls.
They may survive audits. They rarely scale well.
And they carry significant key-person dependency.
In an AI-enabled Finance world, this fragility becomes increasingly unsustainable.
How Finance transformation roadmaps sideline Tax:
Most Finance transformations start where transaction volume is highest:
🔹Procure to Pay
🔹Order to Cash
🔹Record to Report
Tax provisioning often appears later as “Phase 2” or “Wave 3.”
In reality, those phases are usually the first to be delayed, descoped, or quietly dropped when budgets tighten, priorities shift, or program teams change.
And so, the paradox persists:
Direct tax provisioning is:
🔹time-critical in the close
🔹central to financial statement integrity
🔹heavily judgement-laden
🔹highly scrutinized by audit
Yet it remains one of the least industrialized Finance processes.
The shift that’s coming:
The slow adoption of tax provision engines is not a technology failure.
It reflects how hard it is to synchronize:
process, data, systems, judgment, and governance across Finance and Tax.
But as:
🔹cloud ERPs mature
🔹data platforms stabilize
🔹AI-driven Finance accelerates
the cost of spreadsheet-based provisioning will become harder to justify not just in effort, but in:
🔹control risk
🔹close cycle pressure
🔹scalability
🔹audit defensibility
🔹talent dependency
The leadership question should be changing:
From:
“Should we automate Direct tax provisioning?”
To:
“When will our foundations be strong enough to automate it safely, at scale, and with confidence?”
That’s where modern Finance transformation will quietly distinguish the leaders.

Hyatt Family Office takes builder’s approach with strategic private equity investments
The family office deploys capital in thirds to public equities, private equity, and late-stage venture capital.
August 4, 2025
By
Lauren Bailey
Tech-entrepreneur-turned-investor Michael Hyatt approaches his family office investments through a builder’s lens, taking a long view to capital deployment, particularly with private equity allocations.
Private equity investing isn’t for the faint of heart, he said, in an interview with Markets Group. “It takes patience, operational rigor, and a whole lot of nothing. The hardest part is resisting the urge to act. As an operator, I had to completely rewire my entrepreneurial instincts.”
Moving fast to fix problems or build foundations for enterprises comes naturally to entrepreneurs, he continued. “When something broke I jumped in. When something looked promising, I chased it. But as an investor that mindset can backfire.”
Often the smartest move is to wait, watch, and let things unfold, Hyatt added. “I had to rewire my instinct to optimize and control to instead learn to back the right people and give things space. Patience is not natural to most operators (and certainly not me!) but in this game it’s a competitive edge.”
In the 90’s, Hyatt and his brother built Dyadem International, an engineering software firm they later sold to IHS (now IHS Markit) in 2011 for nearly $100M. They also co-founded Toronto-based BlueCat Networks with their father in 2001, after seeing limitations in existing DNS solutions. In 2017, they sold BlueCat to Madison Dearborn Partners for $400M, retaining a significant equity position. In 2022, it was sold again for more than $700M to Audax Private Equity.
He now runs the Hyatt Family Office with his chief investment officer, Elmer Kim, which deploys capital in strategic thirds to its allocations.
From Dragon’s Den to capital deployment
Establishing the family office was a natural next step for Hyatt, a former “dragon” on Next Gen Den, an online iteration of the Canadian Broadcasting Corp.’s popular Dragon’s Den reality television show that sees investors hear pitches from Canadian entrepreneurs seeking seed dollars, similar to the show Shark Tank in the United States.
The office invests a third of its capital across public markets to traditional S&P 500 public equities, another third to private equity, including late-stage growth equity and large institutional rollups, automation, secondaries, and distressed turnarounds.
The bulk of his public and private equity investments are designed for optimal returns with just a little patience and persistence. “Cash pays 3% to 4%. The S&P averages 8-10%. But good private equity should give you 600 – 800 bps above if you’re willing to lock up capital and wait.”
For example, the office recently bought into a private equity fund focused on automation, specifically robotics companies with what he characterized as solid profit profiles. It also invests in distressed debt companies that have successfully navigated turnarounds, as well as funds that do large roll ups. Since selling his company to Madison Dearborn, he’s opted to stay invested in the organization.
“I stick to what I understand. We don’t chase fads. If this were five years ago, we would be discussing blockchain all day. Now it’s [artificial intelligence].”
While Hyatt is a big believer in AI, he believes the industry will experience some fatigue and fallout before the real winners emerge.
The final third of the office’s investments goes to late-stage venture capital, which is where Hyatt brings operational experience. He noted the stark contrast between ownership and partnership, pointing out that the difference really lies in just how much stress is worth the upside.

“You’ve got to ask yourself how much stress you’re really willing to endure. Buying and operating a business means getting in the boat and rowing — it’s a lot harder. You’re aiming for a much higher return, but that also comes with significantly more risk. But if you’re going to fly to different countries you, sit on boards, deal with management turnover, and live through all that operational friction, you better be making a premium to the public markets.”
When sussing out investment strategy, Hyatt takes an approach more akin to an operator, not just betting on outcomes but identifying opportunities to build a lasting footprint. “First, I research if the market is growing, underserved, and if we can help to build a real upside. Then I focus on the team. Can we work with the CEO? Is the management team coachable? Can we have honest, even uncomfortable conversations, and come to a resolution quickly and effectively?”
What he looks for in a partnership are people who can cut through the noise, stay focused on what matters, and do the right thing under pressure. “I don’t invest unless I believe we can move fast, build trust, and create something valuable together.”
The office has backed several startups, including sustainability-driven logistics provider GoBolt, Canadian photonics-based quantum computing company Xanadu, fintech platform Float Financial Solutions Inc., generative AI tax research platform Blue J Legal Inc., cloud-based legal management platform MinuteBox, and data security platform DataStealth.
The Hyatt brothers were also founding partners of the Creative Destruction Lab at the University of Toronto’s Rotman School of Management.
“We just try to back great entrepreneurs in great markets. And when we invest, we assume we’re holding for at least 10 years.”
AI as a gatekeeper
On any given day, Hyatt may get dozens of pitch decks from startups or funds.
To reduce time spent reading through each, he uses an AI tool to find the most compelling proposals. The model is pre-programmed with the lenses he uses when evaluating companies, including business model viability, founder history, competitive landscape, and market dynamics.
“It analyzes the company from all angles, scrapes the web for background intel, checks out the founders, gauges the competitive environment, estimates potential saturation, and ultimately scores the opportunity,” he said.
Within minutes, Hyatt said he gets what would take a team of three associates a full week to produce. Most of the time, he is in full agreement with the tool, but he admits that on rare occasions, he may catch something it missed.
“The technology gives me a sharper lens, a broader perspective, and more time to think strategically rather than just swim in a sea of pitch decks. So, if you’re sending me one, just know: my AI is your first audience. And if it makes the cut, then I’ll grab that coffee.”

There's a risk embedded in most AI implementations that rarely appears in the vendor pitch: knowledge lock-in.
As AI tools accumulate context about your business—your voice, your preferences, your workflows—that context becomes embedded in the platform. Switching becomes increasingly expensive. Not just in migration costs, but in the loss of compounded context that took months to build.
The risk isn't that you chose the wrong model—models are improving quickly, and what's optimal today may not be in twelve months. The risk is that your knowledge isn't portable.
The mitigation is structural: store your knowledge in formats you own, independent of the AI platform. Plain text files, local notes, portable databases. Your knowledge should be separable from whatever model or platform is currently processing it.
This isn't an argument against committing to a platform. Consolidating your AI stack on one platform is still the right operational move for most executives—it's the only way to accumulate the contextual depth that makes AI genuinely powerful.
The distinction is between the platform (which can change) and the knowledge base (which should travel with you). Organizations that architect for portability now will have significantly more flexibility as the AI landscape continues to shift.

The hard part of enterprise AI is not proving that the tool can do something useful.
Most teams have already proved that.
The hard part is turning useful experiments into reliable operations.
That shift changes the work.
An AI experiment can live inside a sandbox, a demo, or a motivated team.
AI-enabled operations need something more durable:
- a named workflow owner
- clear data and system boundaries
- approval gates for high-impact decisions
- exception paths when confidence drops
- audit trails for what happened and why
- metrics tied to cycle time, quality, risk, or capacity
This is where many enterprise AI programs stall.
They move from tool adoption to tool sprawl without redesigning the operating layer around the work.
For leaders planning AI initiatives this quarter, I would use a simple filter before scaling the next pilot:
Can the team explain how this workflow will run on a normal Tuesday?
Who reviews the output?
Who can override the system?
What evidence is logged?
Where does human judgment remain mandatory?
What metric proves the workflow improved?
If those answers are vague, the organization may not have an AI capability yet.
It has an AI experiment with production ambitions.
The path forward is not slower AI adoption.
It is better operational design.
Readiness first.
Governance second.
Workflow redesign third.
Then scale the AI.

The most important consequence of cheaper AI is not lower cost. It is what lower cost makes possible.
The conventional assumption is that as models become cheaper and more open, demand for AI infrastructure will decline.
History suggests the opposite.
When storage became cheaper, companies stored more data. When bandwidth became cheaper, video consumption exploded. As AI inference becomes cheaper, enterprises will not simply spend less to perform the same tasks. They will embed intelligence into far more workflows and run it far more often.
That changes the enterprise AI equation.
In healthcare, lower inference costs could move AI from answering an occasional question to continuously helping people navigate eligibility, benefits, provider networks, medications, care options, and next actions.
That does not reduce infrastructure requirements. It expands them.
More importantly, it increases the value of the system surrounding the models:
• Permissioned data
• Identity and consent
• Governance and escalation
• Specialized tools and agents
• Enterprise workflows
• Integrated action pathways
• Measurement and accountability
As models become more accessible, the model itself becomes less of the differentiator.
The advantage moves to the companies that can orchestrate increasingly abundant intelligence inside trusted, working systems.
Cheaper intelligence will not make enterprise AI less valuable. It will make intelligence ubiquitous and raise the value of everything required to put it to work.

If you cannot explain what your AI did, you do not have a production system.
You have a demonstration.
Enterprise AI Blueprint #011 | AI Observability
Many AI teams focus heavily on whether the final answer is accurate.
But in an enterprise environment, accuracy alone is not enough.
You also need to understand:
• Which data and context were used?
• Which model, agent and tools were involved?
• What actions were taken?
• Which policies and permissions were applied?
• Where did human intervention occur?
• Can the entire decision be reconstructed?
This becomes even more important with Agentic AI.
A chatbot may produce one response.
An AI agent can retrieve information, call tools, update systems and trigger downstream actions.
Without end-to-end observability, organisations may see the outcome, but have no reliable way to explain how it was produced.
Enterprise AI observability should therefore cover more than infrastructure health.
It should provide visibility across the complete decision pipeline:
→ Context
→ Retrieval
→ Reasoning
→ Tool calls
→ Actions
→ Outcome
And it should connect technical telemetry with business impact.
Not only:
“Did the workflow complete?”
But also:
“Was the right decision made, under the right constraints, at an acceptable cost?”
Because when AI moves into production, trust depends on more than performance.
It depends on whether the organisation can observe, explain and govern what the system is doing.
Could your organisation reconstruct an AI-driven decision six months after it was made?

Avoid Vendor Lock-in in AI with Portable Knowledge
This title was summarized by AI from the post below.
Michael Hyatt

Most leaders treat their AI tools as software. The smarter ones are starting to treat them as infrastructure, and infrastructure decisions carry risk.
Gartner has warned that enterprises going all-in on a single AI provider create a deep dependency that erodes their technical agility and their negotiating power on price, terms, and service. That's not a minor inconvenience. It's a structural commitment that gets harder to unwind every month.
Here's what most teams miss. The lock-in isn't only at the model layer. It's in your data, your workflows, and the institutional knowledge your people have poured into one platform. The longer you stay, the deeper it runs.
What's true for the Fortune 500 is just as true for a 15-person company. When your knowledge, your models, and your workflows all live inside one vendor's walls, that vendor sets the rules and you live with them.
The mitigation is straightforward in principle: keep the asset that matters most, your knowledge, in a portable form you control, and treat the model as a swappable component.
The organizations that will scale AI safely are the ones designing for portability now, before the dependency is too expensive to exit.
I unpack the three shifts that make this practical here:

Vendors are exceptionally good at one thing:
Making their solution feel like your problem's answer.
This isn't criticism. It's their job. They present with precision, they benchmark across industries, and they arrive with evidence that's hard to argue with in a room.
The structural problem is what happens after the meeting.
Organizations with strong internal AI ownership walk out asking: does this solve our actual problem?
Organizations over-indexed on vendor relationships walk out asking: how do we implement this?
That single difference in question determines whether AI investment builds capability or complexity.
Vendors operate across clients. They bring breadth. What they can't bring is the one thing that determines whether any solution actually works at your scale — accountability for the outcome after the contract is signed.
That accountability lives internally. Or it lives nowhere.
The most expensive AI decisions I've seen weren't bad technology choices. They were good technology choices for someone else's problem, adopted because the demo was compelling and the internal evaluation process hadn't happened yet.
The organizations building genuine AI advantage have one thing in common: they define the problem internally before any external conversation begins.
The vendor should answer your question.
Not write it.
Where does vendor influence end and internal AI strategy begin in your organization — and is that line clearly drawn?

Choosing an AI vendor is harder than choosing the technology.
Here are the 5 questions that filter out the noise fast.
Choosing an AI vendor is harder than choosing the technology.
Here are the 5 questions that filter out the noise fast.
After running dozens of these conversations, this is the short list I'd hand any business owner before they sign anything.
1. 'Show me a business like mine that you've helped.'
Vague case studies are a red flag. You want a specific example, with specific numbers, and ideally a phone number for the client.
2. 'What's the smallest version of this we can ship in 30 days?'
Anyone insisting on a 6-month build before showing value is selling you risk, not progress. Good partners can carve out a tight pilot.
3. 'What happens to the data, and who owns it?'
If they can't answer in plain language, they haven't thought about it, or they're hoping you don't ask.
4. 'What does the handover look like at the end?'
Will your team be able to maintain it? Or are you locked into them forever? Both can be valid, but you need to know which one you're signing up for.
5. 'What's the failure scenario?'
Every honest partner will tell you what could go wrong. If they say nothing can go wrong, run.
These five questions take ten minutes. They will save you months and a lot of money.
Most vendors won't fail on the technology. They'll fail on these.

What is needed for success is “integrating AI into existing workflows and systems and securing full support from business executives”.
And in a regulated environment, integrating AI into workflows and systems can be challenging.
Apart from technical issues like response times and availability fails, there are problems arising from a lack of buy-in from leadership, and overall lack of trust from users. Security issues are often a late consideration and costs can be unclear.
The reality is, to make AI integration successful, the work put in place to support the model represents most of the effort.
Solid and reliable production systems need security and access control, audit logging, monitoring and alerts, cost tracking, output validation, retry handling and fallbacks, confidence based routing and human escalation paths.
In addition organisations need strong governance, ownership and change management processes in place to ensure confidence and acceptance.
Before you launch into your AI adventure, it’s worth planning for a reliable end state.
And don’t forget to ask the important questions - like who owns the output? Who's accountable when AI is wrong?

Recently, I had a conversation with someone who told me they were looking to move away from a (very well known) tech provider because the product only worked with a certain operating model and that inflexibility was no longer tenable. It's a brave decision - and the right one.
They're not alone. So often, we see technology become the goal - where the business has to bend around it. Too often it means tradeoffs that aren't sustainable. Teams are locked into rigid structures. Reporting doesn't quite tell you what's really going on. Unnecessary complexity. Effort is pushed onto the customer. Siloed channels that make the customer feel like they have to start all over, or worse, like they're dealing with a completely different company.
It's tempting to look to technology for the answer to everything - growth, experience, productivity - but it never is, at least not on its own. AI can absolutely help - once the foundations are right. Get the process working well first, and the technology has something solid to build on.
